articles.body: Trumpy Billionaire Tried to Kill This Movie—Now We Know Why    The Daily Beast

scored.body: With all due respect to Aaron Sorkin, filmmaker Luca Guadagnino has delivered the true sequel to The Social Network with Artificial, an A.I. origin story that’s at once a cautionary tale, horror show, and tragedy. Detailing the rise, fall, and still-skyrocketing re-ascent of OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, the Call Me By Your Name auteur’s latest (world-premiering at the New York Film Festival ahead of its Dec. 25 theatrical release) is a saga of timely terror. If its tonal unevenness sometimes undercuts its urgency, it’s still an engrossing lament that we’re forever doomed to repeat our mistakes—until, that is, we’re literally doomed.Amazon MGM Studios—run by the MAGA-friendly Jeff Bezos—tried to kill Artificial after it was completed (it’s now being distributed by NEON), and given its scathing depiction of its subject, it’s easy to assume that decision was driven by reasons that have nothing to do with the film’s quality. Whatever the case, Guadagnino’s drama doles out a figurative beating to OpenAI and Altman, whom Andrew Garfield embodies as the phoniest and most amoral of toxic tech bros. Having suffered at the hands of a megalomaniac as Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in The Social Network, the star now assumes the role of an agent of apocalyptic calamity, and his compellingly rancid performance is the dark heart of this modern fable. Even so, it’s Anora’s Yura Borisov who runs away with the film as the idealist whose dreams of a brighter tomorrow are shattered by the realities of an avaricious and cold-blooded today.In 2003, math prodigy Ilya Sutskever (Borisov) arrives at the University of Toronto office of famed computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance)—who’ll decades later win the Nobel Prize and be known as the “godfather of A.I.”—and immediately wows him with his genius. Sutskever is convinced that artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a potential reality in his lifetime, and despite his peers’ mockery, his collaboration with Hinton earns them millions in funding from Google, where they strive to achieve what many deem “science fiction.” For Sutskever, AGI heralds paradigm-altering breakthroughs in science, medicine, and other fields that will reap tremendous benefits for mankind. He’s a true believer, and his zealotry earns him a fan in Altman.Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov in “Artificial.” Neon Sutskever thinks that the primary thing standing in the way of his goal is scaling—meaning, he needs more money to ramp up the amount of data he pumps into his A.I. Disregarding Hinton’s reservations, he solves this problem by partnering with Altman and Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), both of whom are won over by a big dinner speech in which Sutskever declares, “Feel the AGI!” As Guadagnino’s camera pans around the table in the lead-up to that proclamation, Artificial captures the alluring promise of the technology and the borderline-religious faith that drives its development. Unfortunately, the spell the director casts breaks every time Musk appears on screen, thanks to a Barinholtz performance that consists of cartoonish faces and clownish gestures.In large part because of the goofy Tesla CEO, Artificial’s tone is slightly off early on. It rights itself once Musk jumps ship on OpenAI because of its slow progress, which threatens to let its formidable competitors reach A.I. first. Garfield’s Altman is totally blasé about this abandonment, pivoting by bringing in (with Sutskever’s seal of approval) Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro). Along with board chairman Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman), the team sets out to change the world responsibly—a mission whose altruism the company’s nonprofit status supposedly safeguards.Blur and Gorillaz frontman Damon Albam’s alternately electronic and orchestral score infuses Artificial with unsettlingly woozy energy, while Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed’s canted angles give the film its edge, and their shot-counter-shot close-ups lend it an unnerving romanticism. With the wind at their back, Sutskever and Altman head for the techno-horizon, but the former is so seduced by the latter’s charm and support—all of it wrapped in florid, soft-spoken encouragements and comforting reassurances—that by the time he realizes that his cohort is consolidating power, crassly monetizing their invention (via ChatGPT), and ignoring warning signs (including with regard to their deal with Microsoft), he’s left with nothing but dire options.Astutely and amusingly written by the surrealist Saturday Night Live writer Simon Rich, Artificial moves efficiently through the recent past until it reaches its Big Bang: Sutskever convincing the board to fire Altman for deceptive and dangerous practices and to install Murati as OpenAI’s new CEO. This is the make-or-break moment for the company and, as Guadagnino’s film suggests, for the industry—if not the entire human race. As those acquainted with the news will know, Altman’s ouster was short-lived, and in the director’s hands, his proverbial resurrection plays out as depressingly inevitable, with only Sutskever unaware until the end that good intentions are no match (in Silicon Valley, or elsewhere) for unchecked greed and ego.Sam Altman is played by Andrew Garfield in the new film. Shelby Tauber/Pool/REUTERS Garfield’s Altman is a weirdo who grows less human as his control over the planet’s most powerful tech increases, and Artificial is wise to not italicize that, as a manipulative and untrustworthy liar who only cares about his own survival, he’s the perfect reflection of his duplicitous A.I.. It’s Borisov, however, who’s truly magnetic as the principled Sutskever, who clings to the hope that safety and security will win out. With a focused intensity that’s an extension of his character’s dogged inability to lie (making him the opposite of an AGI), the actor makes for a deeply sympathetic protagonist, not to mention a depressingly pitiable one once he’s forced to reckon with the nature of his allies and grapple with his own responsibility for the dawning A.I. crisis.Guadagnino can occasionally be too flashy; a shot of Altman and Sutskever hugging in real time, with super-slow-motion background revelry, for example, is unnecessarily showy and distracting. And ultimately, his censure of the men hurtling the Earth toward possible destruction—without a care for anything other than their own narcissism and covetousness—is too familiar to radically open anyone’s eyes. Yet Artificial imagines these tech pioneers in such bold and repugnant hues that it’s still easy to get swept up in Sutskever’s optimism and, consequently, to be wrecked by the rude awakening he receives. Consider it a caustic takedown of the stewards tasked with protecting us from the danger they’ve created, and a scary backstory for a future that looks bleaker with each passing day.Obsessed with pop culture and entertainment? Follow us on Substack and YouTube for even more coverage.

scored.body:
A lesson Steve Jobs took from an old piece of furniture still guides how Apple builds its products, according to the company's new CEO, John Ternus. Before taking charge of Apple, Ternus oversaw its hardware engineering teams through multiple generations of devices. He says the principle holds even for the company's lowest-priced devices.Ternus shared his thoughts soon after the MacBook Neo was launched earlier this year. He brought up a story about the late Apple co-founder that he counts among his favourites, using it to explain why Apple cares so much about parts of a product that buyers rarely see.The Back of a Chest of DrawersAlso Read | Layoffs Are Rising In Tech, But These Skills Are Helping People Unlock Better PayThe anecdote is a simple one. While moving a chest of drawers, Jobs pulled it away from the wall and took a look at its back. He reflected on the carpenter who made it, noting that the back had been finished as beautifully as the rest of the piece, even though nobody was ever likely to see it.

Ternus said the story is never far from his mind, as he feels it captures exactly what Apple does.Since the days of the first Macintosh, Apple has treated the inside of its hardware and its hidden surfaces with as much engineering precision as the outer casing.ALSO READ | John Ternus Net Worth, Salary, Career, Family & More — All You Need To Know About Apple CEONo Shortcuts on the MacBook NeoAccording to Ternus, the MacBook Neo is proof of this approach. Its affordable price, he indicated, has not come at the cost of design or how well it is built."Here is our most affordable Mac we've ever made, and it's absolutely beautiful. And if you open it up and look inside, it's just as beautiful," he said.Ternus noted that this applies to every Apple product, from the iPhone Pro Max to the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and the MacBook Neo is no different. In other words, Apple's entry-level devices are built to the same standards as its flagships.ALSO READ | Who Is John Ternus? Meet Apple's New CEO Taking Over From Tim CookA Hint at Apple's FutureTernus also sees this attention to unseen details as a guide for the road ahead under his leadership.He said that thinking about the story has been good for him, since it probably offers the clearest clue to Apple's future direction. "We're going to keep pushing in that same way," Ternus said.

members.title: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal

representative.headline: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal
representative.body: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments    Managed Services Journal

articles.headline: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments - Managed Services Journal
articles.body: What MSPs can learn from BlueStar’s AI marketing experiments    Managed Services Journal

scored.body: From left: BlueStar’s John Martin, James Korte and Bre Malott lead “Blending Creative Content with Modern Marketing Tools” at VARTECH 2026. An AI tool that writes an ad gets plenty of attention. A tool that takes finished ads and turns them into a client presentation may solve a more immediate problem for a busy marketing team.At BlueStar’s VARTECH 2026 event, James Korte, director of marketing at BlueStar US, described an internal application that does exactly that. Placing a series of social ads into realistic layouts and assembling them in PowerPoint used to take his team 30 to 45 minutes. BlueStar’s homegrown replacement for a paid tool called Ad Mockup Studio now puts the ads in context and exports the presentation with one click.“I hated doing that,” Korte said of the manual version.That example captured a recurring theme of “Blending Creative Content with Modern Marketing Tools,” a BlueStar Academy session hosted by John Martin, senior content marketing manager at BlueStar US, and featuring Korte and Bre Malott, a digital marketing specialist at BlueStar Europe: Let AI handle the repetitive work, and keep people in charge of the decisions that make marketing effective. The panel summed it up with a familiar line from AI’s early days – people want AI to do the laundry, not write the poetry.For MSPs working with limited marketing resources, the session offered several practical ways to apply that approach.Start with a task that eats timeKorte said BlueStar has built roughly 10 internal tools in 2026 using vibe coding – AI-assisted software development in which users describe an application in plain language, then work with an AI tool to build and refine it. His platform of choice is Lovable; Replit is another popular option.One example is Brief Builder. It takes information from a standard project intake form, runs it through BlueStar’s guidance on what makes good marketing and produces creative-brief-style deliverables with starting points for headlines and copy. Korte’s favorite layer: The team instructed the system to channel a handpicked group of great copywriters and marketers from history. He called the result “a creative brief on steroids.”Another tool pulls data from HubSpot, LinkedIn, ClickUp and another platform into a single dashboard. It answers a request BlueStar CMO Dean Reverman had made for years: one view of campaigns and email subscriber activity to bring into board meetings. Korte built it in a matter of hours, largely by plugging in API keys.He also uses a Claude project to generate quarterly bonus documentation for the seven or eight people he manages. Team members submit raw notes on what they accomplished, and the tool selects the most significant items, weights them and produces a formatted, branded document. “Of course, I check it,” Korte said. “It saves me hours.”The common thread is a defined problem. Each tool addresses work the team already understands: preparing a brief, packaging ads, gathering information from separate systems or documenting results.An MSP can use the same starting point. Identify a recurring marketing task, document the inputs and desired output, and ask whether a small tool could remove the manual steps. Monthly campaign reports, QBR slide preparation and case study outlines built from project notes are likely candidates. Count the time spent reviewing and correcting the output as part of the cost – when the panel asked which marketing task takes too much time, one attendee’s answer was “correcting AI.”Take content strategy out of the slide deckA content strategy can lose momentum after the meeting where it’s presented. Korte described the familiar pattern: He builds a strategy deck defining pillars, themes, formats and audiences, walks the team through it, “and then life goes on.” Before long, people forget what the pillars were.“One of the reasons that I’m so infatuated with vibe coding right now … is because I feel like it’s useful for taking strategy out of a PowerPoint slide and putting it into a tool,” he said.BlueStar’s tool uses what the company has told it about its audiences – how many readers care about data capture versus point of sale and payments, for example – to recommend article topics and score their relevance. Once a writer accepts a topic, the tool suggests people to interview, questions to explore and a visual blueprint for the finished piece, from the hero image and bulleted agenda to scannable section formatting.Korte cited an article in progress by BlueStar Academy’s lead trainer about scaling a point-of-sale business from deployments of a handful of locations to 50 or 100. The tool organizes the assignment, but the trainer still conducts the interviews, distills what he learns and writes the article. A designer then uses the blueprint to format it.For an MSP, the value is consistency. Define priority customers, the business problems the company solves and the services it wants to explain, and those decisions can drive an editorial workflow that keeps topic selection on track. A topic score is only as useful as the guidance behind it, though. People still need to decide whether a proposed article answers a real customer question and supports the company’s goals. As the panelists noted, AI can’t decide who you’re selling to or which direction your company is rowing the boat.Give AI your voice and brand standardsMalott described giving ChatGPT her speaking style, words she likes and words she wants to avoid. “I want it to sound like things are truly from me,” she said.Martin, a writer at heart, described a research routine built on two tools. He runs the same prompt in Copilot and Gemini, asking for ideas, statistics, sources and how current the information is. The responses often differ significantly, so he merges the useful material and rewrites it in his own voice or BlueStar’s. “At the end of the day, I want it to sound like it’s from a human being,” he said.For MSPs, that suggests a practical role for AI in organizing research and producing a first pass. Checking the underlying sources and adding the company’s own expertise remain part of the job. Agreement between two AI responses isn’t verification.The same principle applies to visuals. “I don’t think the designs are bad. I think they are cluttered,” said Korte, who has spent more than 20 years designing by hand. AI-generated graphics tend to cram in copy, icons and the same script-style fonts, producing a default look audiences now recognize. The fix is to give the tool references, such as a screenshot of a design, color scheme or typography you like. Malott suggested prompting the AI to treat an ad like a billboard: a big, bold message, less text and a clean layout. As the panel pointed out, much of a designer’s job is removing things from the page.Korte said Claude gets BlueStar’s slides about 80% of the way there when he points it at a folder containing the company’s fonts, colors and graphic elements. When it misuses an element, he uploads a screenshot showing correct usage, and the next result comes closer. An MSP can do the same by gathering approved logos, colors, fonts and examples of effective work in one place, along with guidance on audience and tone.Settle governance before tools spreadBlueStar’s official policy, the panel noted, is that Copilot is the only AI tool approved for sharing company data – even as the marketing team experiments with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Lovable for other work.That mix creates its own problem. Korte’s 15-person U.S. marketing team builds in different tools, so a useful assistant created in one person’s account can’t easily be shared. BlueStar plans to pursue a team account, and Korte described another option under consideration: an internal app built on an AI provider’s API, so the whole team logs in to one tool and the company pays for usage instead of individual subscriptions.Ownership matters, too. Korte acknowledged the security questions vibe-coded apps raise and said he is working out how to move one of his projects off Lovable, using its GitHub integration and a copy of the database. “I don’t plan on not paying for Lovable, but I don’t want to be tied to it either,” he said.MSPs will recognize those issues. The same customers experimenting with vibe-coded tools and personal AI accounts will need help with access controls, data handling, API key management and ongoing maintenance. An MSP that has worked through those questions for its own marketing team is better positioned to answer them for clients.Keep review in the workflowAI also helps with troubleshooting. When a colleague reports a broken HubSpot workflow, Malott now shares a screenshot with AI to pinpoint the missing step, instead of tracing the problem from the beginning.Finished work still needs inspection, though. Korte recalled an AI-generated hero image for a healthcare research article showing a patient in a hospital bed and a nurse nearby. The nurse’s ID badge carried the patient’s photo – a mistake BlueStar didn’t catch until a friend at another company emailed a screenshot. “We’ve got to look more closely at those,” Korte said.For MSPs, review should cover facts, brand details and the small visual elements that can undermine credibility.The session’s strongest lesson was practical: Choose a familiar task, use AI to remove the work around it, and keep people accountable for the result. Skepticism has a place in that process. When an attendee admitted to still being skeptical near the end of the session, the panel’s reply was simple: Good. BlueStar’s examples give MSPs a place to begin, especially when repetitive production work crowds out time to understand customers and create content worth reading.

articles.body: New Mexico Democrats seek ethics probe over Senate GOP AI images    Albuquerque Journal

scored.body:
POLITICS

New Mexico Democrats accuse Senate Republicans of violating AI campaign law

The Roundhouse in Santa Fe on Feb. 3.

Eddie Moore/Journal

The New Mexico Democratic Party has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate whether state Senate Republicans’ use of artificial intelligence-generated images in recent social media posts violates a 2024 state law aimed at curbing political misinformation.The Senate Republicans and state Sen. Jay Block, R-Rio Rancho, have published or shared artificially generated images of Democrats in recent weeks as part of a campaign accusing the majority Democrats of being corrupt.Some of the images include a fake jail mugshot of Senate Pro Tem Sen. Mimi Stewart, D-Albuquerque, House Speaker Javier Martinez, D-Albuquerque, wearing a hammer-and-sickle lapel pin and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland embracing an unspecified man in an orange prison jumpsuit.The fake mugshot suggests Stewart was charged with “hit and run,” a reference to an automobile crash between Stewart and a pedestrian in 2024 that has recently surfaced in news reports. Stewart was never issued a citation or booked into jail, and she stayed on scene until police arrived, interim Santa Fe Police Department Chief told the Santa Fe New Mexican. In a complaint to the ethics commission the Democrats provided Friday, DPNM Chair Sara Attleson said the images violate House Bill 182, which imposes strict disclaimer requirements on AI-generated campaign materials. The law requires artificially generated images to carry conspicuous disclaimers with the following text: “This image has been manipulated or generated by artificial intelligence.”In a statement, Attleson called on the Ethics Commission to investigate and impose any penalties as quickly as possible. State law provides for $1,000 fines for each violation. “Voters should not be misled by public officials or their official offices about what is or isn’t real,” Attleson said. “We are asking the Ethics Commission to enforce the law that is meant to protect faith in our elections.”None of the images on social media carried the required disclaimer, though Facebook has since labeled both as AI generated. Block, who originally posted the fake mugshot of Stewart, also noted that his image was AI-generated at the end of a lengthy Facebook post Sept. 22. Block told Source NM on Monday that the SEC complaint is Democrats’ effort to distract from the real corruption the images seek to highlight.  He also defended his post as protected speech under the First Amendment. “I can’t believe they’re crying over that when they refuse to hold themselves accountable,” Block said of Democrats. “It’s called free speech.”

Late Friday, after New Mexico Democrats announced they’d filed the ethics complaint, Senate Republicans republished their post with the contested images along with the required disclaimer. Still, Sen. Minority Leader Bill Sharer, R-Farmington, in a statement, called the matter “funny.”“The Democrat Party, that consistently fails to hold their own members to account when it comes to breaking the law and violating ethical standards, is taking exception to our efforts to expose their failed leadership and lack of accountability,” he said.”

articles.body: TikTok Expands Off-Platform Ad Network to U.S. Advertisers, Adds AI Campaign Tools Through Claude, Perplexity    Net Influencer

scored.body:
TikTok is bringing its ad network beyond its own app to U.S. advertisers and opening up campaign management to third-party AI platforms, the company announced at Advertising Week New York 2026.

The “TikTok Ad Network” (TTAN) lets U.S. advertisers extend campaigns beyond TikTok to reach audiences across what the company describes as a premium network of nearly 400,000 apps worldwide. TTAN is fully integrated into TikTok Ads Manager and includes brand safety and placement controls.

Alongside the network expansion, TikTok said its “Model Context Protocol” (MCP) tool for advertisers is now available as a connector across several AI platforms and registries, including Claude, Kimi, Manus, Perplexity, Replit, Snowflake, Tencent WorkBuddy, and the IAB Tech Lab Agent Registry. Built on the open “Model Context Protocol,” the tool allows developers to build AI agents directly on top of TikTok’s ads ecosystem to plan, launch, and manage advertising workflows with fewer manual steps. TikTok said advertiser use of the MCP tool for campaign activation and management has grown more than 200% since launch, citing internal data from July through September 2026.

“The TikTok MCP is indispensable to our AI-powered campaign workflows, including how we build campaigns, upload creative, and analyze performance. TikTok is a leader in helping brands leverage AI to grow,” George Velonias, Head of Growth Marketing at Wayfair Canada, said in a blog post.

The announcements were part of a broader set of AI-powered advertiser tools TikTok unveiled at the conference, spanning commerce, lead generation, and creative automation. On the commerce side, TikTok introduced “Buy Direct,” an in-app checkout tool that lets users complete purchases from the For You feed without leaving the app, and “Shopping Assistant,” a conversational AI agent built into multiple TikTok touchpoints that provides real-time guidance on product details, shipping, sizing, and availability. The company also introduced “Agentic Leads,” an AI agent for lead generation available through TikTok Direct Message and on advertiser-owned websites.

On the creative side, TikTok is automating its “Search Ads Campaigns” through Smart+, which extends automation to keyword and creative selection in search ads buying. A related feature, “Smart+ Creative Selection,” consolidates creative sourcing, including advertiser assets, Symphony’s AI-generated creatives, and creator content, into a single approval workflow. TikTok is also expanding GMV Max, its automated ad solution for TikTok Shop sellers, to factor in costs such as affiliate commissions, coupons, and referral fees when optimizing campaigns.

“AI is transforming how advertiser content is created and scaled,” said David Kaufman, Global Head of Monetization Product Partnerships at TikTok. “With our suite of solutions, we are bringing together AI, automation, and creativity to help advertisers improve performance while reducing effort.”

TikTok cited a PF Global economic impact report published last week finding that activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, with 54 million Americans reporting a purchase after watching a TikTok video.

articles.headline: SDKs emerge as key gateway to AI advertising as in-app ad market hits $400 billion - The Economic Times
articles.body: SDKs emerge as key gateway to AI advertising as in-app ad market hits $400 billion    The Economic Times

scored.body: The software development kit (SDK) has emerged as the key control point in the $400 billion in-app advertising market and could give independent adtech platforms an early advantage in the next wave of advertising across AI assistants, lockscreens and agentic commerce, according to a new report by Analysys Mason.The report, The SDK Advantage: How independent adtechs won mobile and are positioned to win AI-native advertising, argues that platforms such as AppLovin, InMobi and Liftoff, which built large SDK footprints across mobile apps, are best positioned to capture advertising on emerging AI-native consumer products.In-app advertising reached around $400 billion in 2025, growing 10.8% year on year and reaching five times its 2017 level, according to the report. It accounted for roughly a third of the $1.18 trillion global advertising market, while users spent more than 90% of their smartphone time inside apps.The shift is significant because traditional web advertising tools have limited applicability inside apps. Apps do not use cookies and are isolated from one another, while Apple’s ATT opt-in rate is around 35%. Safari and Firefox block third-party cookies by default, and Google retired its Privacy Sandbox in October 2025.As a result, first-party signals collected through SDKs have become the most dependable basis for targeting, the report said.The report argues that installed footprint, rather than simply advertising technology, has become the key competitive moat. Independent SDKs can reach up to 44% of Android and 31% of iOS app downloads.AppLovin’s $1.05 billion acquisition of MoPub is cited as an example of deals focused on acquiring installed footprint rather than just technology.The economics of that footprint can be significant. AppLovin generated $5.48 billion in advertising revenue in 2025, up 70%, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of around 82%, according to the report.At the same time, advertising remains heavily concentrated among the largest online platforms. Google, Meta and Amazon account for 70-75% of global online advertising spend, even though the open internet represents around 60% of online time.For publishers, the economics of in-app advertising remain more fragmented: of every $100 spent by an advertiser in-app, publishers receive about 50-55, the report said.The next opportunity could come from AI-native products. The report argues that advertising will become increasingly important as AI products scale because every query carries an inference cost and subscriptions alone may not cover those costs at consumer scale.Published pricing indicates that inference costs have fallen by more than 99% since 2023, potentially making free, ad-supported AI viable.Unlike conventional digital advertising, however, this emerging inventory will not necessarily have a webpage or ad tag. It will instead need to be accessed through code already sitting on the device—potentially strengthening the position of adtech companies with established SDK footprints.“Apps broke the advertising playbook built for the web,” Ujjwal Chaudhry, Partner at Analysys Mason, said. “Without cookies, tracking a user across apps no longer works, and the SDK has become the one place where the audience, the ad and the result can all be measured.”Chaudhry said the next wave of advertising would sit across lockscreens, AI assistants and agentic checkout.“AI products are costly to run, and advertising is the most scalable way to keep them free for consumers,” he said, adding that independent platforms with the widest SDK footprints were best placed to capture this new supply.According to the report, each successive shift in advertising has widened the lead of independent SDK-first platforms rather than resetting the competitive landscape.

articles.headline: Fake ChatGPT, Gemini Sites steal advertising accounts, MFA codes - BleepingComputer
articles.body: Fake ChatGPT, Gemini Sites steal advertising accounts, MFA codes    BleepingComputer

scored.body:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a "human-operated phishing platform" that impersonates advertising products for artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots like Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity, Meta Muse, and Manus.

The products, which claim to offer campaign optimization, spend audits, and business-account connections, are designed with one goal in mind: to capture credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes via spoofed login windows using the browser-in-the-browser (BitB) trick.

"Each product was built around the same action: Connect," Island researchers Oleg Zaytsev and Ofek Ronen said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Clicking it opened a browser drawn inside the real browser. The fake address bar displayed trusted origins such as accounts.google.com or an Okta tenant, while the real browser remained on the phishing domain."

"Behind the interface, the platform kept every password attempt, fingerprinted the device, and let an operator pick which MFA challenge the victim saw next."

One of the websites in question is "museads.ai," which emerged on September 16, 2026, a little over a week after Meta launched Muse, its AI agent designed for personal workflows. Described as "Your AI ads manager for paid media workflows," the platform claimed to help customers reach buyers, connect their ad accounts, and run sponsored placements.

Prominently placed in the spoofed web page is a Prompt Box with a "Connect" button, clicking which triggers a BitB attack to capture a visitor's account credentials for Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows. This is accomplished by drawing a fake window displaying a bogus account sign-in form with the address bar pointing to a legitimate domain (e.g., accounts.google[.]com).

In the background, the victim's device is fingerprinted, and the information is transmitted to the attacker at the endpoint "/api/send/ip" over Socket.IO, after which operator commands and victim data are exchanged based on the login workflow. Armed with the account credentials, the attacker attempts to sign in to the account in real-time.

"Every brand gets its own pitch," the researchers explained. "ChatGPT promises a Monday Google Ads brief. Gemini promises MCC (manager account) and linked-client support. Claude gets its own advertising portal, Perplexity offers campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus offers a private Meta integration."

Users are assessed to be directed to these landing pages via fake invitation emails that impersonate these trusted brands to lend the attacks a veneer of legitimacy.

"Each one in this campaign poses as a believable product, with its own brand, pitch, and sign-in flow," the researchers pointed out. "They also move with the news."

Island said the AI ads pages are part of a broader phishing platform that supports a three-pronged operation, the two others being Google Ads-themed refund claims and payment confirmation, as well as recruitment-related sites for Tesla, Louis Vuitton, Nike, and Adecco.

All the identified websites have been found to share the same technology stack comprising Next.js and Socket.IO, and communicate with the same endpoints. What's more, the threat actors behind the operation have exposed source code for earlier versions of the platform through misconfigured public GitHub repositories.

The AI ads-focused campaign is designed to target agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators, likely with the end goal of monetizing the ads accounts to run their own ad campaigns or sell them for profit, especially when they have a clean spend history.

According to a report published by Mimecast in July 2026, malware families like VietCredCare, DuckTail, NodeStealer, and PXA Stealer have engendered ad account theft at scale, leading to a "widespread commodity crime in the advertising ecosystem" where bad actors drain business budgets and sell accounts with good reputation in underground markets.

"For the victim, the card is the easy part: they can remove it within hours. Getting the account back is not," Island said. "Attackers typically add their own administrators and downgrade the legitimate owner, and recovery can take weeks or months while the account keeps serving ads. For a manager account, the damage reaches the agency’s clients."

To mitigate the threat, organizations are recommended to enable phishing-resistant authentication, review advertising control changes, and scrutinize AI integrations before connecting accounts.

The disclosure comes as Island revealed that threat actors are abusing Google-sponsored results to route unsuspecting users to custom GPTs or shared-AI chat content, which then redirect them to a fake Cloudflare verification page serving ClickFix-style lures to deliver NetSupport RAT.

"The campaign did not require a vulnerability in ChatGPT or Google," Island said. "It abused trusted platforms, attacker-authored content, paid search, and social engineering to move people toward malware delivery."

"Across a three-month observation period ending in August 2026, the broader delivery cluster included about 850 paid-ad landings, 26 lookalike ChatGPT destinations, and 71 Google Ads campaign IDs."

scored.body:
noirlab2624 — Photo Release

Cascading knot structure of historic supernova remnant are uncovered in new observations from the Gemini North telescope in Hawai‘i

6 October 2026

The Gemini North telescope located on Maunakea in Hawai‘i has revealed the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, the likely remnant of the historic supernova seen in the year 1181. The new observations reveal that its famous “firework” filaments are not smooth streaks, but chains of tiny knots.

No, this is not a firework display. This is Pa 30 — the likely remnant of the historic supernova witnessed in the year 1181, now captured here in unprecedented detail by the Gemini North telescope, one half of the International Gemini Observatory, partly funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and operated by NSF NOIRLab. This image was captured with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS), and it shows that the remnant’s unmistakable firework-shaped ejecta take a cascading knot-like structure.

The historic supernova, named SN 1181, is one of only five supernovae in the Milky Way that were observed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. Eight separate texts show that Chinese, Japanese, and Arabic astronomers first observed the supernova between 4 and 6 August 1181. The supernova remained visible in the constellation Cassiopeia for 185 days. According to what we know about how stars end their lives, the colossal explosion would have left something behind. Pa 30, a system composed of a blue central star and surrounding firework-shaped shell, is the top candidate for this supernova remnant.

Pa 30 was only discovered in 2013 through a citizen science campaign to find planetary nebulae in Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) data. It was the 30th nebula found by American amateur astronomer Dana Patchick. Follow-up imaging on the KPNO 2.1-meter Telescope and the Hiltner 2.4-meter Telescope, both located at NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), a Program of NSF NOIRLab, revealed faint, diffuse nebular emission and remarkable radial filaments threading the nebula in a nearly perfect sphere. Based on its estimated age and brightness, scientists consider Pa 30 to be the likely remnant of SN 1181.

Analysis of the new observations from Gemini North, which was led by Timothy Cunningham (Center for Astrophysics — Harvard & Smithsonian) and Ilaria Caiazzo (Institute of Science and Technology Austria), reveals about ten times more filamentary structure in Pa 30 than previously seen. It also shows that the radial filaments are made of consistent chains of tiny knots of gas, rather than smooth streaks as previously thought. This knotty structure suggests that there may have been thermal or density variations in the circumstellar medium that shaped the supernova ejecta as it expanded radially away from the explosion.

Pa 30 is unique among all known supernova remnants. The central star remaining after the explosion, IRAS 00500+6713, is extremely hot, with a temperature of about 200,000°C (~360,000°F). It also possesses very fast stellar winds that move at around 16,000 kilometers per second (~10,000 miles per second).

Surviving remnant stars are expected to be “kicked” away during the powerful supernova explosion. However, the central star of Pa 30 appears almost exactly centered in the remnant. This curious configuration implies that the explosion was quite symmetrical, and it rules out a large kick that could have knocked the star off-center. From this, the researchers conclude that SN 1181 was an extremely rare Type Iax supernova. Unlike the standard high-energy explosions of Type Ia supernovae that wipe out their stars, Type Iax supernovae are lower-energy, incomplete explosions that leave behind a surviving remnant star. Pa 30 is the only known Type Iax remnant in the Milky Way.

The story of SN 1181 is one of humans working together, across time and space, to understand the changing Universe. As new astronomical questions arrive every day, SN 1181 invites us to wonder what mysteries remain unsolved from the distant past.

More informationAnalysis of this data is presented in a paper titled “Detection of knots in the supernova type Iax remnant Pa 30” appearing in The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9cb2

The team is composed of T. Cunningham (Center for Astrophysics — Harvard & Smithsonian [CfA]; now University of Warwick), I. Caiazzo (Institute of Science and Technology Austria), J. C. Raymond (CfA), and S. J. Kenyon (CfA).

NSF NOIRLab, the U.S. National Science Foundation center for ground-based optical-infrared astronomy, operates the International Gemini Observatory (a facility of NSF, NRC–Canada, ANID–Chile, MCTIC–Brazil, MINCyT–Argentina, and KASI–Republic of Korea), NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), the Community Science and Data Center (CSDC), and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory (in cooperation with DOE’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory). It is managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA) under a cooperative agreement with NSF and is headquartered in Tucson, Arizona.

The scientific community is honored to have the opportunity to conduct astronomical research on I’oligam Du’ag (Kitt Peak) in Arizona, on Maunakea in Hawai‘i, and on Cerro Tololo and Cerro Pachón in Chile. We recognize and acknowledge the very significant cultural role and reverence of I’oligam Du’ag to the Tohono O’odham Nation, and Maunakea to the Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians) community.

scored.body:
October 7, 2026 21 min read

Every Canadian business running Microsoft 365 has had the same conversation this fall: do we pay for Microsoft Copilot, stick with the ChatGPT subscription half the team already expensed, or lean into Gemini because it is bundled with Google Workspace? It is not an abstract question anymore. Microsoft now counts more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, OpenAI has pushed ChatGPT’s weekly active user base past 900 million, and Google says its Gemini app has crossed 950 million monthly users. Three very different products, three very different pricing models, and three very different answers to the Canadian data residency question that keeps coming up in procurement meetings.Why This Comparison Matters for Canadian Teams Right NowWhat’s Actually Running Behind Each AssistantThe Model Mix Behind CopilotWhat Powers ChatGPT and Gemini ChatSpecs and Features at a GlancePricing in Canada: What You’ll Actually PayBenchmarks and Adoption Data From Three SourcesMicrosoft 365 Copilot Deep Dive: Agent Mode, Researcher, and AnalystChatGPT for Work: Plus, Business, and the GPT-6.1 Sol RolloutGoogle Gemini and Workspace: Where It Actually FitsData Residency and Privacy for Canadian OrganizationsFive Real-World Use Cases ComparedWhich One Should You Choose? Use-Case RecommendationsHow to Migrate Between Copilot, ChatGPT, and GeminiPros and Cons of Each PlatformThe Verdict: Our Pick for Canadian Teams in 2026Frequently Asked Questions

This comparison breaks down what model actually powers each assistant as of October 2026, what you will pay in Canadian dollars, how each one handles your Word documents and Excel sheets, and where the data residency story genuinely differs between Microsoft, OpenAI, and Google. We also walk through a migration path for teams switching between them and close with a direct verdict for five common Canadian business profiles.

Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

Why This Comparison Matters for Canadian Teams Right Now

The timing is not a coincidence. Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings update confirmed that Agent Mode, the generative workflow that drafts and iteratively revises Word documents, Excel workbooks, and PowerPoint decks from a prompt, is now the default experience inside Copilot across the core Office apps. At the same time, OpenAI has been rolling out GPT-6.1 Sol to ChatGPT Work and Codex users, while Google has quietly started pushing AI Ultra subscribers toward a newer Gemini 4 Argon model. All three vendors shipped meaningful updates inside a six-week window between late August and early October 2026, which is exactly why the comparison keeps resurfacing in IT budget conversations.

For Canadian organizations specifically, there is an extra wrinkle that does not show up in US-focused coverage of this topic: data residency. Microsoft 365 tenants provisioned in Canada can keep core Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams data at rest in the Canada Central and Canada East regions, anchored in Toronto and Quebec City data centers. Neither OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise nor Google Workspace offers an equivalent guaranteed Canadian region for every workload today, which matters enormously for law firms, healthcare providers, and public-sector bodies bound by PIPEDA or Quebec’s Law 25. We dig into exactly where that story is stronger than it looks, and where it is weaker, in the data residency section below.

The keyword Canadians actually type into Google is blunt: copilot vs chatgpt, with Gemini usually added as a third option once someone remembers their company also pays for Google Workspace. That search intent, more than any abstract AI benchmark, is what this guide is built to answer.

What’s Actually Running Behind Each Assistant

None of these three products run on a single, fixed model anymore. All three vendors have quietly moved to multi-model routing, which makes “which model is better” a more complicated question than it was even a year ago.

The Model Mix Behind Copilot

Microsoft Copilot has historically run on OpenAI’s GPT model family by default, with Anthropic’s Claude available for specific scenarios inside Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork. That has changed gradually through 2026. Reporting from mid-2026 described Microsoft routing tens of thousands of Copilot prompts per week inside Excel and Outlook to its own in-house MAI models rather than OpenAI or Anthropic, part of a broader push to cut third-party AI spending. Industry reporting describes this as still a small fraction of total Copilot traffic, with OpenAI and Anthropic continuing to handle most production requests, particularly for anything complex. We cover Microsoft’s in-house model push in more detail in our dedicated look at Microsoft’s MAI models, but the short version for this comparison is: Copilot today is a blend, not a single model, and Microsoft has not published what share of requests go where.

What Powers ChatGPT and Gemini Chat

OpenAI’s own documentation is more specific, and more conservative than a lot of coverage suggests. As of early October 2026, GPT-6.1 Sol is rolling out only to ChatGPT Work and Codex, not to the ordinary Chat interface most Plus subscribers use day to day. GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s most capable model, is reserved for the $100-and-up GPT-6 Pro tier. Everyday Plus-tier conversations are still largely running on the GPT-5.6 Sol class of model unless OpenAI enables a newer one for your account.

Google’s subscription page points AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers toward Gemini 3.1 Pro, paired with a 1-million-token context window, as the flagship model for paying Gemini users. Google has also begun surfacing the newer Gemini 4 Argon model to AI Ultra subscribers specifically, though as of this comparison’s research window Google had not clarified whether Argon would eventually move down into the Pro tier or stay Ultra-exclusive. Gemini 3.8 Flash, a faster and cheaper model, is what shows up in Google Cloud’s API pricing for developers rather than in the consumer Gemini app directly.

The practical takeaway: comparing Copilot to ChatGPT to Gemini is really comparing three different routing systems, each of which quietly swaps the underlying model depending on your plan, your task, and sometimes the week you happen to be using it.

Specs and Features at a Glance

Here is how the three assistants stack up on the specs that actually affect daily use, pulled from each vendor’s current documentation as of October 2026.

SpecMicrosoft CopilotChatGPTGoogle Gemini

Default underlying model (paid tier)Multi-model: OpenAI GPT family, growing share of Microsoft MAI, Anthropic Claude for select scenariosGPT-5.6 Sol class for Plus Chat; GPT-6 Astra on $100+/mo Pro; GPT-6.1 Sol in Work/Codex onlyGemini 3.1 Pro on AI Pro/Ultra; Gemini 4 Argon rolling to AI Ultra

Native Office/Workspace integrationDeepest: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams, OneNote, LoopNone native; browser, desktop app, and API onlyDeep inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Meet

Agent/autonomous workflow modeAgent Mode (default in Word/Excel/PowerPoint), plus Researcher and Analyst agentsAgent-style tasks via Codex and connectors; no document-editing agent modeAgentic browsing features folded in after Project Mariner’s May 2026 shutdown

Standalone chat appCopilot app (consumer) and Copilot Chat (business)ChatGPT web, desktop, and mobile appsGemini app (web, Android, iOS)

Free tier availableYes, limited, inside Windows and Microsoft accountsYes, limited daily usageYes, standard limits, Gemini 3.6 Flash/3.1 Pro capped

Browser-based agent productFolded into Edge/Copilot rather than a separate browserAtlas standalone browser shut down August 9, 2026Project Mariner discontinued May 4, 2026; capability moved into Chrome

Enterprise admin controlsMicrosoft Entra, Purview, tenant-wide policyChatGPT Enterprise admin console, SSO, data controlsGoogle Workspace Admin console, Vault, DLP

Reported scale (2026)30M+ paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats; 150M+ MAU across the first-party Copilot family900M+ weekly active users (some reports put it past 1B by mid-2026)950M monthly active users (Gemini app)

Coding-specific toolingGitHub Copilot is a separate product and subscriptionCodex CLI and desktop app bundled into paid ChatGPT tiersGemini Code Assist, separate from the consumer Gemini app

Canadian-dollar billingYes, Microsoft bills directly in CADNo, billed in USD and converted by your card issuerPartial; Google has introduced CAD pricing for some consumer tiers

Two things jump out immediately. First, Microsoft is the only one of the three billing Canadian customers directly in CAD rather than letting a USD charge hit your statement and your bank set the exchange rate. Second, Copilot’s advantage is entirely about depth of integration into tools your staff already use, not raw context window size, where ChatGPT and Gemini both publish bigger numbers.

Pricing in Canada: What You’ll Actually Pay

This is where the comparison gets genuinely useful for a Canadian buyer, because list prices in USD do not tell you what hits your invoice. Microsoft bills Canadian customers directly in CAD. OpenAI and, mostly, Google still price in USD, which means your actual cost depends on your bank’s conversion rate and, in several provinces, sales tax on top.

PlanPriceBilling currencyNotes

Microsoft 365 Personal (includes consumer Copilot features)CAD $11.50/monthCAD, directPer Microsoft’s Canadian consumer pricing page

Microsoft 365 Copilot (business add-on)CAD $31.90/user/month, paid annuallyCAD, directRequires a qualifying Microsoft 365 business subscription

Microsoft 365 Copilot (enterprise tier)CAD $40.70/user/month, paid annuallyCAD, directPlus applicable provincial tax

ChatGPT PlusUS$20/month (~CAD $28/month converted)USDCanadian trackers report checkout sometimes closer to CAD $24.99 before tax depending on promo

ChatGPT ProFrom US$100/month, up to US$200/monthUSDThird-party Canadian trackers estimate roughly CAD $153 to $280/month after conversion

ChatGPT Business / EnterpriseQuote-basedUSDOpenAI does not publish a flat CAD or USD per-seat Business/Enterprise price

Google AI Plus (Canada-specific tier)CAD $10.99/monthCAD, directIntroduced January 2026, no equivalent tier from Microsoft or OpenAI at this price point

Google AI ProUS$19.99/month (~CAD $27.99 converted)MixedIncludes Gemini 3.1 Pro access and the 1M-token context window

Google AI UltraUS$99.99 to US$199.99/monthUSDNo confirmed standalone CAD price found at time of writing

Add provincial sales tax and the gap widens further. One Canadian pricing tracker calculated that a CAD $28 base subscription lands anywhere from roughly $29.40 after Alberta’s 5% GST to about $32.20 after Quebec’s combined GST and QST. That is a real difference across a 50-person team paying for Plus or Pro seats for a full year, and it is a cost Microsoft’s direct CAD billing avoids by baking it in up front.

The practical read for a budget owner: if your organization is already paying for Microsoft 365, the incremental Copilot add-on at CAD $31.90/user/month is a known, predictable line item billed in home currency. ChatGPT and Gemini both carry currency-conversion uncertainty unless your finance team negotiates a direct enterprise contract.

Benchmarks and Adoption Data From Three Sources

There is no single independent 2026 benchmark that scores Copilot, ChatGPT, and Gemini side by side on office tasks like writing, spreadsheet modeling, and data analysis. That gap is worth stating plainly rather than papering over with a borrowed number. What does exist is adoption and scale data straight from each company’s own 2026 disclosures, which at least tells you where the market is actually voting with its wallet.

Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings materials reported that first-party agent monthly active usage, covering tools like Researcher and Analyst inside Copilot, had increased sixfold year to date, with Agent Mode now the default experience in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.

Separately, Microsoft 365 Copilot specifically passed 30 million paid seats as of its late-September 2026 earnings call, with engagement per user described as nearly doubling year over year and weekly usage approaching the level of Outlook and Teams.

OpenAI’s own figures put ChatGPT at more than 900 million weekly active users as of early 2026, with some secondary reporting citing a figure above 1 billion weekly active users by August 2026, a number OpenAI has not directly restated in the materials reviewed for this comparison.

Alphabet’s July 22, 2026 earnings call reported 950 million monthly active users for the Gemini app, and Google separately said its AI Mode search feature passed 1 billion monthly users around its May 2026 developer conference.

Read those four data points together and a pattern emerges. ChatGPT and Gemini are winning on raw reach, largely because both are free to try and sit inside products billions of people already use, a browser-adjacent chat app and Android/Search respectively. Copilot’s 30 million paid seats is a much smaller number, but it is a far more commercially meaningful one, because every single one of those seats represents a business that opted to pay specifically for the AI add-on inside a productivity suite it was already running. That is a fundamentally different kind of adoption than a free chatbot download, and it is the number worth watching if you are trying to judge enterprise traction rather than consumer buzz.

Microsoft 365 Copilot Deep Dive: Agent Mode, Researcher, and Analyst

Copilot’s biggest product shift in the back half of 2026 is the move to Agent Mode as the default, not optional, experience in the three apps most Canadian office workers touch daily. Instead of a sidebar you prompt for a paragraph at a time, Agent Mode takes a natural-language brief and iterates on a full Word document, Excel workbook, or PowerPoint deck, refining it across multiple passes before handing it back for review. Microsoft describes this as producing expert-quality first drafts, though as with any vendor claim about its own product quality, that should be treated as a marketing characterization rather than an independently verified benchmark.

Alongside Agent Mode, Microsoft has built out named agents that live inside Copilot Chat: Researcher, aimed at synthesizing information across a research brief, and Analyst, aimed at data-heavy work like reconciling spreadsheets or building financial models. Both are first-party agents, meaning Microsoft builds and maintains them directly, as opposed to the custom agents that customers or partners can build on top of Copilot Studio. If you want a closer look at how that custom-agent layer stacks up against Salesforce Agentforce and Gemini Enterprise’s agent-building tools specifically, we cover that separately in our Copilot Studio vs Agentforce vs Gemini Enterprise comparison.

The catch with Copilot, and it is a real one, is that it is not a standalone product in the way ChatGPT or Gemini are. You need an underlying, qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription before the Copilot add-on even becomes purchasable, and the per-user pricing stacks on top of whatever you are already paying for Office apps. For a Canadian business not already standardized on Microsoft 365, that makes Copilot a harder sell on price alone, even before you weigh feature differences.

ChatGPT for Work: Plus, Business, and the GPT-6.1 Sol Rollout

ChatGPT’s advantage over both competitors is flexibility: it is not tied to a specific productivity suite, it runs the same core assistant whether you are in Word, Google Sheets, Slack, or a terminal window via the Codex CLI, and its $20-a-month Plus tier is the cheapest named, publicly listed paid plan among the three once you set aside Google’s newer CAD-priced Plus tier. OpenAI’s October 2026 rollout notes show GPT-6.1 Sol landing first in ChatGPT Work and the Codex coding tool, with OpenAI explicitly stating it is not yet available in ordinary Chat, a distinction that matters if you are deciding whether to upgrade a team that mostly writes documents versus one that mostly writes code.

For teams that already use Excel heavily, our dedicated breakdown of Claude for Excel vs Copilot vs Gemini Sheets goes deeper into spreadsheet-specific functionality than this broader comparison does, and is worth reading alongside this piece if spreadsheets are your primary use case.

The practical downside for Canadian buyers is pricing opacity above the Plus tier. OpenAI does not publish a flat, public CAD or even USD per-seat price for ChatGPT Business or Enterprise, which means budgeting for a team rollout requires a sales conversation rather than a self-serve checkout, something Microsoft’s published per-user CAD pricing avoids entirely for the equivalent Copilot business tiers.

Google Gemini and Workspace: Where It Actually Fits

Gemini’s case is straightforward if your organization already standardized on Google Workspace rather than Microsoft 365: the AI layer shows up natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Meet, in the same way Copilot shows up natively inside Outlook, Word, Excel, and Teams. If you are not already a Workspace shop, bolting Gemini onto a Microsoft-based organization mostly just gives you another standalone chat app, with less of the deep document integration that is Copilot’s main selling point.

Google’s pricing structure is also the most tiered of the three. The CAD $10.99-a-month AI Plus tier, introduced in January 2026, is a genuinely distinct option neither Microsoft nor OpenAI matches at that price point, though Google has reportedly begun tightening what free and AI Plus users can access as of October 9, 2026, limiting them to the Flash and Flash-Lite models while reserving Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the newer Gemini 4 Argon, for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. That is worth flagging for any Canadian small business that signed up for the budget tier expecting ongoing access to Google’s flagship model, since Google appears to be actively narrowing what that tier includes.

Google’s agentic browsing ambitions, once centered on the standalone Project Mariner research prototype, were folded into Chrome’s built-in Gemini side panel after Mariner’s discontinuation on May 4, 2026. That mirrors what happened to OpenAI’s Atlas browser, which shut down entirely on August 9, 2026, with its agent capabilities absorbed back into the core ChatGPT product rather than a separate browser. Neither company, in other words, is currently betting on a standalone AI browser as the delivery mechanism; both have folded that functionality back into their core assistant.

Data Residency and Privacy for Canadian Organizations

This is the section Canadian IT and compliance teams actually care about, and it is also where vendor marketing and technical reality diverge the most.

Microsoft 365’s baseline data residency story is the strongest of the three on paper: core workload data in Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams can be kept at rest in Canadian regions, physically anchored in Toronto and Quebec City. But that is a statement about where your stored Office data lives, not necessarily where every Copilot prompt gets processed. Copilot’s prompt handling, grounding, and model inference steps can still leave Canada depending on the specific feature, tenant configuration, and Microsoft’s regional-processing commitments at the time. One industry analysis suggested Microsoft had signaled in-country Copilot inference for Canada specifically as a 2027 target, which implies full, guaranteed Canadian processing of the AI step itself was not yet universally available as of this comparison’s research window in late 2026.

Google Workspace does not currently offer an equivalent, generally available Canadian data region for Gemini inference, according to the sources reviewed for this piece, and OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise likewise does not provide a standard, generally available Canadian residency region. Both vendors can and do write bespoke contractual data-handling provisions into large enterprise agreements, but neither offers a self-serve, guaranteed Canada-only processing path the way Microsoft’s regional infrastructure at least partially does for the stored-data layer.

For organizations bound by PIPEDA, Quebec’s Law 25, or sector-specific rules in health care, legal services, or the public sector, the honest summary is: none of the three vendors currently guarantees that every byte of an AI interaction, from prompt to inference to response, stays on Canadian soil end to end. Microsoft’s story is meaningfully further along than the other two for stored data, but buyers should get written, product-specific confirmation from whichever vendor they choose rather than assuming a Canadian Workspace or 365 tenant automatically means Canadian AI processing. If sovereign AI and data residency are a top priority for your organization, our related coverage of Cohere vs OpenAI vs Gemini on Canadian data residency digs further into vendor-by-vendor residency commitments, and our look at Canada’s federal AI strategy covers the policy direction the government itself is pushing toward on sovereign AI infrastructure.

Five Real-World Use Cases Compared

Abstract feature comparisons only go so far. Here is how the choice typically plays out across five common Canadian organization profiles.

A mid-sized law firm already on Microsoft 365: Copilot tends to win by default here, not because it is objectively the smartest model, but because contract drafting and redlining already happen inside Word, and the firm’s existing Canadian data-residency posture for client files extends more naturally to Copilot than to standing up a second vendor relationship with OpenAI or Google.

A marketing or creative agency billing by the project: Many agencies gravitate toward ChatGPT Plus or Business specifically because creative brainstorming, ad copy, and client-facing messaging do not need to live inside a Word document, and the flat US$20 Plus price is easy to expense per freelancer or contractor without a Microsoft 365 seat attached.

An accounting or professional-services firm on Google Workspace: For firms that standardized on Workspace rather than Microsoft 365, Gemini’s native presence in Sheets and Docs makes it the lower-friction choice, even though Workspace’s data residency story for AI processing is currently no stronger than OpenAI’s.

A Canadian SaaS startup’s engineering and operations teams: It is common to see a split decision inside the same company, with engineers on ChatGPT Plus or Enterprise for the Codex coding tool and a separate GitHub Copilot subscription for in-editor suggestions, while finance and ops run Microsoft 365 Copilot’s Analyst agent for financial modeling in Excel.

A provincial or municipal public-sector body evaluating all three: Public-sector procurement teams consistently flag data residency as the deciding factor over raw model quality, which tends to push early pilots toward Microsoft given its stronger, if still incomplete, Canadian regional infrastructure story, pending clearer guaranteed-residency commitments from OpenAI and Google.

Which One Should You Choose? Use-Case Recommendations

Pulling the use cases above into direct recommendations:

Choose Microsoft Copilot if your organization is already paying for Microsoft 365 Business or Enterprise plans, your work product lives primarily in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook, and Canadian data residency for stored files is a compliance requirement.

Choose ChatGPT if you need a tool-agnostic assistant that works the same way across writing, coding, and research tasks regardless of which productivity suite your company runs, and you value OpenAI’s broader model lineup and the Codex coding tool.

Choose Gemini if your organization runs Google Workspace rather than Microsoft 365, and you want the AI assistant to show up natively in Gmail, Docs, and Sheets without adding a third vendor relationship.

Run more than one in parallel if, like the vast majority of large organizations tracked in 2026 surveys, your teams already use multiple AI tools for different jobs; a reported 81% of large global organizations now run three or more model families concurrently rather than standardizing on one.

Delay a decision if your primary blocker is guaranteed end-to-end Canadian data residency for AI inference specifically; none of the three vendors fully delivers that today, and Microsoft’s own in-country Copilot inference commitment for Canada is reportedly targeted for 2027 rather than already in place.

If your organization…Lean towardWhy

Already pays for Microsoft 365 Business or EnterpriseMicrosoft CopilotAdd-on pricing stacks cleanly on an existing tenant; deepest Word/Excel/Outlook integration

Already pays for Google WorkspaceGeminiNative inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides without a second vendor relationship

Has no fixed productivity suite, or a mixed-OS teamChatGPTSame experience everywhere; cheapest named paid tier at US$20/month

Writes a lot of code day to dayChatGPT (Codex) or GitHub CopilotCodex is bundled into paid ChatGPT tiers; GitHub Copilot is a separate, editor-native subscription

Is bound by PIPEDA, Law 25, or sector-specific residency rulesMicrosoft 365 Copilot, with written confirmationStrongest Canadian regional infrastructure for stored data, though AI inference residency is not yet fully guaranteed by any of the three

Is a budget-conscious solo operator or very small teamGoogle AI PlusAt CAD $10.99/month it undercuts every other named paid tier, though it is now capped to Flash-class models

Treat this table as a starting point rather than a final answer. The right call still depends on which suite your finance and IT teams have already standardized on, since ripping out an existing Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace deployment just to chase a marginally better chatbot is rarely worth the disruption.

How to Migrate Between Copilot, ChatGPT, and Gemini

Switching AI assistants, or running a pilot of a second one alongside your existing tool, is less disruptive than migrating an entire productivity suite, but there are still a few steps worth following in order.

Audit current usage first. Before adding or dropping a seat, check which teams are actually using Copilot, ChatGPT, or Gemini daily versus which licenses are sitting unused. Microsoft’s own Copilot dashboard defines an active user as someone who used Copilot at least once in the prior 28 days across Teams, Outlook, Copilot Chat, or the core Office apps, a useful baseline metric to pull before any licensing change.

Export anything you need to keep. ChatGPT conversation history, custom GPTs, and saved prompts can be exported from account settings before a seat is cancelled. Gemini’s saved conversations and Gems work similarly inside the Gemini app. Copilot does not maintain a separate chat history in the same way, since most of its output lives inside the Word, Excel, or PowerPoint file it helped create, which is arguably an advantage for continuity since the work product survives independent of the subscription.

Run a 30-to-60-day overlap period. Rather than cancelling one subscription the day a new one starts, overlap both for a billing cycle or two so teams can compare output quality on real work rather than a synthetic test, and so nothing falls through the cracks mid-project.

Re-check data residency commitments for the new tool. If data residency drove the original decision, do not assume it transfers; confirm current, product-specific residency terms directly with the vendor rather than relying on general marketing claims, since all three vendors have been actively changing their regional infrastructure commitments throughout 2026.

Retrain on agent-style workflows, not just the chat box. The biggest practical difference between these tools in late 2026 is not chat quality, it is each vendor’s agent layer: Copilot’s Agent Mode, ChatGPT’s Codex and connector-based tasks, and Gemini’s Chrome-integrated agentic features. Teams migrating between tools should budget time to relearn the agent workflow, not just the conversational interface.

For IT admins verifying who actually holds a Copilot license before a migration, Microsoft Graph PowerShell can pull license assignment directly:

Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "User.Read.All"

Get-MgUser -All | ForEach-Object {

$skus = (Get-MgUserLicenseDetail -UserId $_.Id).SkuPartNumber

if ($skus -contains "Microsoft_365_Copilot") {

[PSCustomObject]@{ User = $_.UserPrincipalName; Licensed = $true }

}

}

Running that kind of audit before a license renewal is the fastest way to find out whether your organization is actually paying for 50 active Copilot seats or quietly carrying 20 unused ones.

Pros and Cons of Each Platform

Microsoft Copilot

Pro: Deepest native integration into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams

Pro: Direct CAD billing with no currency-conversion guesswork

Pro: Strongest, though still incomplete, Canadian data residency story for stored workload data

Con: Requires an existing, qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription before you can even buy it

Con: Model routing is opaque; you cannot choose whether a given prompt hits OpenAI, Anthropic, or Microsoft’s own MAI models

ChatGPT

Pro: Works identically regardless of which productivity suite or operating system you use

Pro: Cheapest named, publicly listed paid tier among the three at US$20/month for Plus

Pro: Codex coding tool bundled into paid tiers without a separate subscription

Con: Billed in USD only, adding currency-conversion uncertainty for Canadian buyers

Con: No published, self-serve CAD or USD per-seat price for Business or Enterprise tiers

Google Gemini

Pro: Native integration across Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Meet for Workspace customers

Pro: Only vendor offering a sub-CAD-$11 paid tier, introduced specifically for the Canadian market in January 2026

Pro: Largest published context window at 1 million tokens on AI Pro and AI Ultra

Con: Google has been actively narrowing what the budget AI Plus tier includes, limiting it to Flash-class models as of October 2026

Con: No confirmed Canadian data residency region for Gemini inference specifically

The Verdict: Our Pick for Canadian Teams in 2026

There is no single universal winner here, and treating this as a simple ranking would misrepresent how differently these three tools are actually built. But the data does point to a clear decision framework. If your organization already runs Microsoft 365, the CAD $31.90-a-month Copilot add-on is the lowest-friction, best-integrated, and most Canada-aware option of the three, and Microsoft’s 30-million-seat figure suggests a lot of other Canadian and North American businesses have reached the same conclusion. If you are not locked into a productivity suite, or your team’s work is more code and research than documents and spreadsheets, ChatGPT’s US$20 Plus tier remains the most flexible and cheapest named option, with the caveat that you are accepting USD billing and less certainty about where your data physically lives. And if your organization already standardized on Google Workspace, Gemini is the natural fit rather than a reason to switch suites entirely.

The one point every Canadian buyer should carry away regardless of which tool they pick: none of the three vendors currently guarantees full, end-to-end Canadian data residency for AI inference, only for certain stored data in Microsoft’s case. Anyone buying on compliance grounds should get that confirmed in writing, product by product, rather than assuming a Canadian tenant or Canadian billing address settles the question.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Microsoft Copilot the same as ChatGPT?No. Copilot is Microsoft’s own product built on a multi-model backend that has historically defaulted to OpenAI’s GPT models but now also routes some requests to Microsoft’s in-house MAI models and, in select scenarios, Anthropic’s Claude. ChatGPT is OpenAI’s own standalone product, run entirely on OpenAI’s models.

Can I use Copilot without a Microsoft 365 subscription?Not for the full business version. Microsoft 365 Copilot is sold as an add-on that requires a qualifying Microsoft 365 Business or Enterprise subscription underneath it. A limited consumer version of Copilot is available separately through Microsoft accounts and Windows.

Which is cheaper in Canada, Copilot or ChatGPT Plus?On paper, ChatGPT Plus at US$20/month, roughly CAD $28 after conversion, is close to Microsoft 365 Copilot’s CAD $31.90/user/month. But that comparison only holds if you already have a Microsoft 365 subscription to attach Copilot to; if you do not, the real cost of adopting Copilot includes the underlying Microsoft 365 plan too.

Does any of these three guarantee my data stays in Canada?Microsoft 365 offers the strongest story for stored workload data, including Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams, through Canadian regions in Toronto and Quebec City, but Copilot’s AI processing itself is not guaranteed to stay in-country for every feature today. Neither Google Workspace nor OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise currently offers a generally available Canadian residency region for AI processing.

What happened to ChatGPT Atlas and Google’s Project Mariner?Both were standalone AI-browser or browser-agent products that their companies shut down in 2026: Atlas on August 9, 2026, and Project Mariner on May 4, 2026. Both companies folded the underlying agentic-browsing technology back into their core products, ChatGPT and Chrome’s Gemini integration respectively, rather than continuing them as separate apps.

Which model actually powers ChatGPT Plus right now?As of early October 2026, OpenAI’s own documentation shows GPT-6.1 Sol rolling out to ChatGPT Work and Codex only, not ordinary Chat. GPT-6 Astra is reserved for the $100-and-up GPT-6 Pro tier. Plus-tier chat conversations are generally still served by the GPT-5.6 Sol class of model unless OpenAI enables something newer for a given account.

Can my team use more than one of these at once?Yes, and it is increasingly the norm rather than the exception. Industry surveys cited in 2026 reporting suggest the large majority of big organizations already run three or more AI model families concurrently for different jobs, rather than standardizing on a single vendor.

Is Gemini included free with Google Workspace?A baseline level of Gemini functionality is built into Workspace, but the more capable AI Pro and AI Ultra tiers, which unlock Gemini 3.1 Pro, the 1-million-token context window, and the newer Gemini 4 Argon rollout, are separate paid add-ons starting at roughly CAD $27.99/month.
