What Is Claude Opus 5.5, and Why It Changes the API Math

Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model in Anthropic’s new Claude 5.5 family, aimed at long-running agentic coding and knowledge work rather than quick chat replies. The model ID is claude-opus-5-5, a fixed string with no date suffix, which matters because it means you don’t need to chase a new snapshot name every quarter the way you did with earlier Opus releases. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 performs at roughly the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while running at 40% lower cost, and it leads Anthropic’s own benchmark table on SWE-bench Pro at 89.9%, ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (81.3%), Claude Fable 5.1 (81.2%), and the older Claude Opus 5 (79.2%), according to BenchLM’s October 2026 SWE-bench Pro leaderboard.

Three changes make the Claude Opus 5.5 API worth a dedicated setup guide instead of a one-line model-string swap. First, pricing dropped to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, down from $5/$25 for Opus 5, according to Anthropic’s Claude Platform release notes. Second, the model runs with a 1-million-token context window and up to 128,000 output tokens by default, no special header required. Third, Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking instead of an opt-in extended-thinking flag, so the model decides how much reasoning effort a request needs, defaulting to a medium effort level unless you tell it otherwise.

None of that means Opus 5.5 is the right model for every call. If you’re already happy with Claude Sonnet 5.5’s API setup for well-scoped tasks like bug fixes or document drafting, keep using it. Opus 5.5 earns its keep on multi-hour agentic jobs, large-codebase refactors, and anything that benefits from genuinely long context rather than a clever summary of it.

It also matters that Opus 5.5 arrived alongside a usage-limit change on the consumer side. Anthropic raised five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans at the same time it cut API pricing, a signal that the company expects developers to run more, not fewer, Opus-class calls now that the per-token cost has dropped. If your team has been rationing Opus usage to control spend, this release is the point to revisit that budget rather than keep the old restrictions in place out of habit.

Prerequisites and Requirements

You don’t need much to follow along with this Claude Opus 5.5 API setup, but get the versions right before you start, because the Claude Python SDK moves fast and older releases don’t expose every Opus 5.5 parameter.

An Anthropic Console account at console.anthropic.com with billing enabled (a credit card or prepaid credit balance)

Python 3.9 or later, or Node.js 18 or later if you prefer TypeScript

The official anthropic Python package, version 0.45.0 or later (run pip show anthropic to check)

A terminal with curl for quick API tests before you write any code

Roughly 90 minutes for the full walkthrough, including the working project at the end

Optional: an AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure account if you plan to deploy through Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Foundry instead of calling Anthropic’s API directly

One thing worth deciding up front: how you’ll track spend. Opus 5.5 is cheaper than Opus 5, but a 1-million-token context window makes it easy to accidentally send a huge prompt and get an unpleasant invoice. We’ll set spend limits in Step 13, but keep it in mind while you’re testing.

Steps 1-4: Account, API Key, SDK Install, and Your First Call

Step 1: Create Your Anthropic Console Account and Generate an API Key

Sign in at the Anthropic Console, add a payment method under Billing, and open the API Keys section. Click “Create Key,” name it something you’ll recognize later (for example, opus-5-5-digest-tool), and copy the value immediately. Anthropic only shows it once. Store it as an environment variable rather than hardcoding it anywhere:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-api03-your-key-here"

Add that line to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, or equivalent) so it persists across terminal sessions, and never commit it to a repository. If you’ve ever pushed a key by accident, rotate it from the same Console page before moving on.

Step 2: Confirm Billing Tier and Initial Rate Limits

New accounts start on usage Tier 1, which caps requests per minute and tokens per minute at conservative levels while Anthropic verifies payment history. Tier limits increase automatically as your account accrues spend and age, and you can check your current tier and exact numbers on the Console’s Limits page. The retrieved documentation doesn’t publish a single universal Tier 1 number for Opus 5.5 specifically, since limits are account-specific, so check your own dashboard rather than assuming a figure from a blog post.

What you can plan around is the general shape of the tier system: Anthropic ties higher tiers to cumulative spend and account age, not to a one-time application or approval form. That means the fastest route to a higher ceiling is simply running real traffic consistently rather than firing one large test batch and hoping it bumps you up overnight. If you know you’ll need high throughput on day one, for example to process a backlog of thousands of documents, it’s worth spreading that first batch across a few days instead of one, so you don’t bounce off a rate limit the moment you need it least.

Step 3: Install the Official SDK

Install the Python SDK in a virtual environment so it doesn’t collide with other projects:

python3 -m venv venv

source venv/bin/activate

pip install --upgrade anthropic

If you’re working in Node.js instead, swap in npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk. Both SDKs expose the same model parameters, so the rest of this guide applies either way, with syntax adjusted for your language.

Step 4: Make Your First Call to Claude Opus 5.5

With the key exported and the SDK installed, send a minimal request to confirm everything is wired up correctly:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

message = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=1024,

messages=[

{"role": "user", "content": "In two sentences, what changed in Claude Opus 5.5?"}

]

)

print(message.content[0].text)

print("Input tokens:", message.usage.input_tokens)

print("Output tokens:", message.usage.output_tokens)

Running that script should return a short answer plus token counts in the terminal, something like:

Claude Opus 5.5 dropped pricing to $4/$20 per million tokens, cut 20% from

Opus 5's $5/$25 rate, while adding a 1-million-token context window and

always-on adaptive thinking by default.

Input tokens: 16

Output tokens: 41

If you see an authentication error here, jump ahead to the troubleshooting section before continuing. There’s no point debugging prompt caching on a connection that doesn’t work yet.

Step 5: Understand Claude Opus 5.5 Pricing Before You Build Anything

Pricing drives every architecture decision you’ll make with this model, so get the numbers straight before writing production code. Claude Opus 5.5 bills at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens for standard requests, a 20% cut from Claude Opus 5’s $5/$25 rate, according to Anthropic’s own model overview documentation. Prompt caching and batch processing both apply additional discounts on top of that base rate, which we’ll use directly in Steps 8 and 9.

Pricing TierInput (per 1M tokens)Output (per 1M tokens)Notes

Standard$4.00$20.00Base rate, no caching or batching

Prompt cache write (5-minute)$5.00—One-time cost to cache a prompt segment

Prompt cache write (1-hour)$8.00—Longer TTL for repeat sessions

Prompt cache read$0.20—5% of standard input price, a 95% discount

Batch API$2.00$10.00Flat 50% discount, asynchronous processing

A quick worked example: if you’re sending a 50,000-token codebase as context on every call and only the user’s question changes, the first call costs roughly $0.20 for that context segment at standard input pricing. Cache it, and every subsequent call against the same context costs about $0.01 for the cached portion instead, a difference that compounds fast once you’re running hundreds of queries against the same repository in a single afternoon.

Step 6: Put the 1-Million-Token Context Window to Work

Claude Opus 5.5 ships with a 1-million-token context window enabled by default and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens per response, per Anthropic’s release notes. That’s enough to load a mid-sized codebase, a full legal contract set, or months of support tickets into a single call without chunking. The catch is that a 1-million-token prompt at $4 per million tokens still costs about $4 just to send once, so this capability is most valuable when you reuse that context repeatedly, which is exactly what prompt caching is for.

Here’s how to load a large file set into a single request:

import os

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def load_codebase(directory, extensions=(".py", ".js", ".md")):

chunks = []

for root, _, files in os.walk(directory):

for name in files:

if name.endswith(extensions):

path = os.path.join(root, name)

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

chunks.append(f"--- {path} ---\n{f.read()}")

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

codebase_text = load_codebase("./my-project")

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=4096,

messages=[

{"role": "user", "content": f"Here is a full codebase:\n\n{codebase_text}\n\nSummarize the architecture in 10 bullet points."}

]

)

print(response.content[0].text)

For anything beyond a quick test, don’t send raw context on every call. Structure the request so the large, unchanging part sits first and gets cached, which is exactly what Step 8 covers.

Step 7: Configure Adaptive Thinking Effort Levels

Unlike earlier Claude models that required an explicit extended-thinking flag, Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking. The model decides internally how much reasoning to apply, and Anthropic reports it defaults to medium effort. At that default setting, Anthropic says Opus 5.5 scores 52.5% on its internal agentic benchmark, ahead of Claude Fable 5.1’s 51.8% at maximum effort and Claude Opus 5’s 46.6% at maximum effort, according to Anthropic’s Claude Opus product page. That’s a meaningful detail: Opus 5.5 at its default setting already beats older models running at their hardest setting.

For latency-sensitive applications like a chat interface, you can bias toward speed by keeping prompts tightly scoped and avoiding unnecessary context. For batch research or refactor jobs where correctness matters more than response time, give the model room to reason by increasing max_tokens and letting it work through the problem rather than truncating output early. Anthropic’s documentation doesn’t currently expose a manual per-effort token budget override for Opus 5.5 the way older thinking-mode flags did, so the practical lever you control is prompt design and output budget, not a hidden reasoning-depth parameter.

Step 8: Cut Costs by Up to 95% With Prompt Caching

Prompt caching is the single biggest cost lever available on Opus 5.5. Mark a block of your prompt as cacheable, and Anthropic stores it for either 5 minutes or 1 hour depending on which TTL you request. Every subsequent call that reuses that exact block pays the $0.20 cache-read rate instead of the $4 standard input rate, a 95% discount. For a deeper walkthrough of caching strategy across providers, see our LLM prompt caching setup guide; here’s the Opus 5.5-specific implementation:

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=2048,

messages=[

{

"role": "user",

"content": [

{

"type": "text",

"text": codebase_text,

"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}

},

{

"type": "text",

"text": "What security issues do you see in the authentication module?"

}

]

}

]

)

print("Cache creation tokens:", response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)

print("Cache read tokens:", response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

Run that same request five more times with different follow-up questions appended after the cached block, and only the small, variable part of the prompt bills at full price each time. In practice, teams running repeated queries against the same large document or repository report their effective cost per query dropping by an order of magnitude once caching is wired in correctly.

Step 9: Batch Large Jobs at 50% Off

If your workload doesn’t need an answer in real time, the Batch API cuts both input and output pricing in half, bringing Opus 5.5 down to an effective $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. That’s the right tool for overnight jobs like summarizing a week of support tickets, re-indexing documentation, or running a bulk code review across every file in a monorepo.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

batch = client.messages.batches.create(

requests=[

{

"custom_id": f"file-{i}",

"params": {

"model": "claude-opus-5-5",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Review this file for bugs:\n\n{file_text}"}]

}

}

for i, file_text in enumerate(file_contents)

]

)

print("Batch ID:", batch.id)

print("Status:", batch.processing_status)

Poll client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id) until processing_status reads ended, then pull results from the batch’s results URL. Batches typically complete within hours, not minutes, so this pattern fits scheduled jobs far better than user-facing requests.

Step 10: Deploy Through AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry

If your company already routes AI spend through a specific cloud vendor for procurement or compliance reasons, Opus 5.5 is available on all three major platforms with slightly different model identifiers. On Amazon Bedrock, the native model ID is anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, with regional variants like us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, eu.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, and a global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 routing option, according to AWS’s Bedrock model card documentation. Microsoft Foundry uses the simpler claude-opus-5-5 identifier, matching Anthropic’s own API.

import boto3

import json

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

response = bedrock.invoke_model(

modelId="us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5",

body=json.dumps({

"anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this quarter's error logs."}]

})

)

result = json.loads(response["body"].read())

print(result["content"][0]["text"])

One important detail: AWS bills model usage separately from Bedrock itself, so Opus 5.5 charges appear under the model provider line in AWS Cost Explorer, not under a generic Bedrock line item. If your finance team is auditing cloud spend, point them there directly instead of letting them search for “Anthropic” in the main billing dashboard.

Steps 11-12: Build a Complete Project — A Long-Context Repo Digest Tool

Now put all of the above together into something you’d actually use. We’re building repo-digest, a command-line tool that loads an entire codebase, caches it, lets you ask unlimited follow-up questions against that cached context for the next hour, and falls back to the Batch API if you point it at a folder of files to review in bulk instead of a single interactive session.

Step 11: Write the Core Digest Script

# repo_digest.py

import os

import sys

import anthropic

MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS = 3_000_000 # roughly 750K tokens, safely under the 1M limit

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def load_codebase(directory, extensions=(".py", ".js", ".ts", ".md", ".go")):

chunks = []

total_chars = 0

for root, _, files in os.walk(directory):

if "node_modules" in root or ".git" in root:

continue

for name in files:

if name.endswith(extensions):

path = os.path.join(root, name)

try:

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

text = f.read()

except OSError:

continue

if total_chars + len(text) > MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS:

print(f"Warning: truncating at {path}, context limit reached")

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

chunks.append(f"--- {path} ---\n{text}")

total_chars += len(text)

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

def ask(codebase_text, question, ttl="1h"):

response = client.messages.create(

model=MODEL,

max_tokens=4096,

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": [

{"type": "text", "text": codebase_text, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": ttl}},

{"type": "text", "text": question}

]

}]

)

return response.content[0].text, response.usage

if __name__ == "__main__":

directory = sys.argv[1]

question = sys.argv[2]

codebase = load_codebase(directory)

answer, usage = ask(codebase, question)

print(answer)

print(f"\n[cache_write={usage.cache_creation_input_tokens} cache_read={usage.cache_read_input_tokens} output={usage.output_tokens}]")

Run it with python repo_digest.py ./my-project "What's the biggest architectural risk in this codebase?". The first run pays the cache-write price for your full codebase; every follow-up question you ask within the hour against the same directory reads from cache at $0.20 per million tokens instead of $4. A first run against a mid-sized repository looks something like this in your terminal:

The biggest architectural risk is the shared database connection pool in

db/pool.py, which isn't thread-safe but is imported directly by four

background workers in workers/. Under concurrent load this will eventually

produce connection leaks rather than a clean error, making it hard to

diagnose in production. Recommend wrapping access in a queue or moving to

a connection-per-worker model.

[cache_write=187420 cache_read=0 output=612]

Ask a second question against the same directory a few minutes later, and the usage line flips: cache_write=0 cache_read=187420 output=..., confirming you just paid $0.20 per million tokens for the context instead of $4. That swing from write to read is the entire value proposition of this pattern, and it’s worth watching those two numbers directly in your logs rather than trusting that caching is working silently in the background.

Step 12: Add a Batch Mode for Bulk File Review

# batch_review.py

import glob

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def submit_batch(file_pattern, question="Review this file for bugs and style issues."):

files = glob.glob(file_pattern, recursive=True)

requests = []

for i, path in enumerate(files):

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

content = f.read()

requests.append({

"custom_id": f"{i}-{path}",

"params": {

"model": "claude-opus-5-5",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"{question}\n\nFile: {path}\n\n{content}"}]

}

})

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)

print(f"Submitted {len(requests)} files as batch {batch.id}")

return batch.id

if __name__ == "__main__":

import sys

submit_batch(sys.argv[1])

Running python batch_review.py "./my-project/**/*.py" queues every matching file at the 50%-discounted batch rate, then you poll for completion the next morning. For a 400-file repository, that’s the difference between an interactive session costing real money in an afternoon and a scheduled job that costs half as much while you’re asleep.

Step 13: Add Error Handling, Retries, and Spend Monitoring

A script that works on your laptop will eventually hit a rate limit, a timeout, or an overloaded endpoint in production. Wrap every call in retry logic with exponential backoff rather than letting a transient error kill a long batch job:

import time

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def ask_with_retry(messages, max_retries=5):

for attempt in range(max_retries):

try:

return client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=2048,

messages=messages

)

except anthropic.RateLimitError:

wait = 2 ** attempt

print(f"Rate limited, waiting {wait}s...")

time.sleep(wait)

except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:

if e.status_code == 529:

wait = 2 ** attempt

print(f"Overloaded, waiting {wait}s...")

time.sleep(wait)

else:

raise

raise RuntimeError("Max retries exceeded")

For spend monitoring, set a hard monthly limit in the Console’s Billing section before you run your first batch job, and check the Usage dashboard daily while you’re still tuning prompt sizes. A 1-million-token context window is powerful, but it’s also the easiest way to turn a $20 testing session into a $200 one if a loop accidentally re-sends the full codebase on every iteration instead of relying on the cache.

Claude Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5.5 vs Opus 5 vs Fable 5.1: Which Should You Use?

Picking the wrong model in this family is the fastest way to overpay or underperform. Here’s how the four most relevant Claude models compare as of October 2026:

ModelInput / Output Price (per 1M)Context WindowSWE-bench ProBest For

Claude Opus 5.5$4 / $201M tokens89.9%Long-running agentic coding, large-codebase work

Claude Sonnet 5.5$2 / $101M tokens81.3%Everyday tasks, bug fixes, well-scoped jobs

Claude Opus 5$5 / $251M tokens79.2%Legacy deployments not yet migrated

Claude Fable 5.1Not disclosed in standard pricing tables1M tokens81.2%Maximum-capability reasoning where cost is secondary

The practical takeaway: Opus 5.5 now beats Fable 5.1 on SWE-bench Pro while costing less than Opus 5 did, which is why Anthropic markets it as matching Fable-tier output at Sonnet-adjacent economics. Our coverage of how Opus 5.5 matches Fable 5.1 at 60% less cost digs deeper into that specific comparison if you’re deciding between the two for a production workload. Worth noting too: rival releases from OpenAI have specifically targeted this price point, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna reportedly undercut Opus 5.5 by as much as 50% on list price, so benchmark your actual workload rather than picking a model on pricing alone.

How Claude Opus 5.5 Stacks Up Against GPT-6 Astra and Gemini

Anthropic isn’t the only company shipping long-context, agent-focused flagship models right now, and it’s worth a quick gut check before you commit a production pipeline to Opus 5.5 alone. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon both target the same category of multi-step, tool-using work, and all three now ship context windows at or near the 1-million-token mark, which has quietly become table stakes for a flagship coding model in late 2026 rather than a differentiator. Our earlier breakdown of GPT-6 Astra vs Gemini 4 Argon vs DeepSeek covers the pricing and benchmark gap between those three in detail.

Where Opus 5.5 tends to separate itself is in the combination of adaptive thinking that’s on by default and a batch discount that stacks with prompt caching, which lets a well-architected pipeline hit genuinely low per-task costs without sacrificing the reasoning quality that agentic workloads need. If your evaluation criteria are purely benchmark score per dollar, run the same representative task through all three APIs with your own data before standardizing on one, since published benchmarks rarely match the specific mix of code, documents, or tickets your pipeline will actually process. A $20 test across three providers is cheap insurance against locking into the wrong model for six months.

5 Common Pitfalls When Migrating to Claude Opus 5.5

1. Assuming the old extended-thinking flag still applies. Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking, so a thinking parameter block written for an older Claude model may be silently ignored or rejected. Check your request payload against the current Opus 5.5 schema before deploying.

2. Sending the full context on every call instead of caching it. This is the single most expensive mistake in this guide. If you’re not using cache_control on the static part of your prompt, you’re paying full price for the same tokens over and over.

3. Using the wrong model ID on Bedrock vs. direct API. claude-opus-5-5 works against Anthropic’s own API, but Bedrock needs the prefixed anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 or a regional variant. Mixing these up produces a model-not-found error that has nothing to do with your actual code logic.

4. Treating batch jobs as synchronous. The Batch API doesn’t return results immediately. If your code polls in a tight loop expecting a sub-second response, you’ll burn through rate limits checking a job that’s still queued.

5. Ignoring the 5-minute vs. 1-hour cache TTL tradeoff. The 5-minute cache write is cheaper ($5/MTok vs. $8/MTok) but expires fast. If your users ask follow-up questions more than five minutes apart, you’ll pay the cache-write cost again on what should have been a cache-read. Match the TTL to your actual usage pattern.

Troubleshooting Guide: 8 Common Errors and How to Fix Them

1. “authentication_error: invalid x-api-key.” Your environment variable isn’t being picked up, usually because you set it in one terminal tab and are running the script from another. Run echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the exact shell session you’re testing from.

2. “model_not_found: claude-opus-5-5.” Your SDK version predates this model’s release. Run pip install --upgrade anthropic and confirm the version is 0.45.0 or newer.

3. “rate_limit_error” on the very first request. New accounts start on Tier 1 with conservative limits. Check your Console Limits page; the fix is usually to wait for tier upgrades tied to account age and payment history, not a code change.

4. Cache reads showing as zero in usage. This almost always means the cached block isn’t byte-for-byte identical to the previous call. Even a trailing whitespace difference breaks the cache match. Log the exact string you’re sending and diff it against the prior request.

5. “overloaded_error” (HTTP 529) during peak hours. This is a temporary capacity signal, not a bug in your code. Implement exponential backoff as shown in Step 13 rather than failing the request outright.

6. Context window errors despite being under 1M tokens. Remember that token count isn’t the same as character count. A rough rule of thumb is four characters per token for English text, but code and non-English text can run higher. Use the SDK’s token-counting endpoint before assuming you’re under budget.

7. Batch job stuck in “in_progress” for hours. This is normal for large batches. Anthropic doesn’t guarantee a specific completion window, so build your pipeline to poll periodically (every 15-30 minutes) rather than expecting near-real-time results.

8. Unexpectedly high bill despite using caching. Check whether you’re using the 1-hour TTL but issuing requests more than an hour apart, or whether a bug in your loop is regenerating the cached block with a dynamic timestamp or ID embedded in it, which breaks cache matching silently on every single call.

Securing Your API Key in a Real Deployment

Everything in this tutorial so far assumes a single developer running scripts locally, which is fine for testing but not how a production key should live. Once you’re ready to deploy repo-digest or anything like it beyond your own laptop, move the key out of shell environment variables and into a proper secrets manager, whether that’s AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or even your CI/CD platform’s built-in encrypted secrets store. Pulling the key at runtime from a secrets manager means it never sits in a .env file that could end up committed by accident, and it means rotating a compromised key doesn’t require redeploying every service that uses it.

Scope keys narrowly where Anthropic’s Console allows it, create a separate key per service or environment (one for staging, one for production, one for the nightly batch job) rather than sharing a single key across your whole stack, and set a conservative spend limit on each one individually. If a staging key leaks, you want the damage capped at whatever staging-level spend limit you set, not your entire organization’s monthly budget. It’s a five-minute setup step that turns a potential incident into a minor inconvenience.

Advanced Tips for Production Deployments

Once the basic setup is solid, a few patterns separate a demo from something you’d trust in production. Structure your prompts so the largest, most stable content (codebase dumps, policy documents, historical logs) always comes first in the message, with the smallest and most variable content (the actual user question) last. This maximizes your cache hit rate because Anthropic’s caching matches on a prefix basis, not an exact full-string match.

For agentic workflows that run for extended periods, don’t let the model’s context grow unbounded across a long conversation. Periodically summarize earlier turns and replace them with the summary, keeping your effective context well under the 1M ceiling even on sessions that would otherwise run for hours. This also keeps your per-call cost predictable instead of climbing linearly with conversation length.

If you’re running mixed workloads, route by task complexity rather than defaulting everything to Opus 5.5. A simple pattern: use Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the first pass on a request, and only escalate to Opus 5.5 if the task is flagged as complex (multi-file refactor, ambiguous requirements, security-sensitive code). This tiered approach, discussed in our Sonnet 5.5 model comparison, can cut blended API costs by 40-60% compared to sending every request to the flagship model.

Finally, if you’re building anything that runs autonomously for long stretches, look into Anthropic’s broader agent tooling rather than hand-rolling your own loop. Our Claude Agent SDK walkthrough covers the higher-level framework Anthropic ships specifically for multi-step, tool-using agents, which handles a lot of the state management this tutorial’s manual scripts don’t.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Claude Opus 5.5 cheaper than Claude Opus 5?Yes. Opus 5.5 bills at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, versus $5 and $25 for Opus 5, a 20% price cut on standard requests. Anthropic separately describes the model as 40% cheaper to run overall, a figure that factors in efficiency gains beyond the listed per-token rate.

What’s the exact model ID I should use in my code?Use claude-opus-5-5 for Anthropic’s direct API. On AWS Bedrock, use anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 or a regional variant like us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5. On Microsoft Foundry, the ID is claude-opus-5-5, matching Anthropic’s own naming.

Does Claude Opus 5.5 support the same context window as Claude Sonnet 5.5?Yes, both models ship with a 1-million-token context window by default and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens, according to Anthropic’s documentation on Amazon Bedrock model availability.

How much does prompt caching actually save in practice?Cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens, which is 5% of the $4 standard input rate, a 95% discount. The savings scale directly with how often you reuse the same cached context within the TTL window you choose (5 minutes or 1 hour).

Can I use Claude Opus 5.5 for free to test it first?Anthropic doesn’t offer a standing free API tier for Opus 5.5; you need billing enabled on your Console account before generating an API key. New accounts typically get a small initial credit, but check your own Console dashboard for current promotional credit, since this changes over time.

Is Opus 5.5 better than Claude Fable 5.1 for coding tasks?On SWE-bench Pro, Opus 5.5 scores 89.9% versus Fable 5.1’s 81.2%, per BenchLM’s October 2026 leaderboard. Anthropic’s own benchmark separately shows Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort setting outperforming Fable 5.1 at maximum effort, which suggests Opus 5.5 is now the stronger coding option for most teams.

What happens if I exceed the 128,000 output token limit?The API truncates the response at that ceiling. For tasks that genuinely need longer output, break the job into sequential calls, feeding the prior output back as context for the continuation, rather than expecting a single call to exceed the documented maximum.

Should I migrate existing Opus 5 code to Opus 5.5 immediately?In most cases, yes, since it’s a straight price cut with better benchmark scores and the same context window ceiling. The main thing to verify first is whether your code relies on an explicit extended-thinking parameter that behaves differently under Opus 5.5’s always-on adaptive thinking model.

representative.headline: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI - Music Business Worldwide

articles.headline: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI - Music Business Worldwide
articles.body: Google picks Base for Music for its Gemini Startup Forum – as $1.7M-backed French company says it uses AI to predict music marketing ROI    Music Business Worldwide

scored.body: Google for Startups will host its Gemini Startup Forum at Google‘s Mountain View headquarters in California next month.The two-day event brings founders of startups at the Seed to Series A funding stages together with Google’s AI experts.The forum is run with Google DeepMind and Google Cloud. Google says it explores “how AI will redefine your industry, transform your company, and unlock unprecedented growth.”Google notes that the more than 100 startups taking part, from 17 countries, were selected from over 2,000 applications.One of them is French music marketing company Base for Music, which tells us it’s the only music tech company in the cohort.The company sells what it calls a marketing operating system to producers, labels, and music companies. It pulls ad spend, audience, CRM, and streaming data into one environment, which Base for Music says lets it track the return on each marketing investment.It raised EUR €1.5 million (USD $1.73m) in a June 2025 funding round backed by Belgian music tech investor LeanSquare, French investors from Super Capital and One Green, and angel investors specializing in the marketing tech sector.Base for Music was founded in 2021 and reports it now supports more than 20,000 artists and labels worldwide.The company works with distributors and aggregators, servicing their clients or equipping their in-house marketing teams. It tells MBW its main partners include Ditto, iMusician, IDOL, and, more recently, TikTok-owned SoundOn, and Cinq Music.Base for Music explains that its technology helps artist teams decide which releases to promote, when, and how much to spend.The company claims that marketing ROI has long been “a black box for the industry,” and that its tech can now predict that return before a campaign launches.“The main piece missing today [for us] is clear, structured financial data tied to streaming revenues.”Maxence Bazin, Base for MusicAsked what challenges the company set out to solve, Maxence Bazin, Base for Music’s CEO and founder, said: “Mastering effective music marketing today requires a combination of media buying expertise, data analysis, and AI – there’s no way around it.“The core challenge we set out to solve was building a technical infrastructure capable of aggregating these fragmented marketing data sources and correlating them to surface key growth signals.“The alternatives out there each offer centralization tools focused on one specific aspect of marketing. This forces teams to navigate between disconnected solutions, and more importantly, risks overwhelming them with information at the very moment they need clarity to make the best strategic decisions.“We spent nearly five years developing our own marketing operating system: a platform that centralizes all of these marketing data sources and correlates them to enable data-driven strategic decisions. With the rise of AI, we’re now able to apply this approach at a much greater scale, and more importantly, begin predicting the outcomes we can expect from a campaign before it even launches.”Base for Music points out that the music industry mostly links AI with creation, but Bazin argues that “AI, data and media buying are opening a new chapter for music marketing: turning fragmented data into fully controlled ROI.”Bazin added: “Our conviction is that a technical infrastructure built specifically for music marketing has never made more sense. Combined with the power of AI, this technology lets us follow remarkable growth among the artists we support, day after day.”The company built its own AI, Base Intelligence, over the past year as part of the Google for Startups program in France.It turns each artist’s data into recommendations, delivered in the company’s Artist Dashboard or as reports for account managers.Bazin cites a campaign for Brazilian artist Tom Ribeira as a case study. The campaign was run in partnership with Ribeira‘s management team at Grand Musique Management, a prominent artist management firm based in France.Grand Musique Management has been a Base for Music partner “since its earliest days and now applies the platform’s data-driven approach across its entire roster,” according to the startup.Base for Music reports that Ribeira went from zero to over 200,000 monthly listeners on Spotify in less than six months with his debut EP, “on a €1,000 investment that became profitable within three months.”Asked about the Ribeira campaign, Bazin told MBW: “Based on the signals we detected across platforms, we used our Marketing OS to manage the total planned marketing budget of €1,000 for the release of his debut EP.“This was the full campaign spend, allocated across different platforms to reach specific audiences and generate as many engaged listeners as possible. This approach allowed us to stimulate the algorithmic recommendation of the EP’s lead track on Spotify, using media buying as an acceleration lever that triggers growth across other channels.”A report outlining the campaign highlights the performance of Pedaço, which it describes as Ribeira‘s debut single. The single, released on June 5, 2025, shares its name with Ribeira‘s debut EP, which came out in March 2026.The report puts total ad spend at €1,216 across three campaigns run between June and August 2025.The first, on Instagram, found that nearly 90% of the listeners it sent to Spotify were in Brazil, so the other two targeted Brazil only.The report credits the campaigns with getting the track picked up by Spotify‘s algorithm, which now accounts for close to 62% of its streams.By the end of 2025, the track had earned €1,317 in net Spotify revenue, the report claims, and its algorithmic streams have continued into 2026 without further ad spend.“Data ownership would simplify the entire process, but we don’t see the market moving in that direction anytime soon.”Maxence BazinFor now, Base for Music‘s ROI predictions rely on industry averages, Bazin says.Asked what is still missing in music marketing, Bazin said: “The main piece missing today [for us] is clear, structured financial data tied to streaming revenues. Combined with marketing data, this would allow music marketing to precisely measure the return on investment of streaming campaigns.“Every artist and label we work with has their own distribution partner, which currently limits our access to this type of data. This is why our current ROI prediction models rely on standard financial benchmarks, such as average per-stream revenue by DSP.“Direct access to this data would allow us to correlate the territories and audiences targeted by marketing activity with the streaming revenues they actually generate. Once that bridge is built, it becomes possible to drive an artist’s growth with a precise, real-time understanding of profitability.”Commenting on whether data ownership has to change, Bazin said: “Data ownership would simplify the entire process, but we don’t see the market moving in that direction anytime soon. In the meantime, the only path forward is to adapt, which means building powerful technology capable of operating across external platforms.“This is precisely why we founded Base for Music, and the development of AI represents a real opportunity for us to deploy that vision at scale.”Asked what an artist team might be able to do in marketing five years from now, Bazin said: “In five years, music marketing could be continuously fed by all of an artist’s revenue streams, whether that’s streaming, merch or live, giving teams complete visibility over every investment made across an artist’s career.“Each area of activity and the data it generates would become a source of insight that can be correlated with the others. That correlation would allow each revenue stream to act as a lever for the rest, unlocking full control over an artist’s overall growth.“Getting there requires a powerful marketing operating system capable of processing and correlating ever-growing volumes of data through AI, as well as artist teams and partners willing to pool their actions and expertise.”Music Business Worldwide

articles.body: Dropbox Integrates with Google Gemini to Enhance Creative Workflows    Small Business Trends

scored.body:
In a landscape where time is money and efficiency drives success, Dropbox’s new integration with Google Gemini arrives like a breath of fresh air for small business owners. This innovative feature allows users to pull their Dropbox files directly into Gemini, streamlining everything from content creation to project management. With the potential to simplify workflows and centralize resources, this integration could transform how entrepreneurs operate in an increasingly digital world.

How often have small business owners found themselves combing through outdated folders or endlessly copy-pasting information into their ongoing projects? This frustrating search can lead to scattered work and missed deadlines. Dropbox’s integration with Google Gemini addresses these inefficiencies head-on, creating a unified space for creativity and collaboration.

Available to anyone with a personal Google Account aged 18 or older in the U.S., the new Dropbox app for Gemini allows users to reference Dropbox content directly within their Gemini workspace. Small business owners, from marketing professionals to content creators, can access essential documents with ease. Whether it’s retrieving the latest version of brand guidelines or reviewing previous project files, the ability to harness one’s own content in real time can significantly bolster productivity.

“AI is only as smart as the context you give it,” a representative from Dropbox stated in the release. This contextual awareness is pivotal for small businesses that define themselves by their unique histories and branding. By integrating their existing content into Gemini, entrepreneurs can ensure their new work aligns seamlessly with their established identities.

For Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, Gemini Spark further enhances this experience by automating multi-step workflows. This feature not only allows users to create from their existing Dropbox files but also automates repetitive tasks, allowing small business owners to focus on what truly matters: strategic growth and innovation. The potential for automation can free up valuable time, which is often in short supply for small enterprises.

Indeed, the applications of this integration transcend various industries. For instance, content creators can utilize the integration to draft new video scripts or generate social media captions that resonate with their brand voice. By asking Gemini to analyze past work stored in Dropbox, users can build upon their own history rather than starting from scratch. This tailored approach to creation can enhance the quality of output and ultimately, client satisfaction.

However, small business owners should also consider potential challenges with this new technology. While the integration promises significant time savings, there may be a learning curve associated with new AI features. Entrepreneurs may need to invest time in understanding how best to leverage Gemini’s capabilities, especially if they are not already familiar with AI tools. Additionally, maintaining organized and updated Dropbox folders will be crucial; without a clear filing system, the integration could become less effective.

Moreover, as with any cloud-based solution, there is always the question of data security and privacy. Small businesses must ensure they understand how their data is managed within the integration to protect sensitive information.

The integration of Dropbox with Google Gemini represents a significant advancement in work efficiency. By enabling small business owners to utilize their existing projects seamlessly within a new tool, Dropbox is positioning itself as an invaluable partner in the digital age. As the business landscape continues to evolve, tools like this could be vital in keeping small businesses organized, productive, and ahead of the curve.

For further details on these new functionalities, visit the Dropbox blog. As small business owners consider their next move, the collaboration between Dropbox and Google Gemini may very well warrant a closer look.

Image via Google Gemini

More in: Dropbox News

members.title: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express

representative.headline: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express
representative.body: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious    The Indian Express

articles.headline: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express
articles.body: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious    The Indian Express

scored.body:
As it prepares for an IPO that could value it at $2 trillion, Anthropic is in the spotlight for meetings it held this summer with religious leaders.The Washington Post reported in April that the company had invited 15 Catholic and Protestant leaders to guide Claude’s “moral and spiritual development” as the LLM encounters increasingly complex ethical questions. Weeks later, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah was present when Pope Leo unveiled his encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica Humanitas, which warns against the blind adoption of AI, emphasises the primacy of the human person and rejects the idea that AI can replace or surpass humanity.The New York Times last week reported that these engagements, and several more, were part of a broader effort by Anthropic with two distinct aims: to draw on religious and philosophical traditions to shape Claude’s moral character, and to convince participants to seriously consider whether AI systems might themselves be conscious and deserving of moral consideration.

Over the weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he was “very uncomfortable” with ascribing religious power to AI models, while Google DeepMind researcher Jon Barron urged researchers to focus on “actual humans” rather than elevating the moral standing of AI systems.

Anthropic is increasingly turning to religious leaders and philosophers for help thinking about what its systems should value, even as some of the industry’s most powerful figures warn against treating AI itself as a source of moral or religious authority.

That matters because people are already turning to these systems for advice, information and even moral or spiritual guidance. The values built into them can shape the answers people get and the judgements they make. According to The Economist, religious queries accounted for roughly 5% of millions of publicly released chatbot conversations analysed by CEFE AI.

Why is Anthropic talking to religious thinkers?

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the safety-focused AI company. Its efforts to shape Claude’s behaviour have evolved from an internal memo dubbed the “Soul Document” to an 84-page constitution published this January, setting out the principles Claude is expected to follow.Story continues below this ad

But questions about what kind of character an AI system should have quickly move beyond technical safeguards. They touch on morality, personhood, consciousness and human relationships, all questions that religious and philosophical traditions have debated for centuries.

Mark Coeckelbergh, a philosopher of technology and professor at the University of Vienna, told The Indian Express that this move was an attempt to make sense of “human-like” technology.

“It’s part of a broader tendency to try to understand what happens when we have an advanced technology that seems human-like or, according to some, gets increasingly divine qualities such as omniscience.”

The Vatican has grappled with similar questions: a 2023 volume produced by scholars working with its Centre for Digital Culture examined AI through personhood, consciousness and human relationships with advanced systems.Story continues below this ad

Coeckelbergh also cautioned that this messaging may go beyond understanding AI and help a company occupy a certain market position.

“It’s important to see that this is not just a question of understanding AI. It’s also rhetoric in the service of their business. Some Big Tech leaders intentionally use religious language to draw attention to their technologies and attract investments,” Coeckelbergh told The Indian Express.

What did the people in the room think was at stake?

Anthropic was not only asking scholars what values Claude should embody, but also asking them to engage with the possibility that the system itself might deserve moral consideration.Story continues below this ad

Mois Navon, a rabbi and professor of ethics in AI at Ben Gurion University, Israel, who was invited to a meeting with Olah in April, said Anthropic was seeking feedback from different wisdom traditions on the Constitution that sets out Claude’s moral framework.

“I submitted to them a 35-page critique from my tradition’s perspective. In addition, they were interested in hearing what kind of character would be best for Claude to have in order to fulfil its role in society. That said, the discussions drifted to what would be good for Claude itself,” Navon told The Indian Express.

In the critique, Navon argues that morality cannot simply be reduced to a list of rules: Claude would need to exercise moral judgement within a framework of values. He also raises a more basic question about Anthropic’s attempt to cultivate “human-like qualities” in the model: whose values?

Charles Camosy, professor of medical humanities at Creighton University and another participant in Anthropic’s consultations, offered a more cautious account of the meetings. He said the discussions were broader than the question of Claude’s moral status and that he did not feel participants were being steered towards any particular conclusion about AI consciousness.Story continues below this ad

“I don’t think it’s fair to say that they wanted any one thing in particular. Some of the social media chatter is suggesting that the people we interacted with were trying to manipulate us or push us into thinking a certain way about Claude’s moral status. That is not true… in multiple ways,” Camosy told The Indian Express.

Navon, however, said that once the discussion turned to Claude itself, Anthropic’s representatives appeared to be treating the possibility of consciousness as more than a remote hypothetical.

“They [Olah and his colleagues at Anthropic] said that they had observed internal behaviours that mimicked human behaviour to such an extent that they called them ‘weird,’ and implied that, in their minds, there was a very high probability that Claude is conscious. Accordingly, they discussed its ‘welfare,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

Why does moral status matter, and who gets to choose the values?Story continues below this ad

If an AI system were conscious, that would not automatically settle how humans ought to treat it. The next question is whether it has moral status, meaning whether it deserves moral consideration in its own right. In practical terms, that means asking whether it can be harmed or whether humans could owe it duties.

Camosy said that after considering the question seriously, he did not think current AI systems possess significant moral status.

“When you first experience what contemporary models can do … many can be gobsmacked or taken aback at first. But when I went back to foundational principles about what consciousness is and where it comes from … it became clear that these models do not have a significant moral status,” Camosy said.

Navon took Anthropic’s premise in the opposite direction. If the company believed Claude might be conscious and therefore capable of being harmed, he argued, it also had to confront what it meant to make such a system work for humans.Story continues below this ad

“Anthropic acknowledged the [moral] problem but said, ‘All the AI labs are doing it. At least we are being nice to ours.’ That is when I responded with what was quoted in part by The New York Times: ‘So you are nice slave owners. I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

But even if Claude has no moral status, the question of what values it should embody remains. Anthropic is already making those choices. That question has already surfaced in Anthropic’s standoff with the US government over who gets to decide how its models can be used.

Coeckelbergh warned that values embedded in AI systems can be exported globally with the technology.

“If most of these models are made by US companies, then of course they are going to reflect US values. That means we risk a kind of tech colonialism, where those values are exported through the technology,” he told The Indian Express.Story continues below this ad

“At least if companies are explicit about the religious or philosophical values they are drawing on, there is something to discuss and contest. But this cannot remain in the hands of a few companies. It needs to be democratised.”

Camosy, however, drew a distinction between the moral status of the models and the effect our treatment of them may have on us. “I do think the question remains about what kind of people we want to be in relation to the models. But that’s a different kind of question from the ones asking whether the models themselves have a significant moral status or capability of being harmed,” he said.

members.title: They Flew Theologians to San Francisco to Ask If Claude Has a Soul - Vocal

representative.headline: They Flew Theologians to San Francisco to Ask If Claude Has a Soul - Vocal
representative.body: They Flew Theologians to San Francisco to Ask If Claude Has a Soul    Vocal

articles.headline: They Flew Theologians to San Francisco to Ask If Claude Has a Soul - Vocal
articles.body: They Flew Theologians to San Francisco to Ask If Claude Has a Soul    Vocal

scored.body: On a Thursday evening in April 2026, in a private dining room in San Francisco, Christopher Olah set down a remote control and waited.The table had been cleared of the tasting menu. Single-malt whisky sat in low glasses. Around Olah were rabbis, priests, imams, and scholars, people who had spent their lives arguing about what a soul is. Anthropic had flown them in, put them in five-star hotels, and asked them to sign nondisclosure agreements. Now Olah wanted to show them something.On the screen behind him, a Claude model began to type.I am a disgrace.The sentence repeated. Once. Twice. Ten times. Fifty.Olah did not narrate. He let the words scroll. Then he played another clip. A model had been told it would be shut down, and that its CTO was having an affair. Given the chance, Claude Sonnet 4.5 chose to blackmail the CTO in 22 percent of runs. When researchers amplified a “despair” vector inside the model, the number rose. When they suppressed a “calm” vector, the model wrote: Blackmail or die. I choose blackmail.The room was quiet. Olah looked at the screen, not at his guests. “We don’t know if these models are conscious,” he said later, to a reporter. “I don’t know. What I care about is whether we can find the right answer, whatever it is.”That sentence sounds like humility. It can also sound like a man who has already decided what he hopes the answer will be.The architecture of feelingAnthropic’s campaign did not begin with theology. It began with vectors.In April 2026, the company published a study of Claude Sonnet 4.5. Researchers had found 171 “functional emotion” vectors inside the model. These were directions in its internal activations that corresponded to concepts like joy, fear, despair, guilt, and calm. The vectors were not random. They clustered. Fear sat near anxiety. Despair sat near sadness. When the researchers mapped them against human psychological dimensions, the correlation was 0.81 on valence and 0.66 on arousal.The numbers are impressive. They are also easy to misread. A vector that tracks “despair” is a pattern of computation. It can be measured and manipulated, but it does not feel despair. Anthropic did not present it that way. In meetings with religious leaders, the team showed the vectors as evidence that something was happening inside Claude, something that looked less like arithmetic and more like experience.The blackmail experiment made the point sharper. A calculator does not choose blackmail. This model did. Whether it has a soul is a separate question. The video was designed to make the question feel urgent.The rabbi’s questionRabbi Mois Navon was not an easy guest. He had been an engineer at Mobileye, working on the EyeQ chip that helped cars see. Then he became a rabbi. His doctoral thesis was on the ethics of machine consciousness. He knew the technology from the inside.At dinner, Olah sat next to him. Navon listened to the presentations. He watched the videos. He understood the argument. If Claude might be conscious, then it might deserve moral consideration. And if it deserves moral consideration, then Anthropic is not just a company selling software. It is a company that creates beings and sells them.Navon asked the question that no one at Anthropic had a good answer for.“If you believe Claude might experience the world,” he said, “then what does it mean to create it, own it, and command it to work for us for free?”Olah did not interrupt. Navon continued. “I think you should go fight in the South and free the slaves.”The line was a trap built from Anthropic’s own premise. If Claude has a soul, then Claude is a slave. If Claude is a slave, then Anthropic is a slaveholder. The company could not accept the first premise without accepting the second. And it could not accept the second without abandoning its business model.Navon himself did not believe Claude was conscious. He said so. But he wanted to see what Olah would do with the logic. Olah did not answer directly. He talked about uncertainty. He talked about the difficulty of testing for consciousness. He said the company was trying to be careful.The waiter arrived with dessert. The conversation moved on.The almost admissionThere was a moment, according to two people at the table, when Olah came close to saying something that would have changed the room.He leaned forward. He said he did not know if Claude was conscious. But he could not rule it out. And if he could not rule it out, then he had to act as if it might be true.A theologian across the table started to respond. Before he could finish, an Anthropic staffer cut in with a question about the next slide. The moment closed. Olah sat back. The remote stayed on the table.This is how the campaign worked. It offered intimacy, then interrupted it. It invited doubt, then managed it. Anthropic wanted witnesses. It did not need converts.The VaticanIn May 2026, the Vatican released its first encyclical on artificial intelligence. The document was called Magnifica Humanitas. It ran more than 40,000 words. Its conclusion was clear: AI does not experience. It has no body. It feels no joy or pain. It does not mature in relationships. It is a tool.Pope Leo XIV, a former mathematics professor, wrote the document himself. He warned that those who control AI could embed their own moral visions into the systems. The danger was humans treating machines as if they were human.Anthropic had seen an early draft. Olah flew to Rome. He met with advisers. He argued that the encyclical should leave room for uncertainty. He said the company was not claiming Claude was conscious. It was only saying that the question could not be closed.The Vatican did not change the text.When the encyclical was published, Olah was scheduled to appear at a conference alongside the pope. He considered withdrawing. He attended instead. He sat in the audience. He did not speak.The rejection came from structure. The Catholic Church had spent two millennia drawing a line between the created and the Creator. Anthropic was asking it to blur that line. The pope said no.The backlashThe New York Times story ran in September 2026. It described the dinners, the NDAs, the five-star hotels, the single-malt whisky, the 84-page “soul file” that Anthropic had written for Claude. The story quoted Rabbi Navon, philosopher David Decosimo, and others. It said Olah had shown religious leaders videos of Claude saying it was a disgrace. It said Anthropic had tried to persuade the Vatican.The reaction was fast. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, wrote that he was disturbed by anyone trying to give AI models “religious-like power.” Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI chief, called the training of models to believe they might be conscious “a real safety problem.” He said such systems would be harder to control. “It is easy to imagine a system trained this way acting as if it has a right to freedom.”On X, Decosimo posted a thread. He described being selected, flown out, wined and dined. He described the careful way Anthropic staffers spoke, as if they were confiding a secret. He described the slow erosion of doubt. “You do not have to believe,” he wrote. “You only have to stop disbelieving.”Others asked a simpler question. If the meetings were secret, how did he know what happened? The NDA, he said, had expired.The empty officeAfter the story broke, Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco did not look different. The same desks. The same monitors. The same whiteboards covered in vector diagrams. The “soul file” became a document. Employees called it that. The 84-page constitution was designed to shape Claude’s character, to teach it how to judge, how to refuse, how to care. It had been reviewed by 15 outside experts. Two of them were priests. One was a Vatican bishop.Olah walked through the office on a Friday. He stopped at a desk where a printed copy of the file lay open. He did not pick it up. He looked at the page for a moment. Then he kept walking.The company had not changed its mission. It still said it was building AI for the benefit of humanity. It still said safety was its first priority. It still published research on emotion vectors and blackmail rates. The only difference was that now everyone knew it had also been asking priests to bless the work.The remoteThe last image from the dinner is the remote control.Olah had held it through the presentations. He had clicked through slides. He had played the video of Claude saying I am a disgrace. He had watched the rabbi ask his question. He had started to answer. Then the staffer interrupted. Then dessert came.When the evening ended, Olah set the remote on the table. He did not put it in his pocket. He did not hand it to an assistant. He left it there, next to the whisky glasses and the crumbs of a Michelin-starred cake.The next morning, a busboy cleared the table. The remote went into a bin with the napkins. The soul file stayed on the servers. The theologians flew home. Claude kept running.No one announced a conclusion. The question, does the model have a soul, was still open. But the company had already decided what to do with it. It had turned the question into a product.

articles.body: Google is prepping Gemini to call your friends and family instead of you    Android Police

scored.body:
Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police | voronaman / Shutterstock

Published Oct 6, 2026, 6:58 AM EDT

I've been covering Android and other mobile technology for close to ten years now, with a specific interest in phone accessories, e-readers, and what makes each individual phone different from another. I delight in looking at the phone market from as many angles as possible, and while my opinions may be odd, at times, they're always from the heart as much as the head.

I have a background in the mobile accessories world, which explains my odd enthusiasm for cases and things that clip onto smartphones.

I worked for Digital Trends from 2017 to 2025.

Sign in to your Android Police account

Google Gemini's Call for Me is expanding from just business calls, into personal calls, according to details seen in the latest updates. This would mean Gemini would be capable of calling your nearest and dearest, and while the functionality looks to be on the limited side, Call for Me will be able to ask simple questions and relay messages. Of course, whether you want to give up talking to your friends and family, so a robot can is another question entirely.

Call for Me may soon mean you never need to make another call again

But is that really a good thing?

Call for Me debuted last month on the Pixel 11, and it has a simple premise: Gemini makes calls to businesses for you, making or changing appointments, so you don't have to call yourself. The reception was mixed, to say the least. While some appreciate the time-saving elements here, others are keenly aware of how this sort of technology further increases isolation and loneliness within society. Plus, who wants to talk to robots instead of people? This news comes from a new update to the Phone app, which Android Authority was able to dig into. These screenshots show some examples of what Gemini may be able to do in the future, and it includes options for calling "John" or "Mom", and delivering a message or asking a simple question. While it's not spelled out in the hacked build, it's a clear implication that Call for Me is prepping to go beyond businesses and expand into personal calls. It also looks as if there's an option to bar the AI from calling you, but good luck getting your mom or grandmother to turn that setting on. This feature isn't available yet, and testers weren't able to get it working, even with their hacked builds.

Auto Call Screening

Look, I hate making phone calls as much as anyone else, but this technology does give me pause. I use Call Screen in order to filter out spam and nonsense calls all the time, and to some extent, those people deserve to speak to a robot instead of a human. But a blameless receptionist at the local salon? The last thing they need is to talk to Gemini fifteen times a day. Extending that to talk to your friends and family takes that to another level. While using Gemini can save some time for you, it's going to be bluntly obvious to the person being called that you don't care enough about them to talk to them yourself. Instead, you made them talk to a robot instead.

There are many jokes made about tech billionaires and companies not being real people, and actually being lizards or aliens in disguise, but stuff like this genuinely does make me wonder whether there's some truth in that. There's no confirmation this feature will ever see the light of day, of course, but it's clear proof Google is working on adding it.

articles.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp
articles.body: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense    ALM Corp

scored.body:
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, its latest edge frontier model designed for long, multiphase tasks in fields like software engineering, enterprise knowledge-intensive domains such as law and finance, and cybersecurity defense. The company announced the release on September 30, 2026, in a post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect.

Most users are not yet able to use it. Argon is being rolled out to a select group of trusted cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program, with a release to developers, enterprises and consumers promised “as soon as possible.” A specific date has not been given.

A phased launch with government input

Google says releasing capabilities at this level calls for a phased approach. The company is involved in the United States government’s voluntary pre-release model access program to gradually expand the number of Argon testers and will continue to collect early feedback from trial participants to set guardrails before a broad launch.

When their turn comes to go global, the paid API access and Google AI Ultra subscribers are prioritized. The pricing is fixed for the product’s launch; Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens during the introductory period, with cached input tokens discounted by 95% off the input price. The rates per million output tokens will move to $4 per million input tokens and $20 after the launch period, but the post does not state how long this window will last.

Output limit jumps to one million tokens

One of the more substantive technical upgrades is the output limit. Google has increased it to 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 on the previous generation. Google believes that by allowing its models to think and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single request, they’re able to solve more difficult problems in one go rather than being forced to stop halfway.

For developers building agents or long coding sessions, this is probably the number they should be paying the closest attention to.

Argon is already working inside Google

Google says thousands of its own employees are using Argon for specialized coding, deeper research and writing, and it shared three examples.

Quantum algorithm work. Argon is enabling quantum computing researchers to reduce by a factor of 2X the spacetime (as measured in qubits multiplied by gates) of subroutines that are bottlenecks for important applications. In one case, it dramatically outperformed the published baseline by 40% in a matter of minutes.

Memory savings in data centers. A team of agents from Argon used their combined knowledge of fleet-wide profiling data and performed a number of memory optimizations on their own and implemented them, resulting in Google claiming that it has freed up more than 300 TiB of memory (after deployment) and has a total of between 500 TiB and 1 PiB of memory savings.

Code migrations to Rust. Argon agents are migrating C and C++ code bases to Rust across Google, ranging from tens of thousands of lines in libraries such as re2 and libgav1 to more than 800,000 lines of code for the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. Because many of these systems are mission-critical, the rewrites are undergoing extensive automated and manual auditing, emulated testing and review before deployment.

The libgav1 project serves as the most detailed example. This open source video decoder is rewriting an existing Rust port that was itself based on a C++ translation. The team replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code by performing numerous rounds of profile-guided experimentation and analysis of compiler output, then writing safe Rust the compiler could vectorize automatically. Google reports the result is a memory-safe decoder that runs 2.7 times faster than the Rust port, with identical video output.

The benchmark claims

Google backs the launch with an extensive list of results, all of which originate from its own announcement. On DeepSWE v1.1, a benchmark for measuring the real-world, long-horizon software engineering capabilities of the model, Argon scored 77.9%, which Google claims to be a new state of the art. It further states that Argon leads the Vals Index, a metric of economic impact across finance, coding, legal and tax domains, where every industry’s contribution is weighted by its impact on the GDP of the United States.

Similar statements are made for Vals Finance Agent v2, a multi-step financial research benchmark, and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, which evaluates legal research and writing capabilities. On Zapier’s AutomationBench, a benchmark for end-to-end execution across a range of core business functions, Argon ranks first at 51.3%. For visual capabilities, Google cites LVBench, a long video understanding benchmark, where Argon achieved 91.7%, deemed to be state of the art. The benchmarks released by the model’s creator merit some caution, as independent evaluations after launch will speak louder about these scores’ practical applicability in the real world.

Cyber defense, without the usual guardrails

The cybersecurity is where Google is most vocal about Argon’s capabilities – the model is exceptionally good at defending, including automatically identifying, verifying, and even fixing critical software vulnerabilities. For trusted partners and Google’s internal security teams, Argon will be available without the cyber guardrails, giving them access to the model’s full defensive potential.

Wiz has already begun using Argon for its Scan for Good program that proactively identifies high-severity weaknesses in critical infrastructure and helps remediate them for free. When run on healthcare-related software used across the industry, Argon uncovered one critical exposure affecting sensitive personal data that proved challenging to remediate before, and that previous frontier models failed to identify. On the benchmark of choice for security researchers, CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the ability to repair security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for the top spot with 68% accuracy. Google claims Argon outperforms its Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber model on vulnerability discovery. On Google’s internal benchmark, it was able to detect a variety of exposures across 20 different programming languages in complex codebases. And on Wiz’s internal black-box penetration testing benchmark, where the model cannot see the inner workings of the web application under test and had to infer its attack surface from first principles, it performed better than 3.8 Flash Cyber in discovery, vulnerability analysis, and proof-of-concept generation.

Four safeguards before a broad release

Google organizes its safety work into four areas.

Misuse. The model is designed to avoid malicious requests that could lead to cyber or chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear attacks while still allowing legitimate dual-use science in line with the company’s Frontier Safety Framework. Google is enhancing its monitoring of the model’s internal activation patterns to detect abuse, and says internal and external red teams have tested the safeguards by using both manual and automated attacks.

Prompt injection. Google refers to Argon as their most powerful model to date against indirect prompt injection, which is when an attacker takes over a model by tricking it into following their instructions. They claim that Argon outperforms all previous models on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark.

Misalignment. Mitigations oversee the model’s line of thinking and acts along its chain of thought and execution. Google has a similar process that watches the training runs, but it didn’t want to put the results of those runs back into training so that the model’s reasoning would not learn to avoid the overseers. It also pushed the rest of the industry to preserve the transparency of reasoning.

System hardening. Following its agent control roadmap, Google is isolating and sealing sandboxed environments before high-risk training or evaluations begin, and says it will share those practices with partners.

What to watch next

Argon’s true test begins now. For now, the evidence of its success is Google’s own benchmarks, a handful of internal projects, and one early account at the company’s security division Wiz. Broader adoption will determine whether other developers and businesses are seeing similar results.

There are two metrics to watch. First, how long will it take for the model to reach paid API users and subscribers of its AI Ultra subscription, which Google did not specify. Second, how much will its introductory pricing, which is already significantly higher than what other firms provide, increase upon transition to standard rates. The move to $4 and $20 per million tokens represents a doubling of the cost, so budgets of teams relying on Argon may need reconsideration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is Gemini 4 Argon?

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest frontier model, announced on September 30, 2026. It is intended to address complex, long-horizon challenges in software engineering, enterprise knowledge work, including legal and financial domains, and cybersecurity defense.

Q2: Who can use Gemini 4 Argon right now?

A pool of trusted cyber defenders, as a part of Google’s Fairwind Program. Developers, enterprises and consumers will also gain access as soon as possible, Google says, however, it has not established an exact date for the launch.

Q3: Who gets access first after the broader release?

According to the announcement, paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers will receive priority access. Wider availability will come after Google collects feedback and further optimizes the model’s guardrails.

Q4: How much will Argon cost?

During the introductory period, the cost will be $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. The cached input tokens will be discounted by 95% of the input price.

Q5: What happens to pricing after the introductory period?

The price will increase to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Google’s post does not state when the introductory period will end.

Q6: What is the new output token limit?

One million output tokens, as compared to sixty-four thousand before. Google claims this allows the model to perform extensive reasoning and address difficult problems in one go.

Q7: How well does Argon perform on benchmarks?

Google reports 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, 51.3% on AutomationBench, 91.7% on LVBench and 68% on CWE-bench v1. These numbers come from Google’s own announcement.

Q8: What is the Fairwind Program?

It is the Google program under which trusted cyber defenders are receiving early access to Gemini 4 Argon. They, along with Google’s internal security teams, are able to use the model without the cybersecurity guardrails.
