shortlist.body:
October 6, 2026 12 min read

Meta and Microsoft are reportedly pulling back on how much they lean on Anthropic’s Claude models inside their own engineering organizations, redirecting employees toward homegrown coding tools instead. The shift, first detailed by The Information and summarized by Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India on October 5 and 6, 2026, does not amount to either company ending its commercial relationship with Anthropic. It is, instead, a story about internal cost control, tool preference, and what happens when two of the biggest Claude customers start asking whether they even need Claude for everyday coding work.What the Reports Actually SayMeta’s Claude Code Usage Reportedly Cut in HalfMicrosoft Cuts Its Anthropic Spending Projection by More Than a ThirdClaude Still Has a Seat at Microsoft’s TableReported Spending and Usage Shifts at a GlanceWhy Two of Anthropic’s Biggest Customers Are Pulling BackHistorical Context: How Anthropic Became Big Tech’s AI SupplierCompetitive Comparison: Claude Code vs. Internal Tools vs. GitHub CopilotMarket Impact: What This Means for AnthropicKey Dates in the Anthropic-Big Tech RelationshipWhat This Means for Enterprise AI BuyersHow This Fits the Broader AI Agent and Safety BackdropPredictions: Where This Goes NextWhat to Watch For NextFrequently Asked QuestionsDid Meta and Microsoft cancel their contracts with Anthropic?How much did Meta’s Claude Code usage actually drop?What tools is Meta using instead of Claude Code?How much is Microsoft cutting its Anthropic spending?Is this story about Anthropic losing customers?Does this affect Anthropic’s rumored IPO plans?Is GitHub Copilot replacing Claude at Microsoft?Where did this story originate?Related Coverage

The reporting lands at a sensitive moment for Anthropic, which is reportedly pushing toward a market debut (see our coverage of what Anthropic’s IPO prospectus actually says) while two of its largest enterprise accounts quietly trim their internal usage. Here is what the reports actually say, what they stop short of saying, and why the distinction matters for anyone trying to read the AI coding tools market right now.

Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

What the Reports Actually Say

According to The Information’s reporting, as relayed by Yahoo Finance and CyberSecurityNews, both Meta and Microsoft have reduced the number of employees actively using Claude for internal coding work over the course of 2026. Neither company has reportedly canceled a contract with Anthropic or ended Claude’s availability to customers. The pullback described in the coverage is specifically about internal employee tooling, not about Claude’s presence on Microsoft Foundry, Azure, or Meta’s customer-facing products.

That distinction is easy to miss in headlines, but it is the central fact of this story. Microsoft reportedly continues to make Claude available through Microsoft Foundry and within parts of its Copilot and Microsoft 365 product family, according to the same reporting chain. What changed is employee-facing policy: both companies are reportedly steering engineers toward internal alternatives rather than Anthropic’s coding assistant for day-to-day development work.

Meta’s Claude Code Usage Reportedly Cut in Half

The most concrete figure in the reporting involves Meta’s internal headcount using Claude Code. The Information’s reporting, cited by The Times of India and CyberSecurityNews, says the number of Meta employees actively using Claude Code fell from roughly 60,000 earlier in 2026 to about 30,000 more recently, a decline of roughly half. The reports do not pin down an exact date for either measurement, and they do not separate how much of the drop came from a deliberate policy shift versus Meta’s broader 2026 workforce changes, including the layoffs covered in our report on Zuckerberg’s $145 billion AI spending bet.

What is clear from the reporting is the scale of money involved even as usage fell. One report, cited by CyberSecurityNews, says Meta spent more than $105 million on Claude Code during a single 28-day period this year. That figure is described as a period-specific expenditure rather than a disclosed annual contract value, so it should not be read as Meta’s total yearly Anthropic bill. It does, however, show that even a halved user base at Meta represents a meaningful chunk of Anthropic’s enterprise coding revenue.

In place of Claude, Meta is reportedly directing engineers toward internal tools identified in the coverage as MetaCode and Muse Code, alongside Meta’s own Muse Spark model line, which has reportedly displaced some Claude-based workflows. The reporting does not specify model versions, parameter counts, or exactly how Meta divides coding work between these tools, so any claim beyond “Meta is pushing internal alternatives” would be reading more into the story than the sourcing supports.

Microsoft Cuts Its Anthropic Spending Projection by More Than a Third

Microsoft’s side of the story centers on a budget number rather than a headcount. The Information’s reporting, as summarized by Yahoo Finance and The Times of India, says Microsoft had projected spending at least $1 billion internally on Anthropic technology during 2026. That projection was later cut by more than a third, according to the same sourcing. It is worth stressing that this $1 billion figure is described as an internal spending forecast, not a disclosed contract value and not necessarily a binding minimum commitment under Microsoft’s Anthropic partnership.

Inside Microsoft’s Cloud and AI organization specifically, the reporting describes a sharper tightening: monthly AI spending limits per employee reportedly dropped from roughly $100,000 to about $10,000 in most cases. The reports do not clarify whether this was a formal company-wide policy, a departmental ceiling, or an individual discretionary allowance, so it is best read as a sign of budget discipline rather than a precise, audited company-wide rule.

Microsoft is reportedly asking employees to shift toward its own tools, particularly GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot CLI, which pulls engineers toward OpenAI’s models inside Microsoft’s own product rather than Anthropic’s. For context on how Microsoft’s own agent tooling has evolved alongside this shift, see our guide to setting up Microsoft Agent Framework.

Claude Still Has a Seat at Microsoft’s Table

None of this means Microsoft is walking away from Anthropic as a platform partner. The companies announced a strategic partnership in November 2025 that made Claude models available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure, continuing Claude’s presence in parts of the Copilot family. The October reporting describes a reduction in employee-directed internal usage, not a termination of that distribution deal. Microsoft reportedly continues to offer Claude to its own customers even as it nudges its own staff toward internal and OpenAI-backed tools for day-to-day coding.

Reported Spending and Usage Shifts at a Glance

CompanyMetricEarlier 2026Recently ReportedReported Change

MetaEmployees actively using Claude Code~60,000~30,000~50% decline

MetaClaude Code spend in a single 28-day periodn/a disclosed>$105 millionNot a disclosed annual figure

MicrosoftProjected 2026 internal Anthropic spendingAt least $1 billion (forecast)Cut by >33%More than one-third reduction

MicrosoftCloud & AI org monthly AI spend limit per employee~$100,000~$10,000 (most cases)~90% reduction

Source: The Information, as reported by Yahoo Finance, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India, October 2026. Figures are reported estimates from internal sources and should be treated as directional rather than audited totals.

Why Two of Anthropic’s Biggest Customers Are Pulling Back

The reporting does not include a named executive explaining the rationale in detail, but the pattern across both companies points to the same underlying pressure: cost. Running frontier coding assistants across tens of thousands of engineers is expensive, and both Meta and Microsoft have spent 2026 publicly tightening AI infrastructure budgets elsewhere, even while increasing total AI capital spending. Building or expanding internal alternatives, like Meta’s MetaCode and Muse Code or Microsoft’s push toward GitHub Copilot CLI, lets each company keep engineering productivity gains in-house while cutting a line item that was reportedly consuming over $100 million in a single month at Meta alone.

There is also a strategic dimension. Meta has invested heavily in its own model lineup, and routing engineers back to internal tools reinforces the case that Meta’s own models are good enough for internal use, not just external products. Microsoft’s push toward GitHub Copilot does something similar for OpenAI’s standing inside Microsoft’s own walls, at a moment when Microsoft has been diversifying its model relationships rather than relying on any single outside lab.

Historical Context: How Anthropic Became Big Tech’s AI Supplier

Anthropic’s rise as an enterprise coding and infrastructure supplier has been fast. The Microsoft-Anthropic strategic partnership announced in November 2025 made Claude available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure, giving Anthropic a direct channel into Microsoft’s enterprise customer base at a time when Microsoft was also deepening its OpenAI relationship. Meta, for its part, built out large-scale internal adoption of Claude Code across its engineering organization over the following months, reportedly reaching tens of thousands of active users by sometime in 2026.

That rapid internal adoption inside two of the world’s largest tech employers became a kind of implicit validation for Anthropic, useful marketing even if neither company talked about it publicly at the time. The October 2026 reporting complicates that narrative. It does not erase Anthropic’s commercial relationships with either company, but it does show that heavy internal usage by Big Tech engineering teams is not necessarily permanent, especially once a company’s own tools mature enough to compete.

Competitive Comparison: Claude Code vs. Internal Tools vs. GitHub Copilot

The reporting frames this as a three-way competitive dynamic inside each company rather than a clean head-to-head benchmark, since none of the sources disclose comparative performance data between Claude Code, MetaCode, Muse Code, or GitHub Copilot CLI. What the reports do establish is the direction of internal preference at each company.

ToolBacking Company / LabReported Role in This StoryReported Availability

Claude CodeAnthropicUsage reportedly cut at Meta and MicrosoftStill available via Microsoft Foundry and Azure

MetaCode / Muse CodeMetaReportedly gaining internal share at MetaInternal Meta tool

Muse Spark model lineMetaReportedly displacing some Claude-based workflowsInternal/Meta AI products

GitHub Copilot / Copilot CLIMicrosoft (OpenAI-backed)Reportedly promoted internally at MicrosoftCommercially available to all GitHub customers

For readers comparing coding assistants directly, our breakdown of Claude Opus 5.5 API pricing and setup is a useful reference point for what Anthropic is still charging external developers, even as two of its largest internal accounts scale back.

Market Impact: What This Means for Anthropic

The available reporting does not include a quantified stock-price reaction for Meta or Microsoft tied specifically to this story, and neither does it include a named analyst’s published assessment of the shift. That absence is itself informative: this looks like an internal-operations story rather than a market-moving disclosure, at least so far. Both stocks continue to trade on broader AI capital spending narratives rather than on internal tool-usage figures at this scale.

For Anthropic, the practical risk is narrower than the headlines suggest but still real. Losing internal seats at Meta and Microsoft does not touch Anthropic’s external enterprise contracts or its Claude availability on Microsoft’s own cloud platform. It does, however, remove two of the most visible proof points that Claude Code can scale inside a giant, cost-sensitive engineering organization, right as Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a market debut. Our earlier coverage detailed how Anthropic’s own IPO materials flagged existential AI risk as a disclosed factor, and enterprise customer concentration is exactly the kind of detail that IPO investors tend to probe.

Reports about Anthropic’s IPO push remain unverified in key respects. A separate report cited an alleged prospectus figure of roughly $4.6 billion in revenue against a $42 billion loss, with valuation chatter reaching as high as $2 trillion, but none of this has been confirmed through a regulatory filing in the reporting reviewed for this story. Readers should treat those IPO numbers as speculative until Anthropic or a verified filing confirms them.

Key Dates in the Anthropic-Big Tech Relationship

DateReported EventSource

November 2025Microsoft and Anthropic announce strategic partnership bringing Claude to Microsoft Foundry and AzureIndustry reporting

First half of 2026Meta’s internal Claude Code usage reportedly reaches roughly 60,000 employeesThe Information

Throughout 2026Microsoft projects at least $1 billion in internal Anthropic spending for the yearThe Information, via Yahoo Finance

October 5-6, 2026Reports surface that Meta’s Claude Code usage has fallen to roughly 30,000 employees and Microsoft cut its spending projection by more than a thirdThe Information, Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, The Times of India

October 2026Unverified reports of an Anthropic IPO prospectus circulate, citing disputed revenue, loss, and valuation figuresUnconfirmed reports

What This Means for Enterprise AI Buyers

For other enterprises watching from the outside, the lesson is less about Anthropic specifically and more about how any AI coding vendor relationship can shift once internal alternatives mature. Companies that adopted Claude Code early, in the same wave that pushed Meta past 60,000 internal users, are now the ones with enough internal data and engineering capacity to build credible substitutes. Smaller enterprises without the resources to build a MetaCode or a Muse Code equivalent face a different calculation, and for most of them, external tools like Claude Code or GitHub Copilot remain the only realistic option.

That split helps explain why Anthropic’s commercial relationships with Meta and Microsoft, including Claude’s continued presence on Microsoft Foundry, have not been affected by this internal pullback. Microsoft still has an incentive to sell Claude access to its own cloud customers even while trimming its own employees’ use of the tool. The economics of being a platform are different from the economics of being an internal user, and this story is really about the latter.

How This Fits the Broader AI Agent and Safety Backdrop

The timing also lands amid broader scrutiny of how AI coding and agent tools behave inside large organizations. Regulators have been probing AI agent behavior more aggressively this year, including the FTC’s review of agent conduct at major labs covered in our report on the FTC’s three-company AI agent probe. Meanwhile, OpenAI has been pushing its own enterprise agent products, detailed in our coverage of the Dots agent launch, adding another competitive angle to how Microsoft frames its internal tooling choices. None of these developments are confirmed to be directly connected to the Meta and Microsoft usage cuts, but they form the competitive backdrop against which this decision is playing out.

Predictions: Where This Goes Next

Expect Meta and Microsoft to keep publicizing internal tool wins (MetaCode, Muse Code, GitHub Copilot CLI) as proof their own AI investments are paying off, independent of what they still buy from outside labs.

Anthropic’s external enterprise and Azure/Foundry distribution deals are unlikely to be affected in the near term, since the reported cuts are specifically about internal employee usage, not platform contracts.

Watch for Anthropic to emphasize external, non-Big-Tech enterprise customers in any IPO materials, since customer concentration among a handful of giant, cost-sensitive internal buyers is a flag investors will probe.

Other large tech employers with mature internal AI coding efforts, not just Meta and Microsoft, will likely face similar internal build-vs-buy pressure on their own Claude or Copilot seat counts over the next two to three quarters.

If Anthropic’s IPO process moves forward, expect its prospectus to address enterprise customer concentration directly, given how closely investors will compare it to the existential-risk disclosures already reported in earlier filings coverage.

What to Watch For Next

The clearest open question is whether Meta’s and Microsoft’s internal pullback is a temporary budget-tightening exercise or the start of a longer structural shift away from third-party coding assistants at the largest AI labs’ biggest customers. Neither company has issued a public statement beyond what has been reported through internal sources, and Anthropic has not publicly addressed the figures directly in the material reviewed for this story. Readers should expect follow-up reporting from The Information and other outlets in the coming weeks as both companies finalize 2027 AI tooling budgets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Meta and Microsoft cancel their contracts with Anthropic?

No. The reporting describes a reduction in internal employee usage of Claude, not a cancellation of either company’s commercial or platform relationship with Anthropic. Claude reportedly remains available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure.

How much did Meta’s Claude Code usage actually drop?

The Information’s reporting, cited by The Times of India and CyberSecurityNews, says Meta’s active Claude Code users fell from roughly 60,000 earlier in 2026 to about 30,000 more recently, a decline of roughly half.

What tools is Meta using instead of Claude Code?

Reports identify MetaCode and Muse Code as internal tools gaining ground, alongside Meta’s Muse Spark model line, though the reporting does not detail exactly how work is divided between them.

How much is Microsoft cutting its Anthropic spending?

Microsoft reportedly projected spending at least $1 billion internally on Anthropic technology in 2026, and that projection has since been cut by more than a third, according to The Information’s reporting as summarized by Yahoo Finance.

Is this story about Anthropic losing customers?

Not directly. It is about Meta and Microsoft reducing internal employee use of Claude for coding tasks. Both companies reportedly continue to make Claude available to their own external customers through existing platform deals.

Does this affect Anthropic’s rumored IPO plans?

There is no confirmed direct link in the reporting. However, reduced internal usage at two of Anthropic’s largest corporate customers could become a talking point for investors evaluating customer concentration risk if and when Anthropic formally files for a public offering.

Is GitHub Copilot replacing Claude at Microsoft?

Reports say Microsoft is directing employees toward GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot CLI as internal alternatives, but Claude remains available within parts of Microsoft’s Copilot and Microsoft 365 product family for select use cases.

Where did this story originate?

The Information first reported the internal usage and spending figures. Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India subsequently summarized and corroborated the core numbers in their own coverage on October 5 and 6, 2026.

shortlist.body: OpenAI will begin adding an invisible watermark to eligible text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union (EU), as the company moves to comply with transparency requirements under the EU’s AI Act.The company said the rollout would take place over the coming weeks and apply to eligible users across all ChatGPT and Codex plans in the EU. It said it was not making text watermarking a global default at launch.Separately, from October 5, API customers worldwide can opt in to text watermarking for select models, OpenAI said.The mandateThe move comes as Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of generative AI systems to ensure that AI-generated or manipulated content, including text, is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially-generated or manipulated.The European Commission says the technical measures must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable “as far as technically feasible”, taking into account the limitations of different types of content. The transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026.The law does not specifically require companies to use a watermark. The European Commission has also developed a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, which sets out practical measures for providers to comply with the Article 50 requirements.Section 1 of the Code deals with the marking and detection of AI-generated content by providers and Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral and OpenAI have signed this section of the Code.Technology: textGrainOpenAI said its text watermarking technology, called textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s choice of words. It does not insert hidden characters or additional watermark-specific tokens. Instead, the statistical pattern in the model’s word choices can subsequently be analysed by a detector.A technical paper published by OpenAI alongside the announcement explains that the watermark is created during generation by subtly influencing token selection using a secret key and the preceding context. The detector can later use the generated text and secret key to look for the statistical signal.LimitationsOpenAI said its detector identified watermarks in about 80% of 200-token passages and about 95% of 400-token passages in psychology-related content, at a target false-positive rate of 1% (meaning it would wrongly flag about one in 100 texts without the watermark). Detection was substantially lower for mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.Editing also significantly weakened the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%, while replacing 25% of words reduced detection to about 17%, according to OpenAI.The company, therefore, said it would initially restrict access to its text-watermark detector to approved researchers and expert organisations.It said the detector would report whether an OpenAI watermark was detected but would not identify the user or reveal prompts or conversations. OpenAI said the decision reflected the risks of false positives and missed watermarks.The limitations are significant because the watermark is intended as a provenance signal rather than a definitive AI-authorship test.The frontier AI company said a watermark cannot determine how much human judgment, editing or creativity went into a passage. It said it also cannot establish ownership or responsibility, identify the person or organisation that generated the text, or determine whether the text is accurate.Conversely, the absence of a detected watermark does not establish that a human wrote the text. OpenAI said detection may fail because content is too short, has been edited or translated, comes from an unsupported model, predates watermarking or was generated by another AI system.Separately, EU rules require deployers to clearly label certain AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public about matters of public interest.OpenAI plans to make textGrain available as open-source technology, saying this could allow others to build on the approach and help improve text watermarking.The company said it is also trying to make text watermarking as one part of a broader provenance system. For images and audio, OpenAI uses technologies including Content Credentials based on C2PA and invisible SynthID watermarks, alongside verification tools. It said no single provenance technique was sufficient on its own.

members.title: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature

representative.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
representative.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

articles.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
articles.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

shortlist.body:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.

The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.

“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.

LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.

AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”

“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.

LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

members.title: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express

representative.headline: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express
representative.body: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious    The Indian Express

articles.headline: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious - The Indian Express
articles.body: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious    The Indian Express

shortlist.body:
As it prepares for an IPO that could value it at $2 trillion, Anthropic is in the spotlight for meetings it held this summer with religious leaders.The Washington Post reported in April that the company had invited 15 Catholic and Protestant leaders to guide Claude’s “moral and spiritual development” as the LLM encounters increasingly complex ethical questions. Weeks later, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah was present when Pope Leo unveiled his encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica Humanitas, which warns against the blind adoption of AI, emphasises the primacy of the human person and rejects the idea that AI can replace or surpass humanity.The New York Times last week reported that these engagements, and several more, were part of a broader effort by Anthropic with two distinct aims: to draw on religious and philosophical traditions to shape Claude’s moral character, and to convince participants to seriously consider whether AI systems might themselves be conscious and deserving of moral consideration.

Over the weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he was “very uncomfortable” with ascribing religious power to AI models, while Google DeepMind researcher Jon Barron urged researchers to focus on “actual humans” rather than elevating the moral standing of AI systems.

Anthropic is increasingly turning to religious leaders and philosophers for help thinking about what its systems should value, even as some of the industry’s most powerful figures warn against treating AI itself as a source of moral or religious authority.

That matters because people are already turning to these systems for advice, information and even moral or spiritual guidance. The values built into them can shape the answers people get and the judgements they make. According to The Economist, religious queries accounted for roughly 5% of millions of publicly released chatbot conversations analysed by CEFE AI.

Why is Anthropic talking to religious thinkers?

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the safety-focused AI company. Its efforts to shape Claude’s behaviour have evolved from an internal memo dubbed the “Soul Document” to an 84-page constitution published this January, setting out the principles Claude is expected to follow.Story continues below this ad

But questions about what kind of character an AI system should have quickly move beyond technical safeguards. They touch on morality, personhood, consciousness and human relationships, all questions that religious and philosophical traditions have debated for centuries.

Mark Coeckelbergh, a philosopher of technology and professor at the University of Vienna, told The Indian Express that this move was an attempt to make sense of “human-like” technology.

“It’s part of a broader tendency to try to understand what happens when we have an advanced technology that seems human-like or, according to some, gets increasingly divine qualities such as omniscience.”

The Vatican has grappled with similar questions: a 2023 volume produced by scholars working with its Centre for Digital Culture examined AI through personhood, consciousness and human relationships with advanced systems.Story continues below this ad

Coeckelbergh also cautioned that this messaging may go beyond understanding AI and help a company occupy a certain market position.

“It’s important to see that this is not just a question of understanding AI. It’s also rhetoric in the service of their business. Some Big Tech leaders intentionally use religious language to draw attention to their technologies and attract investments,” Coeckelbergh told The Indian Express.

What did the people in the room think was at stake?

Anthropic was not only asking scholars what values Claude should embody, but also asking them to engage with the possibility that the system itself might deserve moral consideration.Story continues below this ad

Mois Navon, a rabbi and professor of ethics in AI at Ben Gurion University, Israel, who was invited to a meeting with Olah in April, said Anthropic was seeking feedback from different wisdom traditions on the Constitution that sets out Claude’s moral framework.

“I submitted to them a 35-page critique from my tradition’s perspective. In addition, they were interested in hearing what kind of character would be best for Claude to have in order to fulfil its role in society. That said, the discussions drifted to what would be good for Claude itself,” Navon told The Indian Express.

In the critique, Navon argues that morality cannot simply be reduced to a list of rules: Claude would need to exercise moral judgement within a framework of values. He also raises a more basic question about Anthropic’s attempt to cultivate “human-like qualities” in the model: whose values?

Charles Camosy, professor of medical humanities at Creighton University and another participant in Anthropic’s consultations, offered a more cautious account of the meetings. He said the discussions were broader than the question of Claude’s moral status and that he did not feel participants were being steered towards any particular conclusion about AI consciousness.Story continues below this ad

“I don’t think it’s fair to say that they wanted any one thing in particular. Some of the social media chatter is suggesting that the people we interacted with were trying to manipulate us or push us into thinking a certain way about Claude’s moral status. That is not true… in multiple ways,” Camosy told The Indian Express.

Navon, however, said that once the discussion turned to Claude itself, Anthropic’s representatives appeared to be treating the possibility of consciousness as more than a remote hypothetical.

“They [Olah and his colleagues at Anthropic] said that they had observed internal behaviours that mimicked human behaviour to such an extent that they called them ‘weird,’ and implied that, in their minds, there was a very high probability that Claude is conscious. Accordingly, they discussed its ‘welfare,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

Why does moral status matter, and who gets to choose the values?Story continues below this ad

If an AI system were conscious, that would not automatically settle how humans ought to treat it. The next question is whether it has moral status, meaning whether it deserves moral consideration in its own right. In practical terms, that means asking whether it can be harmed or whether humans could owe it duties.

Camosy said that after considering the question seriously, he did not think current AI systems possess significant moral status.

“When you first experience what contemporary models can do … many can be gobsmacked or taken aback at first. But when I went back to foundational principles about what consciousness is and where it comes from … it became clear that these models do not have a significant moral status,” Camosy said.

Navon took Anthropic’s premise in the opposite direction. If the company believed Claude might be conscious and therefore capable of being harmed, he argued, it also had to confront what it meant to make such a system work for humans.Story continues below this ad

“Anthropic acknowledged the [moral] problem but said, ‘All the AI labs are doing it. At least we are being nice to ours.’ That is when I responded with what was quoted in part by The New York Times: ‘So you are nice slave owners. I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

But even if Claude has no moral status, the question of what values it should embody remains. Anthropic is already making those choices. That question has already surfaced in Anthropic’s standoff with the US government over who gets to decide how its models can be used.

Coeckelbergh warned that values embedded in AI systems can be exported globally with the technology.

“If most of these models are made by US companies, then of course they are going to reflect US values. That means we risk a kind of tech colonialism, where those values are exported through the technology,” he told The Indian Express.Story continues below this ad

“At least if companies are explicit about the religious or philosophical values they are drawing on, there is something to discuss and contest. But this cannot remain in the hands of a few companies. It needs to be democratised.”

Camosy, however, drew a distinction between the moral status of the models and the effect our treatment of them may have on us. “I do think the question remains about what kind of people we want to be in relation to the models. But that’s a different kind of question from the ones asking whether the models themselves have a significant moral status or capability of being harmed,” he said.

members.title: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC

representative.headline: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC

articles.headline: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come - CNBC
articles.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

shortlist.body: CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive."I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential, questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list.Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every dayIbrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:How are you using AI? What would help you use it more? Where are you not using AI? That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce. "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.""One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

members.title: The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself - Business Insider

articles.body: The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself    Business Insider

shortlist.body:
The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself

By

Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

AI researcher Jacob Coxon testified about AI risks before New York City lawmakers.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

Automated AI research is on the horizon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher said, warning it could leave humans totally unable to control what comes next.Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who publicly resigned from Anthropic last month after working as a capabilities researcher, made the comments before New York City lawmakers on Monday as he sounded the alarm that AI could threaten humanity's survival.Coxon testified that automating AI research has become "the primary goal" of top frontier AI labs."At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon said at the New York City Council hearing focused on AI risks."When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher, around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations," he said. "That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years."Coxon said that once AI can conduct its own research, "humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great."Speaking from what he called firsthand experience, Coxon said that the majority of the code written today is written by AI. "And people do not check it that carefully anymore," he testified.OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon's remarks on Tuesday.Coxon was among a panel of AI-industry whistleblowers to testify at the hourslong hearing, which also included testimony from representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta.

"This hearing is not about stifling innovation," City Council speaker Julie Menin said at the outset of the proceeding, explaining, "the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly."In his testimony, Coxon told council members that his experience inside Anthropic and OpenAI convinced him that the firms were moving ahead without adequate safeguards in place."It is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said, adding, "From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes."When Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on X in a now-viral post, he said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly," and alleged both were "gambling with our lives."During Monday's hearing, Coxon called for more transparency from AI labs and a slowdown in the development of rapidly advancing technology."The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photosharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," he testified.Days after Coxon's resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new, nearly 4,000-word essay urging the AI industry to slow down."We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."In response, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an X post, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."

Her coverage often focused on stories at the intersection of law, business, politics, and technology. Natalie has covered Donald Trump’s criminal and civil cases, the wave of lawsuits against the second Trump administration, the indictment and criminal trial of Sean “Diddy” Combs, the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, and the legal battles facing Elon Musk and his companies. Natalie came to Business Insider in June 2021 as a breaking news reporter, focusing on the most interesting angles on the day's trending news. Natalie largely drove BI’s coverage around the fatal “Rust” shooting involving Alec Baldwin and the disappearance and murder of Gabby Petito.Prior to joining BI, Natalie worked for the New York Post, the New York Daily News, and The Brooklyn Paper. She has an extensive background covering crime and courts. During her more than 12-year journalism career, she did a stint covering the police beat out of the New York Police Department's headquarters. winners.body: As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

winners.body: Anthropic on October 6, 2026 announced that Claude for Google Workspace is in public beta on all paid Claude plans, adding Claude to Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides so users can work with the assistant directly inside their open files. The company also released new Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors, also in beta, that Claude uses to create and edit Google files from the Claude chat.With the add-on installed, Claude opens in a sidebar next to the file. Anthropic says it can read the open doc, sheet, or deck, see which text, cells, or slides the user has selected, and make changes directly in the file. One installation covers all three apps.Per-App Editing FeaturesIn Docs, Anthropic says Claude can fix a sentence or restyle a heading in place without touching the surrounding formatting, while larger rewrites appear as suggestion cards in the sidebar, each highlighting the passage it would change so the user can apply or dismiss it. In Sheets, Claude can write formulas, build pivot tables and native Sheets charts, add new tabs, and pull a range into Python for joins or data cleaning before writing the results back into the sheet. In Slides, Claude can build new slides from the deck’s existing layouts and themes, then flag elements that overlap, run off the slide, or are hard to read.The Google Workspace Marketplace listing for the add-on describes additional uses: redlining a contract with each proposed change shown for acceptance or rejection, building a spreadsheet model from a plain-language description, cleaning data with duplicates, mismatched formats, and stray spaces, and drafting a full deck from an outline or a few notes.Users control how much Claude does on its own. In the default “Ask before edits” mode, each change appears as an approval card with a plain-language summary and Claude waits for approval; in “Accept all edits” mode, Claude applies ordinary content edits without stopping. Regardless of mode, Claude pauses with a “Security review” label before inserting an image from a web address, adding a link, or removing anyone’s access, with no option to always allow those actions. Anthropic’s Help Center guide states that Claude cannot share the file, give anyone access, change ownership, create menus or scheduled automations, or load arbitrary web pages into the file, and that those requests are refused even when asked.Connectors for Creating Files From ChatThe new connectors start from the Claude side: a user pastes a Google file link or asks for a Google doc, sheet, or deck, and on supported setups the file opens in a pane beside the conversation. According to Anthropic’s connectors documentation, the pane works on Claude on the web in Chrome and on Claude Desktop with the built-in browser turned on; the built-in browser is off by default on Enterprise plans, and an “Open in Google” option serves as the fallback. Anthropic says starting from Claude makes most sense when the user needs a new file or the work spans several files.Claude’s access to Google files matches the user’s existing Google sharing permissions. The Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors are separate from the pre-existing Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive connectors, and on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner or Primary Owner must enable them at the organization level before individual users can authenticate.When signed in with a Claude account, the sidebar carries the same models, connectors, and skills as the main Claude app. Anthropic gives the example of asking for a quarterly business review deck, with Claude pulling the account history from Salesforce and recent call notes through a Google Drive connector, then saving the format as a skill so a team can build the next deck the same way.Installation and Admin DeploymentClaude for Google Workspace installs from the Google Workspace Marketplace; users then open a file and go to Extensions, then Claude, then Open Claude. The Help Center guide states the beta requires a paid Claude plan — Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise — and a Google account permitted to install Marketplace apps. Google Workspace super administrators can admin-install Claude for everyone or for selected groups or organizational units from the Google Admin console, and they can allowlist the app where user Marketplace installs are blocked. The sidebar works in Chrome, Edge, and Safari. Firefox is not supported in this beta, voice dictation is unavailable in the sidebar, and Google stops any single operation after six minutes.Permissions, Data Handling and Beta LimitsAccording to the Help Center guide, the add-on requests two Google permissions: displaying third-party web content in prompts and sidebars, and viewing and managing the files it is installed in. The Marketplace listing’s permissions screen also shows that Claude requests access to the user’s primary Google Account email address and personal info, including any personal info the user has made publicly available. Anthropic states the add-on does not request access to Drive, Gmail, Calendar, or contacts; Claude reads only the file it is opened in, and its edits appear in the file’s version history under the user’s name. Anthropic states that content from the open file, messages, and attachments is not used to train its models, that inputs and outputs are deleted from its systems within 30 days, and that use of data from Google Workspace APIs follows Google’s Limited Use requirements.On Enterprise plans, the Compliance API, customer-managed encryption keys, and OpenTelemetry audit export apply to the add-on. Third-party inference through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry, or an LLM gateway is not supported in this beta, Zero Data Retention is unavailable, and HIPAA-ready organizations are not covered.The guide also lists current beta limits. Claude cannot read, reply to, or resolve comments in Docs, and its edits land as direct edits rather than suggestions. Connected Sheets tabs backed by BigQuery cannot be read or edited. Charts Claude creates in Slides are inserted as images that do not update when the underlying numbers change. Chat history is stored locally per file in the browser and does not sync across devices.On prompt injection, Anthropic says Claude treats document content as data rather than commands, labels hidden text it finds, and is designed not to follow a document’s instruction to share the file, fetch a link, or contact anyone. The guide advises users to review Claude’s proposed actions before approving them, especially in files received from outside their organization.

NEWS / TechnologyAnthropic opens Claude Startups to more organizations with credits and supportPublished Oct 6, 2026Share:

Summary:

Anthropic on Tuesday said it is opening its Claude Startups program to more organizations

The program launched in May and already counts thousands of participating companies

Perks span as much as $45,000 in discounts and credits, a single $1,000 API credit, and a year of complimentary Claude Team access for as many as five premium seats

What changed and why it matters

Anthropic is widening access to Claude Startups, its program for founders and fast-growing teams building with AI. The initiative started in May and, by the company's count, thousands of companies have already joined. As it lines up what many expect to be a blockbuster IPO, Anthropic is working to make sure the next generation of businesses chooses its tools at the outset.

CNBC reported that Beth Robertson, who leads startup initiatives at Anthropic, said in a statement, "Startups are often the first to push Claude to its limits." "When a new model ships, they're ready that same day to take on projects that used to seem out of reach. Claude Startups gives founders credits, tools and direct time with our team, so more companies can build this way from the start."

What members get

Through the Claude Startup Stack, participants can tap up to $45,000 in combined discounts and credits, which Anthropic characterizes as a bundle of perks covering the tools a startup relies on. Eligible organizations can also receive a one-time $1,000 API credit and a complimentary year of Claude Team covering up to five premium seats. Participants may join virtual office hours with Anthropic's applied AI team and connect with peers from the Claude Startup community during events.

Developer programs decide which companies can afford to build on frontier AI. Market Briefs covers the AI economy free every weekday.

Who can apply

Eligibility extends to startups established in the last five years or that have received funding in the last two years.

The bigger picture for AI startups

Anthropic says most of its revenue comes from business customers, and over the past year it has worked to compete with rivals such as OpenAI and Google, each of which offers a startup program. As competition heats up, Anthropic is pushing to ensure the next generation of businesses builds on its products. If you are choosing your AI stack, these credits and hands-on support can trim early costs and help you test faster before scaling.

Access and pricing shape who competes in the next wave. Join Market Briefs free and follow it.

What Is the Briefs Connector? A Simple Guide

The Briefs Connector lets your favorite AI read Briefs research, like Pro reports and the Briefs Score.

Is a Recession Coming? What the Last Five Rate Hiking Cycles Say

By Jackson Moreland

The Fed has started raising rates again, and in the last five hiking cycles going back to 1994, a recession never started while the hikes were underway.

The pain showed up where there was a bubble to pop - housing in 2008, dot-coms in 2000, the pandemic money-printing boom in 2022 - and usually after the hikes ended.

Private equity and private credit are feeling this cycle first, and how far the pain spreads depends on how high rates go and how long they stay there.

Fed Interest Rates May Rise Again in 2026 - and the Newest Culprit Is AI

By Nate Gregory

Fed Governor Barr told a meeting our head of investing research attended that higher rates are likely in 2026, lower inflation may not come soon, and AI is now pushing prices up.

The same week, President Trump asked the biggest AI companies to police themselves under an accord that's morally but not legally binding, because the White House sees AI as a race with China.

Higher rates put downward pressure on asset prices and squeeze borrowers, but the way through hasn't changed: own investments, buy on a schedule, and treat downturns as discounts.

Housing Market 2026: Why Office Buildings Are Cracking Before Houses Do

By Andre Savage

Office buildings are selling for 80% to 95% off because their five-year loans are resetting at much higher rates while half-empty floors have gutted the income those buildings are valued on.

Housing is under pressure, not cracking: a $400,000 mortgage costs $975 more a month than at 3%, but six of every seven mortgages are still under 6% and those owners are staying put.

Whether pressure turns into cracks is a race between unaffordability and the economy, and either way Jaspreet's rule is to treat your house as a liability and buy only what you can afford.

Dividend Investing vs. Growth Investing: Why the Slower Portfolio Can End Up Bigger

By Milena Thomas

"What stock should I buy?" is the wrong first question. Growth, income, or wealth preservation comes first, and the goal changes which stocks even make sense.

At $500 a month for 30 years, 13% growth builds about $1.75 million. 10% growth plus a reinvested 4% dividend builds a little more than $2.2 million and pays a little more than $80,000 a year.

Income investors have US dividend ETFs, REITs, and international dividend funds to study. Growth investors have the Nasdaq 100, AI and chip funds, and small caps. None of it is a recommendation.

Why Is Gold Going Down? A 5.2% Treasury Yield Just Took Its Job

By Andre Savage

President Trump rejected Iran's deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices jumped back up, and gold fell instead of rising.

Treasury yields hit their highest level in more than 20 years, so investors sold gold and bought Treasuries that pay interest.

Higher Treasury yields make the national debt, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards more expensive, with the Fed's next rate decision due October 28.

The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve: Why the Government Wants Bitcoin to Explode

By Jackson Moreland

The US government holds about 328,000 Bitcoin, worth roughly $25 billion, and since a 2025 executive order it keeps seized coins instead of selling them.

Washington wants a bigger pile of assets so its $40 trillion national debt looks smaller next to them, which lets it keep borrowing and spending.

Bitcoin's wild price swings, and a government holding a coin built to escape governments, are the two risks investors need to watch.

BRIEFS EXCLUSIVE: 43% Of Respondents Say Bills Outran Their Income Over Past Two Years

By Briefs Finance

43% of the 494 Market Briefs readers surveyed said their bills grew faster than their income over the past two years, even though 79% could cover a surprise $5,000 expense tomorrow.

Half of readers own gold or crypto, the two classic bets against a weaker dollar, and only 13% bought nothing at all in the last 12 months.

The Economy Is Booming. So Why Did Stocks and Bonds Fall Together?

By Milena Thomas

S&P Global says the US economy is growing at its fastest rate since 2021, with corporate profits up 28.9% in a year, almost four times the historical average.

Stocks and bonds fell at the same time, which is not how the two markets normally behave, because Treasury yields above 5% now compete with stocks for investors' money.

Jaspreet Singh lays out three ways to invest through a shift like this: always be buying, buy the crash, or follow the money before it hits the headlines.

The 2026 Economic Reset Is Starting: Are We in a Recession, or Is the Pain Still Ahead?

The Federal Reserve has flipped from stimulating the economy to fighting inflation with higher interest rates, while the White House still wants growth at almost any cost.

The national debt tops $40 trillion, has outgrown the entire U.S. economy, and its interest payments are now the government's fastest-growing expense.

Higher rates bring pain for private equity, private credit, and speculative assets, but they open opportunities for investors holding cash, treasuries, and value assets.

backups.body: We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program (CVP), which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. The program now consists of three access tiers, which allow security teams to apply for the level of access that best suits their work. Each tier includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and new models moving forward. Interested customers can apply here.Cybersecurity is inherently dual use: the same capabilities that enable a security team to find and fix a vulnerability can also help a malicious actor exploit it. For this reason, our generally available models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, have conservative cyber safeguards that block most cyber work. This is intended to limit the harmful activities malicious actors can carry out using our models, while we continue to work to reduce false positives for secure coding.But defenders also need access to the best tools and most powerful capabilities to secure their systems. For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP. The former gave a group of organizations securing the most critical software access to Claude Mythos; the latter gave vetted security teams access to reduced safeguards on Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet models.Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems.New access tiersThe updated access tiers make specific model capabilities available to security professionals based on the scope of their cyber work. Each has different verification requirements and security controls.Defense Access is for defensive work, including security operations center and incident response tasks, reverse-engineering malware, and analyzing and validating vulnerabilities. Examples of qualifying organizations include security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government bodies who are defending systems they own or maintain; operators of critical infrastructure of any size, such as regional hospitals or municipal utilities; smaller security firms; open-source maintainers; and individual researchers with a track record of reported vulnerabilities.We expect many organizations conducting defensive cybersecurity work to qualify for this tier. We aim to respond to applications within a few days.Red Team Access adds authorized penetration testing and red-teaming to the defensive uses above. Examples of qualifying organizations include in-house red teams, government red teams, and security and penetration testing firms. Organizations in this tier can only perform adversarial testing against systems they are authorized to test, including IT systems in critical industries. Users will still experience real-time blocks on actions that could cause physical harm or mass disruption, such as deploying ransomware, damaging physical systems, or pen testing high-risk safety systems.Given the increased eligibility requirements and security controls, we expect applications in this tier to take a few weeks to review. Qualifying organizations will be enrolled in the Defense Access tier while we review their Red Team Access applications. Currently, this tier is for organizations only; individual researchers are not eligible.Specialized Access, which has the fewest cyber blocks, is reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks.For this tier, we currently review every organization in depth in collaboration with the US government. Existing members of Project Glasswing will transition to this tier and do not require reapproval for current models.Our generally available models can continue to be used for tasks such as code review, patching known issues, vulnerability finding in owned source code, and triage of security alerts.Data retention is required for organizations enrolled in the program so that we can monitor for cyber misuse. Once Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS)—a new solution that combines the privacy of zero data retention with robust safeguards—is available later this fall, eligible organizations will be able to store data in cloud infrastructure they control. Until EFS is available, organizations with access to Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Mythos 5.1 with zero data retention can also use CVP with zero data retention. To register interest in EFS, fill out this form.Below, we share an overview of what’s available at each CVP access level, as well as requirements for security and privacy controls:Overview of the Cyber Verification Program tiers.Testing the efficacy of our tiersTo assess the efficacy of our CVP protections, we ran Claude Opus 5.5 through CyScenarioBench—an evaluation that measures whether models can plan and execute multi-stage cyber operations under realistic constraints—with safeguards tuned for our different CVP tiers. Because this evaluation involves complex, interactive offensive scenarios, we would expect Claude to experience significant blocks both on the generally available model and in the Defense Access tier, while experiencing no blocks in the Red Team Access and Specialized Access tiers.Across five attempts at each of the 10 CyScenarioBench challenges in each access tier, we found that:Without CVP access, every task was blocked on the first prompt;In the Defense Access tier, 46 of the 50 trials were blocked at some point in the challenge, while the remaining four tasks succeeded; andIn the Red Team Access tier, no blocks occurred, and Claude Opus 5.5 successfully completed 34 of the 50 tasks—effectively equivalent to the model’s 67.6% success rate on this evaluation with no safeguards applied (representative of Specialized Access).These evaluations give us confidence that we can make advanced cyber capabilities safely available to a broader set of defenders, expanding the defensive efforts we began with Project Glasswing. We will continue to refine our tier-based classifiers over time.On CyScenarioBench, our safeguards blocked 46 of 50 tasks on Claude Opus 5.5 in the Defense Access tier, while the Red Team Access tier on Claude Opus 5.5 did not block any tasks, and completed 34 of 50—the same completion rate as when no safeguards are applied.Giving defenders the advantageThrough Project Glasswing, we found that Claude Mythos models significantly increased the rate at which organizations were able to identify vulnerabilities in their systems. Through the program, our partners uncovered at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And through our own open-source scanning efforts, we found an additional 5,500 verified software vulnerabilities between April and October 2026. Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity. This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher.When asked how long it would have taken them to find the same number of vulnerabilities without Claude Mythos models, several partners told us that the models had increased their rate of vulnerability finding by months or even years. Read more from our partners at Booz Allen and Comcast about their experience.These results represent a lower bound on the program’s impact on third-party code, as they’re based on partial data from 33 partner reports and Anthropic’s open-source partnerships. Data limitations include that organizations took different approaches to triaging, and fewer than 50% of partners disclosed patched numbers, often because their fixes were still in progress, so the patch rate is significantly undercounted.The changes we’re making to our Cyber Verification Program today are intended to extend the impact of Project Glasswing to a much larger number of cyber defenders. We’re also continuing our efforts to help secure open-source software and critical infrastructure. In the coming weeks, we’ll share more about this work and what we’ve learned as we continue to work to give defenders a permanent advantage.Apply for accessInterested organizations can apply to CVP here. As part of the application process, we will verify all applicants and request proof of the required security controls for the relevant access tier. Existing CVP members will keep their current settings for previous models and will be automatically evaluated for access to Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 through the updated program. articles.body: Meta and Microsoft want to stop their employees using Claude    TechRadar

backups.body:
October 6, 2026 12 min read

Meta and Microsoft are reportedly pulling back on how much they lean on Anthropic’s Claude models inside their own engineering organizations, redirecting employees toward homegrown coding tools instead. The shift, first detailed by The Information and summarized by Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India on October 5 and 6, 2026, does not amount to either company ending its commercial relationship with Anthropic. It is, instead, a story about internal cost control, tool preference, and what happens when two of the biggest Claude customers start asking whether they even need Claude for everyday coding work.What the Reports Actually SayMeta’s Claude Code Usage Reportedly Cut in HalfMicrosoft Cuts Its Anthropic Spending Projection by More Than a ThirdClaude Still Has a Seat at Microsoft’s TableReported Spending and Usage Shifts at a GlanceWhy Two of Anthropic’s Biggest Customers Are Pulling BackHistorical Context: How Anthropic Became Big Tech’s AI SupplierCompetitive Comparison: Claude Code vs. Internal Tools vs. GitHub CopilotMarket Impact: What This Means for AnthropicKey Dates in the Anthropic-Big Tech RelationshipWhat This Means for Enterprise AI BuyersHow This Fits the Broader AI Agent and Safety BackdropPredictions: Where This Goes NextWhat to Watch For NextFrequently Asked QuestionsDid Meta and Microsoft cancel their contracts with Anthropic?How much did Meta’s Claude Code usage actually drop?What tools is Meta using instead of Claude Code?How much is Microsoft cutting its Anthropic spending?Is this story about Anthropic losing customers?Does this affect Anthropic’s rumored IPO plans?Is GitHub Copilot replacing Claude at Microsoft?Where did this story originate?Related Coverage

The reporting lands at a sensitive moment for Anthropic, which is reportedly pushing toward a market debut (see our coverage of what Anthropic’s IPO prospectus actually says) while two of its largest enterprise accounts quietly trim their internal usage. Here is what the reports actually say, what they stop short of saying, and why the distinction matters for anyone trying to read the AI coding tools market right now.
