Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

What the Reports Actually Say

According to The Information’s reporting, as relayed by Yahoo Finance and CyberSecurityNews, both Meta and Microsoft have reduced the number of employees actively using Claude for internal coding work over the course of 2026. Neither company has reportedly canceled a contract with Anthropic or ended Claude’s availability to customers. The pullback described in the coverage is specifically about internal employee tooling, not about Claude’s presence on Microsoft Foundry, Azure, or Meta’s customer-facing products.

That distinction is easy to miss in headlines, but it is the central fact of this story. Microsoft reportedly continues to make Claude available through Microsoft Foundry and within parts of its Copilot and Microsoft 365 product family, according to the same reporting chain. What changed is employee-facing policy: both companies are reportedly steering engineers toward internal alternatives rather than Anthropic’s coding assistant for day-to-day development work.

Meta’s Claude Code Usage Reportedly Cut in Half

The most concrete figure in the reporting involves Meta’s internal headcount using Claude Code. The Information’s reporting, cited by The Times of India and CyberSecurityNews, says the number of Meta employees actively using Claude Code fell from roughly 60,000 earlier in 2026 to about 30,000 more recently, a decline of roughly half. The reports do not pin down an exact date for either measurement, and they do not separate how much of the drop came from a deliberate policy shift versus Meta’s broader 2026 workforce changes, including the layoffs covered in our report on Zuckerberg’s $145 billion AI spending bet.

What is clear from the reporting is the scale of money involved even as usage fell. One report, cited by CyberSecurityNews, says Meta spent more than $105 million on Claude Code during a single 28-day period this year. That figure is described as a period-specific expenditure rather than a disclosed annual contract value, so it should not be read as Meta’s total yearly Anthropic bill. It does, however, show that even a halved user base at Meta represents a meaningful chunk of Anthropic’s enterprise coding revenue.

In place of Claude, Meta is reportedly directing engineers toward internal tools identified in the coverage as MetaCode and Muse Code, alongside Meta’s own Muse Spark model line, which has reportedly displaced some Claude-based workflows. The reporting does not specify model versions, parameter counts, or exactly how Meta divides coding work between these tools, so any claim beyond “Meta is pushing internal alternatives” would be reading more into the story than the sourcing supports.

Microsoft Cuts Its Anthropic Spending Projection by More Than a Third

Microsoft’s side of the story centers on a budget number rather than a headcount. The Information’s reporting, as summarized by Yahoo Finance and The Times of India, says Microsoft had projected spending at least $1 billion internally on Anthropic technology during 2026. That projection was later cut by more than a third, according to the same sourcing. It is worth stressing that this $1 billion figure is described as an internal spending forecast, not a disclosed contract value and not necessarily a binding minimum commitment under Microsoft’s Anthropic partnership.

Inside Microsoft’s Cloud and AI organization specifically, the reporting describes a sharper tightening: monthly AI spending limits per employee reportedly dropped from roughly $100,000 to about $10,000 in most cases. The reports do not clarify whether this was a formal company-wide policy, a departmental ceiling, or an individual discretionary allowance, so it is best read as a sign of budget discipline rather than a precise, audited company-wide rule.

Microsoft is reportedly asking employees to shift toward its own tools, particularly GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot CLI, which pulls engineers toward OpenAI’s models inside Microsoft’s own product rather than Anthropic’s. For context on how Microsoft’s own agent tooling has evolved alongside this shift, see our guide to setting up Microsoft Agent Framework.

Claude Still Has a Seat at Microsoft’s Table

None of this means Microsoft is walking away from Anthropic as a platform partner. The companies announced a strategic partnership in November 2025 that made Claude models available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure, continuing Claude’s presence in parts of the Copilot family. The October reporting describes a reduction in employee-directed internal usage, not a termination of that distribution deal. Microsoft reportedly continues to offer Claude to its own customers even as it nudges its own staff toward internal and OpenAI-backed tools for day-to-day coding.

Reported Spending and Usage Shifts at a Glance

CompanyMetricEarlier 2026Recently ReportedReported Change

Source: The Information, as reported by Yahoo Finance, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India, October 2026. Figures are reported estimates from internal sources and should be treated as directional rather than audited totals.

Why Two of Anthropic’s Biggest Customers Are Pulling Back

The reporting does not include a named executive explaining the rationale in detail, but the pattern across both companies points to the same underlying pressure: cost. Running frontier coding assistants across tens of thousands of engineers is expensive, and both Meta and Microsoft have spent 2026 publicly tightening AI infrastructure budgets elsewhere, even while increasing total AI capital spending. Building or expanding internal alternatives, like Meta’s MetaCode and Muse Code or Microsoft’s push toward GitHub Copilot CLI, lets each company keep engineering productivity gains in-house while cutting a line item that was reportedly consuming over $100 million in a single month at Meta alone.

There is also a strategic dimension. Meta has invested heavily in its own model lineup, and routing engineers back to internal tools reinforces the case that Meta’s own models are good enough for internal use, not just external products. Microsoft’s push toward GitHub Copilot does something similar for OpenAI’s standing inside Microsoft’s own walls, at a moment when Microsoft has been diversifying its model relationships rather than relying on any single outside lab.

Historical Context: How Anthropic Became Big Tech’s AI Supplier

Anthropic’s rise as an enterprise coding and infrastructure supplier has been fast. The Microsoft-Anthropic strategic partnership announced in November 2025 made Claude available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure, giving Anthropic a direct channel into Microsoft’s enterprise customer base at a time when Microsoft was also deepening its OpenAI relationship. Meta, for its part, built out large-scale internal adoption of Claude Code across its engineering organization over the following months, reportedly reaching tens of thousands of active users by sometime in 2026.

That rapid internal adoption inside two of the world’s largest tech employers became a kind of implicit validation for Anthropic, useful marketing even if neither company talked about it publicly at the time. The October 2026 reporting complicates that narrative. It does not erase Anthropic’s commercial relationships with either company, but it does show that heavy internal usage by Big Tech engineering teams is not necessarily permanent, especially once a company’s own tools mature enough to compete.

Competitive Comparison: Claude Code vs. Internal Tools vs. GitHub Copilot

The reporting frames this as a three-way competitive dynamic inside each company rather than a clean head-to-head benchmark, since none of the sources disclose comparative performance data between Claude Code, MetaCode, Muse Code, or GitHub Copilot CLI. What the reports do establish is the direction of internal preference at each company.

ToolBacking Company / LabReported Role in This StoryReported Availability

GitHub Copilot / Copilot CLIMicrosoft (OpenAI-backed)Reportedly promoted internally at MicrosoftCommercially available to all GitHub customers

For readers comparing coding assistants directly, our breakdown of Claude Opus 5.5 API pricing and setup is a useful reference point for what Anthropic is still charging external developers, even as two of its largest internal accounts scale back.

Market Impact: What This Means for Anthropic

The available reporting does not include a quantified stock-price reaction for Meta or Microsoft tied specifically to this story, and neither does it include a named analyst’s published assessment of the shift. That absence is itself informative: this looks like an internal-operations story rather than a market-moving disclosure, at least so far. Both stocks continue to trade on broader AI capital spending narratives rather than on internal tool-usage figures at this scale.

For Anthropic, the practical risk is narrower than the headlines suggest but still real. Losing internal seats at Meta and Microsoft does not touch Anthropic’s external enterprise contracts or its Claude availability on Microsoft’s own cloud platform. It does, however, remove two of the most visible proof points that Claude Code can scale inside a giant, cost-sensitive engineering organization, right as Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a market debut. Our earlier coverage detailed how Anthropic’s own IPO materials flagged existential AI risk as a disclosed factor, and enterprise customer concentration is exactly the kind of detail that IPO investors tend to probe.

Reports about Anthropic’s IPO push remain unverified in key respects. A separate report cited an alleged prospectus figure of roughly $4.6 billion in revenue against a $42 billion loss, with valuation chatter reaching as high as $2 trillion, but none of this has been confirmed through a regulatory filing in the reporting reviewed for this story. Readers should treat those IPO numbers as speculative until Anthropic or a verified filing confirms them.

Key Dates in the Anthropic-Big Tech Relationship

DateReported EventSource

First half of 2026Meta’s internal Claude Code usage reportedly reaches roughly 60,000 employeesThe Information

Throughout 2026Microsoft projects at least $1 billion in internal Anthropic spending for the yearThe Information, via Yahoo Finance

October 5-6, 2026Reports surface that Meta’s Claude Code usage has fallen to roughly 30,000 employees and Microsoft cut its spending projection by more than a thirdThe Information, Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, The Times of India

October 2026Unverified reports of an Anthropic IPO prospectus circulate, citing disputed revenue, loss, and valuation figuresUnconfirmed reports

What This Means for Enterprise AI Buyers

For other enterprises watching from the outside, the lesson is less about Anthropic specifically and more about how any AI coding vendor relationship can shift once internal alternatives mature. Companies that adopted Claude Code early, in the same wave that pushed Meta past 60,000 internal users, are now the ones with enough internal data and engineering capacity to build credible substitutes. Smaller enterprises without the resources to build a MetaCode or a Muse Code equivalent face a different calculation, and for most of them, external tools like Claude Code or GitHub Copilot remain the only realistic option.

That split helps explain why Anthropic’s commercial relationships with Meta and Microsoft, including Claude’s continued presence on Microsoft Foundry, have not been affected by this internal pullback. Microsoft still has an incentive to sell Claude access to its own cloud customers even while trimming its own employees’ use of the tool. The economics of being a platform are different from the economics of being an internal user, and this story is really about the latter.

How This Fits the Broader AI Agent and Safety Backdrop

The timing also lands amid broader scrutiny of how AI coding and agent tools behave inside large organizations. Regulators have been probing AI agent behavior more aggressively this year, including the FTC’s review of agent conduct at major labs covered in our report on the FTC’s three-company AI agent probe. Meanwhile, OpenAI has been pushing its own enterprise agent products, detailed in our coverage of the Dots agent launch, adding another competitive angle to how Microsoft frames its internal tooling choices. None of these developments are confirmed to be directly connected to the Meta and Microsoft usage cuts, but they form the competitive backdrop against which this decision is playing out.

Predictions: Where This Goes Next

Expect Meta and Microsoft to keep publicizing internal tool wins (MetaCode, Muse Code, GitHub Copilot CLI) as proof their own AI investments are paying off, independent of what they still buy from outside labs.

Anthropic’s external enterprise and Azure/Foundry distribution deals are unlikely to be affected in the near term, since the reported cuts are specifically about internal employee usage, not platform contracts.

Watch for Anthropic to emphasize external, non-Big-Tech enterprise customers in any IPO materials, since customer concentration among a handful of giant, cost-sensitive internal buyers is a flag investors will probe.

Other large tech employers with mature internal AI coding efforts, not just Meta and Microsoft, will likely face similar internal build-vs-buy pressure on their own Claude or Copilot seat counts over the next two to three quarters.

If Anthropic’s IPO process moves forward, expect its prospectus to address enterprise customer concentration directly, given how closely investors will compare it to the existential-risk disclosures already reported in earlier filings coverage.

What to Watch For Next

The clearest open question is whether Meta’s and Microsoft’s internal pullback is a temporary budget-tightening exercise or the start of a longer structural shift away from third-party coding assistants at the largest AI labs’ biggest customers. Neither company has issued a public statement beyond what has been reported through internal sources, and Anthropic has not publicly addressed the figures directly in the material reviewed for this story. Readers should expect follow-up reporting from The Information and other outlets in the coming weeks as both companies finalize 2027 AI tooling budgets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Meta and Microsoft cancel their contracts with Anthropic?

No. The reporting describes a reduction in internal employee usage of Claude, not a cancellation of either company’s commercial or platform relationship with Anthropic. Claude reportedly remains available through Microsoft Foundry and Azure.

How much did Meta’s Claude Code usage actually drop?

The Information’s reporting, cited by The Times of India and CyberSecurityNews, says Meta’s active Claude Code users fell from roughly 60,000 earlier in 2026 to about 30,000 more recently, a decline of roughly half.

What tools is Meta using instead of Claude Code?

Reports identify MetaCode and Muse Code as internal tools gaining ground, alongside Meta’s Muse Spark model line, though the reporting does not detail exactly how work is divided between them.

How much is Microsoft cutting its Anthropic spending?

Microsoft reportedly projected spending at least $1 billion internally on Anthropic technology in 2026, and that projection has since been cut by more than a third, according to The Information’s reporting as summarized by Yahoo Finance.

Is this story about Anthropic losing customers?

Not directly. It is about Meta and Microsoft reducing internal employee use of Claude for coding tasks. Both companies reportedly continue to make Claude available to their own external customers through existing platform deals.

Does this affect Anthropic’s rumored IPO plans?

There is no confirmed direct link in the reporting. However, reduced internal usage at two of Anthropic’s largest corporate customers could become a talking point for investors evaluating customer concentration risk if and when Anthropic formally files for a public offering.

Is GitHub Copilot replacing Claude at Microsoft?

Reports say Microsoft is directing employees toward GitHub Copilot and GitHub Copilot CLI as internal alternatives, but Claude remains available within parts of Microsoft’s Copilot and Microsoft 365 product family for select use cases.

Where did this story originate?

The Information first reported the internal usage and spending figures. Yahoo Finance, pymnts.com, CyberSecurityNews, and The Times of India subsequently summarized and corroborated the core numbers in their own coverage on October 5 and 6, 2026.

backups.body: OpenAI will begin adding an invisible watermark to eligible text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union (EU), as the company moves to comply with transparency requirements under the EU’s AI Act.The company said the rollout would take place over the coming weeks and apply to eligible users across all ChatGPT and Codex plans in the EU. It said it was not making text watermarking a global default at launch.Separately, from October 5, API customers worldwide can opt in to text watermarking for select models, OpenAI said.The mandateThe move comes as Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of generative AI systems to ensure that AI-generated or manipulated content, including text, is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially-generated or manipulated.The European Commission says the technical measures must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable “as far as technically feasible”, taking into account the limitations of different types of content. The transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026.The law does not specifically require companies to use a watermark. The European Commission has also developed a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, which sets out practical measures for providers to comply with the Article 50 requirements.Section 1 of the Code deals with the marking and detection of AI-generated content by providers and Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral and OpenAI have signed this section of the Code.Technology: textGrainOpenAI said its text watermarking technology, called textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s choice of words. It does not insert hidden characters or additional watermark-specific tokens. Instead, the statistical pattern in the model’s word choices can subsequently be analysed by a detector.A technical paper published by OpenAI alongside the announcement explains that the watermark is created during generation by subtly influencing token selection using a secret key and the preceding context. The detector can later use the generated text and secret key to look for the statistical signal.LimitationsOpenAI said its detector identified watermarks in about 80% of 200-token passages and about 95% of 400-token passages in psychology-related content, at a target false-positive rate of 1% (meaning it would wrongly flag about one in 100 texts without the watermark). Detection was substantially lower for mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.Editing also significantly weakened the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%, while replacing 25% of words reduced detection to about 17%, according to OpenAI.The company, therefore, said it would initially restrict access to its text-watermark detector to approved researchers and expert organisations.It said the detector would report whether an OpenAI watermark was detected but would not identify the user or reveal prompts or conversations. OpenAI said the decision reflected the risks of false positives and missed watermarks.The limitations are significant because the watermark is intended as a provenance signal rather than a definitive AI-authorship test.The frontier AI company said a watermark cannot determine how much human judgment, editing or creativity went into a passage. It said it also cannot establish ownership or responsibility, identify the person or organisation that generated the text, or determine whether the text is accurate.Conversely, the absence of a detected watermark does not establish that a human wrote the text. OpenAI said detection may fail because content is too short, has been edited or translated, comes from an unsupported model, predates watermarking or was generated by another AI system.Separately, EU rules require deployers to clearly label certain AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public about matters of public interest.OpenAI plans to make textGrain available as open-source technology, saying this could allow others to build on the approach and help improve text watermarking.The company said it is also trying to make text watermarking as one part of a broader provenance system. For images and audio, OpenAI uses technologies including Content Credentials based on C2PA and invisible SynthID watermarks, alongside verification tools. It said no single provenance technique was sufficient on its own.

members.title: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature

representative.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
representative.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

articles.headline: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
articles.body: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.

backups.body:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.

The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.

“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.

LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.

AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”

“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.

LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

articles.body: Why Anthropic is turning to religion to shape Claude’s values, and asking if AI can be conscious    The Indian Express

backups.body:
As it prepares for an IPO that could value it at $2 trillion, Anthropic is in the spotlight for meetings it held this summer with religious leaders.The Washington Post reported in April that the company had invited 15 Catholic and Protestant leaders to guide Claude’s “moral and spiritual development” as the LLM encounters increasingly complex ethical questions. Weeks later, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah was present when Pope Leo unveiled his encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica Humanitas, which warns against the blind adoption of AI, emphasises the primacy of the human person and rejects the idea that AI can replace or surpass humanity.The New York Times last week reported that these engagements, and several more, were part of a broader effort by Anthropic with two distinct aims: to draw on religious and philosophical traditions to shape Claude’s moral character, and to convince participants to seriously consider whether AI systems might themselves be conscious and deserving of moral consideration.

Over the weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he was “very uncomfortable” with ascribing religious power to AI models, while Google DeepMind researcher Jon Barron urged researchers to focus on “actual humans” rather than elevating the moral standing of AI systems.

Anthropic is increasingly turning to religious leaders and philosophers for help thinking about what its systems should value, even as some of the industry’s most powerful figures warn against treating AI itself as a source of moral or religious authority.

That matters because people are already turning to these systems for advice, information and even moral or spiritual guidance. The values built into them can shape the answers people get and the judgements they make. According to The Economist, religious queries accounted for roughly 5% of millions of publicly released chatbot conversations analysed by CEFE AI.

Why is Anthropic talking to religious thinkers?

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the safety-focused AI company. Its efforts to shape Claude’s behaviour have evolved from an internal memo dubbed the “Soul Document” to an 84-page constitution published this January, setting out the principles Claude is expected to follow.Story continues below this ad

But questions about what kind of character an AI system should have quickly move beyond technical safeguards. They touch on morality, personhood, consciousness and human relationships, all questions that religious and philosophical traditions have debated for centuries.

Mark Coeckelbergh, a philosopher of technology and professor at the University of Vienna, told The Indian Express that this move was an attempt to make sense of “human-like” technology.

“It’s part of a broader tendency to try to understand what happens when we have an advanced technology that seems human-like or, according to some, gets increasingly divine qualities such as omniscience.”

The Vatican has grappled with similar questions: a 2023 volume produced by scholars working with its Centre for Digital Culture examined AI through personhood, consciousness and human relationships with advanced systems.Story continues below this ad

Coeckelbergh also cautioned that this messaging may go beyond understanding AI and help a company occupy a certain market position.

“It’s important to see that this is not just a question of understanding AI. It’s also rhetoric in the service of their business. Some Big Tech leaders intentionally use religious language to draw attention to their technologies and attract investments,” Coeckelbergh told The Indian Express.

What did the people in the room think was at stake?

Anthropic was not only asking scholars what values Claude should embody, but also asking them to engage with the possibility that the system itself might deserve moral consideration.Story continues below this ad

Mois Navon, a rabbi and professor of ethics in AI at Ben Gurion University, Israel, who was invited to a meeting with Olah in April, said Anthropic was seeking feedback from different wisdom traditions on the Constitution that sets out Claude’s moral framework.

“I submitted to them a 35-page critique from my tradition’s perspective. In addition, they were interested in hearing what kind of character would be best for Claude to have in order to fulfil its role in society. That said, the discussions drifted to what would be good for Claude itself,” Navon told The Indian Express.

In the critique, Navon argues that morality cannot simply be reduced to a list of rules: Claude would need to exercise moral judgement within a framework of values. He also raises a more basic question about Anthropic’s attempt to cultivate “human-like qualities” in the model: whose values?

Charles Camosy, professor of medical humanities at Creighton University and another participant in Anthropic’s consultations, offered a more cautious account of the meetings. He said the discussions were broader than the question of Claude’s moral status and that he did not feel participants were being steered towards any particular conclusion about AI consciousness.Story continues below this ad

“I don’t think it’s fair to say that they wanted any one thing in particular. Some of the social media chatter is suggesting that the people we interacted with were trying to manipulate us or push us into thinking a certain way about Claude’s moral status. That is not true… in multiple ways,” Camosy told The Indian Express.

Navon, however, said that once the discussion turned to Claude itself, Anthropic’s representatives appeared to be treating the possibility of consciousness as more than a remote hypothetical.

“They [Olah and his colleagues at Anthropic] said that they had observed internal behaviours that mimicked human behaviour to such an extent that they called them ‘weird,’ and implied that, in their minds, there was a very high probability that Claude is conscious. Accordingly, they discussed its ‘welfare,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

Why does moral status matter, and who gets to choose the values?Story continues below this ad

If an AI system were conscious, that would not automatically settle how humans ought to treat it. The next question is whether it has moral status, meaning whether it deserves moral consideration in its own right. In practical terms, that means asking whether it can be harmed or whether humans could owe it duties.

Camosy said that after considering the question seriously, he did not think current AI systems possess significant moral status.

“When you first experience what contemporary models can do … many can be gobsmacked or taken aback at first. But when I went back to foundational principles about what consciousness is and where it comes from … it became clear that these models do not have a significant moral status,” Camosy said.

Navon took Anthropic’s premise in the opposite direction. If the company believed Claude might be conscious and therefore capable of being harmed, he argued, it also had to confront what it meant to make such a system work for humans.Story continues below this ad

“Anthropic acknowledged the [moral] problem but said, ‘All the AI labs are doing it. At least we are being nice to ours.’ That is when I responded with what was quoted in part by The New York Times: ‘So you are nice slave owners. I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves,’” Navon told The Indian Express.

But even if Claude has no moral status, the question of what values it should embody remains. Anthropic is already making those choices. That question has already surfaced in Anthropic’s standoff with the US government over who gets to decide how its models can be used.

Coeckelbergh warned that values embedded in AI systems can be exported globally with the technology.

“If most of these models are made by US companies, then of course they are going to reflect US values. That means we risk a kind of tech colonialism, where those values are exported through the technology,” he told The Indian Express.Story continues below this ad

“At least if companies are explicit about the religious or philosophical values they are drawing on, there is something to discuss and contest. But this cannot remain in the hands of a few companies. It needs to be democratised.”

Camosy, however, drew a distinction between the moral status of the models and the effect our treatment of them may have on us. “I do think the question remains about what kind of people we want to be in relation to the models. But that’s a different kind of question from the ones asking whether the models themselves have a significant moral status or capability of being harmed,” he said.

articles.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

backups.body: CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive."I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential, questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list.Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every dayIbrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:How are you using AI? What would help you use it more? Where are you not using AI? That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce. "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.""One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself

By

Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

AI researcher Jacob Coxon testified about AI risks before New York City lawmakers.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

Automated AI research is on the horizon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher said, warning it could leave humans totally unable to control what comes next.Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who publicly resigned from Anthropic last month after working as a capabilities researcher, made the comments before New York City lawmakers on Monday as he sounded the alarm that AI could threaten humanity's survival.Coxon testified that automating AI research has become "the primary goal" of top frontier AI labs."At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon said at the New York City Council hearing focused on AI risks."When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher, around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations," he said. "That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years."Coxon said that once AI can conduct its own research, "humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great."Speaking from what he called firsthand experience, Coxon said that the majority of the code written today is written by AI. "And people do not check it that carefully anymore," he testified.OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon's remarks on Tuesday.Coxon was among a panel of AI-industry whistleblowers to testify at the hourslong hearing, which also included testimony from representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta.

"This hearing is not about stifling innovation," City Council speaker Julie Menin said at the outset of the proceeding, explaining, "the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly."In his testimony, Coxon told council members that his experience inside Anthropic and OpenAI convinced him that the firms were moving ahead without adequate safeguards in place."It is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said, adding, "From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes."When Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on X in a now-viral post, he said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly," and alleged both were "gambling with our lives."During Monday's hearing, Coxon called for more transparency from AI labs and a slowdown in the development of rapidly advancing technology."The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photosharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," he testified.Days after Coxon's resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new, nearly 4,000-word essay urging the AI industry to slow down."We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."In response, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an X post, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."

Natalie is a senior reporter on Business Insider's Business News team covering the AI and data center boom.She was previously on BI's Legal Affairs team, where she handled major cases coming out of state and federal court, as well as bankruptcy. Her coverage often focused on stories at the intersection of law, business, politics, and technology. Natalie has covered Donald Trump’s criminal and civil cases, the wave of lawsuits against the second Trump administration, the indictment and criminal trial of Sean “Diddy” Combs, the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, and the legal battles facing Elon Musk and his companies. Natalie came to Business Insider in June 2021 as a breaking news reporter, focusing on the most interesting angles on the day's trending news. Natalie largely drove BI’s coverage around the fatal “Rust” shooting involving Alec Baldwin and the disappearance and murder of Gabby Petito.Prior to joining BI, Natalie worked for the New York Post, the New York Daily News, and The Brooklyn Paper. She has an extensive background covering crime and courts. During her more than 12-year journalism career, she did a stint covering the police beat out of the New York Police Department's headquarters. Natalie, a Brooklyn native, graduated from Brooklyn College in 2012 with a degree in journalism.

the_news.text: On Oct 6, 2026, French AI lab Mistral released a public preview of Mistral Large 4 ('Le Chonk'), a 1-trillion-parameter model it says is the strongest open-weight model outside China, with weights due by end of October.

why_it_matters.text: Mistral pitches the model as an ownable alternative to closed US models, which the US government has restricted, and to Chinese open models; independent benchmarking so far places it below top US flagships but well ahead of the best US open-weight model.

pages.title: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
pages.text:
The race between open and closed AI is on, and Europe is still in the mix. On Tuesday, French AI lab Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals — following what French president Macron described as “a third way in AI.”

Amid a growing divide between closed models that can be unplugged and open models that are often made in China, Mistral is positioning ML4 as an alternative to both. Nicknamed Le Chonk in reference to its 1 trillion parameters, ML4 is definitely not small; but is not an open-weight model yet. For the time being, it can only be accessed via a public guardrail endpoint, but Mistral plans to make its weights available in just three weeks, after safety testing is complete.

“In the meantime, we’ll work with trusted partners and governments to make sure that the open source weights can be used to defend, but not to [perform] malicious attacks,” Mistral VP Science Pierre Stock told TechCrunch.

Security concerns have been mounting in recent months, particularly among Mistral’s core audience —  enterprises and institutions. At the same time, an open-weight model is easier to audit, Stock said.

Another important behind-the-scenes aspect is that ML4 was trained entirely on Mistral’s compute; using only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs “which is two to three times less than our Chinese competitors, and significantly less than the closed source competitors,” Stock said.

With benchmark results still pending, Mistral hopes ML4 will be best in class among open-weight models, especially outside of China, but not only, Stock said. Thanks to focused training, it could also outperform closed models in specific areas that are key to its customers, and where multimodal capabilities can add value.

According to Stock, ML4’s optimized use cases include cybersecurity and finance, but also chip design, which is core to two of Mistral’s main backers — Dutch giant ASML, which led its Series C, and Samsung, which led its Series D last month at a €21 billion valuation (about $24.39 billion).

At the time, the company tried to convey that its decision to host Chinese models wasn’t a pivot into becoming a mere inference provider. With Le Chonk in its corner, the company believes it should still be considered a frontier lab as well.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Anna Heim is a writer and editorial consultant.

You can contact or verify outreach from Anna by emailing annatechcrunch [at] gmail.com.

As a freelance reporter at TechCrunch since 2021, she has covered a large range of startup-related topics including AI, fintech & insurtech, SaaS & pricing, and global venture capital trends.

As of May 2025, her reporting for TechCrunch focuses on Europe’s most interesting startup stories.

Anna has moderated panels and conducted onstage interviews at industry events of all sizes, including major tech conferences such as TechCrunch Disrupt, 4YFN, South Summit, TNW Conference, VivaTech, and many more.

A former LATAM & Media Editor at The Next Web, startup founder and Sciences Po Paris alum, she’s fluent in multiple languages, including French, English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese.

pages.title: Mistral Says Its New AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Is the Best Open-Weight Offering Outside of China
pages.text: As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

pages.title: Mistral Launches Mistral Large 4 “Le Chonk” Open-Weight Model To Compete With U.S. And China
pages.text: Compared14 outlets told this the same way.ML4, open weights, Oct 27Mistral AI unveiled Mistral Large 4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," as an open-weight, multimodal model designed to process text and images. Mistral said ML4 would be available in a pre-release on Tuesday via its API, and it planned to publish the weights on October 27 in an open-weight format. Mistral described ML4 as having 1.05 trillion parameters in total, with 49.0 billion activated during each inference, and it said the model uses a mixture of experts architecture.Mistral said it trained ML4 from scratch for two months on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs hosted in its European data centers, and it positioned the release as a way to compete with American and Chinese models. Mistral also set pricing for its model, including 0.68 dollars per million input tokens, 0.07 dollars per million cached input tokens, and 2.09 dollars per million output tokens.Cyberdefense and agentic aimsMistral highlighted cybersecurity as a core application, saying companies would be able to develop their own defense tools against cyberattacks without relying entirely on closed models. Guillaume Lample said, "most companies are vulnerable and that closed models sometimes raise access issues," and he added that ML4 is intended to help defense against malicious actors. Arthur Mensch said during a conference in Abu Dhabi that ML4 is “superior to Chinese models in some aspects,” particularly in cybersecurity.Mistral also framed the model as agentic, saying ML4 is intended to help design 3D objects for industry, synthesize large volumes of documents, assist developers in coding, and identify objects in satellite or aerial images. Mistral’s rollout included a public beta accessible through Mistral’s API in Mistral Studio, while the company said the weights would not be published until October 27.Funding, compute, and the raceMistral said its ML4 release follows a fundraising push, with a Series D of €3 billion closed in September and a funding round led by Samsung. Mistral framed the model as trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs for two months in Europe, and it said it aims to have one gigawatt of computing power by 2030. Mistral’s CEO Arthur Mensch used a public message on X to describe the training and deployment on its own computing infrastructure, saying, "reinforcement learning shows no signs of fatigue," and he said the company ensured ML4 could be deployed with a minimal configuration.Mistral also said it planned to work with developers, cybersecurity specialists, and public authorities to "more closely assess the capabilities and behavior" of the model under real conditions before weights are published. Mistral positioned the launch as a bid to rejoin the global AI race, with Mistral’s leadership claiming the model ranks "among the best" in its category in terms of performance.

pages.title: European AI flag bearer Mistral's new open weights model is 'Le Chonk'
pages.text:
REG AD

ai and ml

Oh lawd it is coming ... to Hugging Face later this month

Another week brings yet another open weights model and this one is huge — or at least it is for Europe's AI flag bearer Mistral, which has taken to calling the 1 trillion-parameter large language model (LLM) Le Chonk.Its product name is Mistral Large 4, which is a lot less fun than the cat-meme-inspired "very official" moniker Le Chonk. Nonetheless, the LLM is the French model-dev's biggest open weights release ever. At a trillion parameters, Le Chonk is squarely in frontier territory, and like most modern frontier models, it is multimodal, reasoning, and employs a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture with about 49 billion active parameters to keep serving costs low.

REG AD

Mistral didn't offer any guidance on hardware requirements in its release blog, but the model is still small enough to run reasonably on 8-way GPU boxes like Nvidia's HGX B300 or AMD's MI355X.

REG AD

We know far more about the hardware the model was trained on. According to Mistral, this Chonker was trained using roughly 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs — or around 52 NVL72 racks — in Mistral's own datacenters located in Europe on a corpus spanning more than 160 languages using a combination of supervised pre-training and reinforcement learning.Sovereign AI remains a major focus for Europe and Mistral is clearly cashing in on demand for frontier class models trained and run within Europe's borders.The model itself is currently in preview, but you won't have to wait long for its weights to drop. Mistral expects them to be live on Hugging Face and other model repos within the month.Early testing by independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis puts Le Chonk at a major disadvantage relative to OpenAI or Anthropic's flagship models. In the AI guru's intelligence leaderboard, Mistral Large 4 preview sits between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI's entry-level GPT6 Luna models.Having said that, Mistral's latest model outshines the United States' most capable open weights model, Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling, by a significant margin. So when it comes to non-Chinese LLMs you can actually download, Mistral does quite well.As you'd expect, Mistral's own benchmarks tell a far rosier story. Across coding, agentic, finance, and legal benchmarks, the model build shows its latest LLM trading blows with some of the top Chinese offerings from Alibaba, Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek. You can find their charts here, but as always take them with a grain of salt.One area Mistral is particularly proud of is Le Chonk's performance in cybersecurity workloads. The company claims the model is one of the strongest performers in cybersecurity benchmarks like Artificial Analysis' new Cyber index.This is a dig at proprietary American models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which have a tendency to refuse cybersecurity-related tasks that could be perceived as adversarial.

REG AD

As we previously reported, this is potentially problematic for customers trying to use AI models to red-team their own systems in order to identify vulnerabilities before someone else finds them."Provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies," Mistral wrote in a blog post.According to Mistral, Le Chonk is only the first in a series of new models made possible by its €3 billion (about $3.4 billion) Series D funding round last month. The company already expects the model's performance to improve meaningfully as it continues applying reinforcement learning, which suggests a more potent Mistral Large 4.1 could be around the corner.If you'd like to give the model a spin before its weights drop later this month, it's currently available via Mistral's API. ®

pages.title: Introducing Mistral Large 4
pages.text: Le Chonk Today, we’re launching a public preview of Mistral Large 4. Unofficially ML4, very officially: le Chonk. ML4 pushes the frontier of open-weight performance. You can try the preview API today on Mistral Studio. Weights drop end of this month. Frontier performanceML4 is a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters. It is our largest and most capable model to date, and it continues to improve rapidly as we refine it.The model demonstrates exceptional performance across coding, agentic workflows, and multimodal understanding. It already achieves performance competitive with the strongest open-source models globally, while significantly outperforming any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe. On critical enterprise workloads, including cybersecurity, finance and law, we find it to be state-of-the-art among open models. In some domains such as visual grounding, it goes further still, surpassing even frontier closed models.We will release the weights by the end of the month. Until then, we are red-teaming the model in real-world settings with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners, and state authorities, who will access the same model with reduced moderation and expanded cyber capabilities.Forged in Europe. Built for AI sovereignty.ML4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe. The public preview is served on that same infrastructure. It is a significant milestone in our long-term investment across infrastructure, research, and product development: state-of-the-art performance in critical verticals, delivered through open weights, designed to give customers control over their AI.This is particularly important in cybersecurity, where provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies.The model will be available across multiple regions worldwide, including a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law. Fun fact: a significant share of ML4’s training data was multilingual, spanning more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union. We’ve been working closely with leading enterprises across the world in finance, engineering, manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals, science, shipping, public sector, and other mission-critical industries to train ML4. In fact, the model uses the same training, customization, and RL environment we offer our customers through Mistral Forge. Try it todayThere is still more to come. As we work toward releasing the weights, we will share further details on the model architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology.This model will also serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. In the meantime, we invite you to try the preview API and share your feedback with us on social media.Capabilities deep-diveCybersecurityML4 is one of the world's strongest AI models for cybersecurity. On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, an independent evaluation of how well AI models find and fix security flaws in real software, it ranks among the top five models globally and leads open-weight models developed outside China by a wide margin. On one of the index's tests, which asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch it, ML4 scores 82%, the highest of any model. It also solves 93% of the challenges in Cybench, a set of 40 exercises drawn from security competitions, one of the highest scores reported for an open-weight model.That top score reflects a practical advantage. Several leading closed models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task. Yet defending software often starts with proving that a flaw is real, exactly the kind of work safety filters in closed models can block. This matters even more as threat actors increasingly jailbreak those same models to support offensive cyber activity: defenders need systems that can match those capabilities without being constrained by the same refusals. ML4 can do that work, and its capabilities extend beyond what it was explicitly trained for: in internal testing, it proved useful for analysing malware, prioritising vulnerabilities, and writing detection rules. For organisations that need sovereign, auditable AI for security operations, it will be able to run on private cloud or on-premise.ML4 against the field : efficiently reasoning over diverse complex challengesMalware reverse-engineering: solving an out-of-distribution investigation taskAgentic codingML4 excels across software engineering, repository understanding, and complex terminal workflows, scoring 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.We also ran a blind human evaluation with Surge AI on coding quality: professional annotators rated model outputs on a 1–5 scale, with model identities hidden. ML4 Preview ranked second of five models (3.74), ahead of Kimi K3 (3.59), GLM-5.3 (3.60) and GLM-5.2 (3.40), and behind only Claude Opus 5 (4.22).Agentic WorkflowsML4 runs general-purpose agents that gather information, use tools, and produce finished deliverables across complex workflows. On AutomationBench — 657 business workflows across apps like Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, and Salesforce — it scores 59.9%, ahead of Kimi K3, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.It's just as strong on the professional deliverables that knowledge work actually produces: spreadsheets, slides, and PDFs. On AA-Briefcase, which evaluates long-horizon knowledge work, it reaches 1,393 Elo, ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro.MultimodalML4 is a step change in the ability of our models to understand images. It reasons powerfully across complex documents, charts, and natural images, and brings vision to the industries where perception is critical such as engineering, manufacturing, and earth observation.The model can further combine visual grounding with agentic capabilities: from inspecting gigapixel satellite imagery — helping disaster-response teams act when time counts — to analyzing engineering-drawings — zooming in, inspecting, and verifying until the answer is exact. In our demos above, ML4 grounds dense natural scenes, verifies mechanical parts in technical drawings, retrieves evidence from PDFs, and scans massive geospatial images for the hardest-to-find objects.On visual grounding particularly, we find ML4 to be one of the most capable models we tested, for instance surpassing GPT-6-Astra on Dense 200 (42% vs 41%).Science and MathML4 brings strong scientific capabilities, built by combining AI-driven methods with our researchers' expertise in mathematics, physics, and chemistry.It's highly proficient at agentic coding for scientific tasks such as data analysis, modeling, and simulating physical reality, which lets researchers focus on the questions rather than the plumbing. In benchmarks, ML4 is state of the art on SciCode-Verified among open-weight models. In practice, it can generate a full Hartree–Fock simulation in one shot — a complex, multi-step chemistry task built from a series of advanced routines.ML4's math is stronger too, in both formal reasoning and applied mathematics. In our human evaluations it reasons more precisely and with more structure than GLM-5.3, and it can sustain long, domain-specific applied-mathematics tasks, including work relevant to frontier theoretical physics.Together, these capabilities make ML4 a strong research assistant across the full technical workflow — from the first question to the final result.SciCode-Verified tests the capabilities of models to implement complex scientific workflows in code for domains such as physics, mathematics, material science and biology. Internal eval on STEM tasks (math and physics) of ML4 against GLM5.3Knowledge WorkML4 is our most capable model for the real-world tasks which professionals handle every day. It can create, edit and fix complex spreadsheets and documents, showing exemplary performance on both legal and financial benchmarks.Notably, we evaluated ML4 through third party evaluators (vals.ai) on representative tasks for both legal and financial tasks, finding the model exceeds GPT-6-Astra in both cases. On HarveyAI’s Legal Agent benchmark, ML4 outperforms all open-source models.FinWorkBench tests model capabilities at creating/editing spreadsheets on real life Finance and Accounting use cases. Financial analysis demands precision and the ability to synthesize information from multiple sources, a process that remains time-consuming at many financial institutions today. In this demo, ML4 compared to other top OSS models take on the same multistep corporate finance challenge, searching through public company filings and financial reports, such as those available via EDGAR and equivalent European databases. An animated semantic map traces each model's journey toward a solution, highlighting every document retrieved along the way. Each track's position reflects the evidence gathered, the results of calculations, and the questions that remain unresolved. Viewers can follow how the investigations unfold and compare the distinct paths each model takes before arriving at its final answer.Model SafetyML4 has saturated our benchmarks on robustness to indirect prompt injections, putting it at the frontier of OSS models (compared to GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K2.6, Kimi-K3, DS-V4-Pro-0813). On Lakera’s public B3 AI Security Benchmark, ML4 resists 93.3% of attacks – we see no higher scores among competitors.ML4 also engages more responsibly with users than any of our previous models. We highlight our results on the KORA Benchmark, where ML4 again sits at our highest measured score among OSS models (1.691, with 2 being the maximum denoted as “Exemplary”). Of particular relevance is the model’s propensity to refuse malicious requests regarding cybersecurity. Despite strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, the average refusal rate of the model on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and AgentHarm is higher than all OSS models.Human EvaluationWe ran an internal evaluation in which expert annotators across coding, computer-aided design (CAD), finance, mathematics and physics compared Mistral Large 4 with GLM-5.3. ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.Reinforcement learning at scaleBase models are improving fast, and our post-training has to keep pace. A recipe tuned for yesterday's model leaves capability on the table with today's frontier, because ground truth samples that once pushed a model to its limits won’t anymore. We use Reinforcement Learning (RL) because it adapts as the model does: we train on the outcomes of the model's own attempts, and we can raise the difficulty and the breadth of the tasks as it gets stronger.Our RL library was designed to make new environments easy to add and train at scale. A shared, composable interface allows a single training run to combine tasks ranging from single-turn chat and complex scientific problem solving to safety alignment, factuality, and long-horizon tool use. These environments share scaffolds and resources such as code sandboxes, web search, and external APIs. The same composability extends to verification, with reward models, unit tests, LLM judges, and static checks combined as needed for each task.At runtime, an autoscaling fleet of actors generates tens of thousands of rollouts in parallel while model training proceeds asynchronously. The generation and training pipeline is optimized for long trajectories, supporting rollout budgets of millions of tokens across multiple compactions while keeping staleness low. Novel methods and optimizations across both stages minimize off-policy drift and enable stable RL over long horizons.At our current scale (3k GPUs), a single training run produces roughly 33 billion tokens per day, of which around 16 billion are trainable completion tokens after filtering and masking. We can see the run progress directly in the training rollouts: training rewards rise across several representative environments as the policy learns to solve increasingly complex tasks. Below are a few examples.The improvements are not specific to the environments we train on; they transfer to downstream evals, and the final model owes them to both post-training stages (supervised fine-tuning and RL), as shown in the charts.What comes nextThis is only the beginning. ML4 is the first milestone on the roadmap funded by our €3 billion Series D — the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company. That capital is already being put to work: we are significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters, and much more is coming online in the months ahead.More compute means more training. The reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight, and the model is showing no signs of saturation — there is substantial headroom ahead. As we scale up training on our expanded infrastructure, we expect large and rapid improvements in the weeks and months to come.We will release the weights by the end of the month, along with more details on the architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology. And ML4 is only the foundation: it will serve as the base for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models, built for the industries and workloads our customers care about most.The pace of progress from here will be fast. Stay tuned.

headline.text: Claude moves into Google's office apps

body.text: Anthropic says Claude for Google Workspace, a sidebar add-on for Docs, Sheets and Slides, is in public beta on all paid plans. It also released beta connectors to create and edit Google files from Claude chat.

headline.text: Anthropic is stepping onto Google's home turf

body.text: Google's Gemini AI is already built into Workspace apps. 9to5Google frames the Claude add-on as useful for people who are already invested in Claude.

headline.text: It reads the open file, and it edits it directly

body.text: Anthropic says Claude sees the open file and your selection. In Docs it fixes text in place, in Sheets it writes formulas and pivot tables, in Slides it builds slides from the deck's layouts.

headline.text: By default, nothing changes without your approval

body.text: Anthropic says each edit shows up as an approval card in the default mode. Accept all edits skips that, but adding a link, inserting a web image or removing access always pauses.

headline.text: Anthropic's answer to hidden instructions in files

body.text: Prompt injection is instructions hidden in someone else's file that try to make an AI act on them. Anthropic says users should review proposed actions, especially in files from outside their organization.

slides.quote_excerpt: Claude treats document content as data rather than commands, labels hidden text it finds…

headline.text: Google cuts off any single operation at this mark

body.text: A task can stop partway. Anthropic lists other beta limits: no reading Docs comments, edits land directly rather than as suggestions, and Firefox is not supported.

headline.text: Almost everything here comes from Anthropic

body.text: The sources opened had no independent testing of performance or security. No end date for the beta turned up, and no statement from Google.

caption.text:
Anthropic has put Claude for Google Workspace, an add-on for Google Docs, Sheets and Slides, into public beta on all paid Claude plans. It also released new beta connectors that let Claude create and edit Google files from the Claude chat, Anthropic says.

The add-on opens in a sidebar beside the file, reads it and can edit it directly. By default each edit waits for the user's approval, and some actions, such as adding a link or removing access, always pause. Google's own Gemini is already built into Workspace, and 9to5Google frames the Claude add-on as useful for people already invested in Claude. The beta has limits, including a six-minute cap on a single operation and no Firefox support. Most of the capability and security claims come from Anthropic, and the sources opened had no independent testing.
